"LAY the cat on lightly, please," said the Dela- ware wife-beater to the Sheriff who was about to apply the lash to his back; "lay it on lightly and you will soothe my angry feelings." "Soothe your angry feelings, sir," said the Sheriff. "Yes; a soft tan, sir, turneth away wrath." "So, you are studying for the stage, my dear ?" "Oh, yes. I have been working for several months." "I suppose it is very hard work ?" "In- deed it is. You have no idea how tiresome it is to sit around a dressmaker's all day long, having one new costume fitted on after another."

" Y ou are charged,; remarked the to a tramp, "for stealing an accordian. Are you guilty ?" "Yes, your honour; I must admit the charge." "Did you steal it to play on l" "I did not," replied the prisoner, in a hurt tone of voice; "I hope your honour does not take me for a musician."

MILKMAN-•-" Johnny, did you put water in the milk this morning ?" New assistant—" Yes, sir." "Don't you know that is wicked, Johnny l" "But you told me to mix water with the milk." "Yes, but I told you to put the water in first and pour the milk into it. Then, you see, we can tell people we never put water in our milk." " YOUNG men," says Mr. Cooper, "if it were the last word I had to address to you in the worldl it would be, Don't get into debt. It will make a sneak of you, it will make a slave of you. Keep out of debt, if you dine often on short commons."

COUNT MOLTKE not long ago, leaving the Reichstag early, did not find his carriage waiting, and so took a cab to his office. On alighting he drew out his purse to pay his fare, when the cab- man whipped up his horse and dashed away, crying —" No gold, Herr Field-Marshal I The honour is sufficient !" But Moltke luckily had noticed the driver's number, by which means he found out his name and address, and next day he sent him his photograph with the autograph inscription, " Moltke, to his cabman, March 9, 1884."

"Because there's small-pox in Montreal. Some of you fellers never seem to read the papers." "You're safe enough," answered the passenger. "Don't you see it's got a hole in it? That's where it's been vaccinated."

"That may be, Brown," retorted Jones, with great asperity ; "but my wife, sir, says I am a gentleman, and I shall certainly believe my own wife before a low, sneaking cur like you. If a man cannot believe his own wife, pray, who can he believe?" [Neither of their wives knew them when they arrived at their respective homes.]

A aux, who was hunting a house to move into, was asked if he had paid his rent to his former landlord. "Yes, sir," he said, rather hesitatingly. "Can't you get a recommendation ?" "Oh, yes, air. I can get Mr. Smith my landlord, to give me a recommendation." "How do you know you can ?" "Oh, I know I can, 'cause he want's me to get out." MRS. FOG—" Why will you go about the house in your shirt sleeves? You wouldn't do it any- where else; then why should you do it here? don't you know that it offends good taste? Mr. Fogg—" My dear, I didn't suppose there was any good taste here to offend." Mrs. F.—" You forget that I have changed considerably since I first be, same acquainted with you, my love."

The first wife knocked all the romance (but of me, the second taught me humility--" " And your present wife ?" "Made a phil- ,ssopher out of me. I can hear other people's troubles with a great deal of self-complacency."

div.p: CATHERINE BOOTH,
MOTHER OF THE SALTATION ARMY.

The abridged edition of the " Life of Mrs. Booth, the lother of the Salvation Army," by Mr. Booth-Tucker, published by the Salvation Army Publishing Company, is a most interesting volume. Whether or not our sympathies are with her from a religions point of view, everyone must acknowledge that she was both a good and remarkably clever woman. Few enthusiasts have enne through the world, carrying out to such perfection axioms based on conduct as did the late Mrs. Booth. Her motto, " Do as I do," was not, as is the case with many teachers of morality in the England of to-day. " Do as I ray." Early and late she laboured in the great vine- yard. She claimed no infallibility, only common sense. She made mistakes, but that only led her to greater wisdom. Her home life set a splendid example which many are,at least, in miniature, trying to imitate. I will Prvieavour to give a short sketch from which the book of the shadowland of a life of which each type has been al- most realised, and nearly every protnise fulfilled.

div.head: Cll' ILDHOOD.
div.p: Cll' ILDHOOD.

Kate Mumford, or, as she is more familiarly known, Catherine Booth, was born at Ashborne, in Derbyshire, on January 17, 1829. She was the only daughter in a iamily of five, her youngest brother alone surviving, the elder three having died during infancy. At a very early age flashes of the spirituality. genius, and energy, that were destined to make so indelible a mark upon the world, surprised and gladdened Catherine's mother, her- self a remarkable woman, Who no doubt handed down ro her daughter many of the intensly practical and c.itirageous traits in her well developed character One of the earliest recollections of my life (says Mrs. Booth), in fact, the earliest, is that of being taken into a worn by my mother to see the body of my little brother who had just died. I mu.st have been very young at the time, scarcely more than two years old, I can remember to this day the feelings of awe and solemnity with which the sight of death impressed my 'a by mind. Indeed. the effee produced on that occa- sion has lasted to this very hour. lam sure that many parents enormously under-estimate the capacity of children to retain impressions made upon them in early ,lays.

An early illustration of the sense of responsibility, which :was the strongest trait in Catherine's character. ..ras one day manifested. While running along the road .cith hoop and stick she saw a drunkard being dragged e the lock-up by a constable. A jeering rook) was hot- fly the unfortunate culprit. His utter loneliness and nisery appealed powerfully to her. It seemed that he ,ad not a friend in the world. Quick as lightning Catherine sprang to his side, and marched down the -treet with him,determined that he should feel that there was at least one heart that sympathised with him, whether it might be for his fault, or his misfortune that oe was suffering. The knight-errant spirit which she manifested when, s a mere child. she threw down the gauntlet to the mocking crowd, and dared to take the part of the lonely mstled criminal, was most peculiarly typical of the Oman who afterwarcis stood by the side of her bus- ,}and, helping him to face the score of his day and gener- ion, until unitedly,with character vindicated and name liessed, they had climtd to a position of successful :chievement almost o Moue in the world's history.

div.head: Fon MAN AND BEAST.
div.p: Fon MAN AND BEAST.

Like her other benevolences, Mrs. Booth's kindness to animals took a practical turn. "If I were you," she would say to the donkey boys at the seaside resorts— where in later years she went to lecture—" I should like to feel when I went to sleep at night that I had done my very best for my donkey. I would like to know that I had been kind it, and had given it the best food I could afford ; in fact, that it had had as jolly a day as though I had been the donkey, and the donkey I." And she always enforced her argument with the gift of a threepenny cr sixpenny bit which helped to make it pala- table. If in her walks or drives Mrs. Booth happened to notice any horses left out to graze which looked over- worked and ill-fed, she would send round to the dealers for a bushel of corn. stowing it away in some part of the house. Then when evening fell she would sally forth with a child or servant, carrying a supply of food to the field in which the poor creatures had been observed, watching with the utmost satisfaction while they had a " real good tuck-in." It is not to be wondered at that 'he horses were soon able to recognise her, and would run along the hedge whenever their benefactress passed by, craning their necks and snorting their thanks, te 11- sunrise and perplexity of those who were not in the secret.

div.head: E&IPOLEONIC IDRA.I
div.p: THE E&IPOLEONIC IDRA.I

History was one of Mrs. Booth's most favourite studies. "Napoleon." she tells us, " I disliked with all my heart, because he always seems to me to be the ern- hOdiment of selfish ambition. I could discover no evi- dence that lie had attempted to confer any benefit upon his own nati-m, much lesson any of the countries he had conquered with his sword. Possibly this may have been in some measure due to the prejudice of the EnOsh his- torians, whose works I stuolied, and who, doubtless, strove to paint his character in the darkest colours. Be this as it may, my dislike to him was not based on any national antipathy, but on what I reckoned to be the supremely selfish motives that actuated his life. I could nct but contrast him with °tsar, who, though by no means an attractive character according to my notions, yet appeared desirous of benefitting the people whom he corquer(d. His efforts for their civilisation together with the laws and public works he introduced ontheir behalf, seemed to me to paliate the merciless slaughter of his wars and the loss of life and property that accom- vanied his operations. He appeared to me to desire the g;)ocl of his country, and not merely his own aggrandise- inent."

div.head: STUDYING THE BIBLE.
div.p: STUDYING THE BIBLE.

Especially was Mrs. Booth's mother always anxious to encourage her daughter in the study of the book which she leoked upon as the supreme fountain of wisdom. It was from the Bible that Catherine received her earliest lessons. Before she was twelve years old she had read the sacred book from cover to cover eight times through, thus laying the foundation of that intimate knowledge of, and exceptional familiarity with the divine revela- tion which made so profound an impression on all who knew her. Thirty years later how completely the posi- tion was reversed, and the weeping mother sat in a densley-crowded chapel, listening for the first time to her daughter. as with power and demonstration of the Spirit she exPounded from the pulpit to her eagerly- listening audience those same scriptures which she ha,' •tudied at her mother's knees, and which had become, indeed, when breathed from her lips quick and powerful ' nd sharper than any two-edged sword, piercing even to the dividing asunder of soul and spirit, and of the joints and marrow, a discerner of the thoughts and in- ,ents of the heart. To the end of her lifn Mrs. Booth maintained this intense love and reverence for the Scrip- ures, and her last and most valued gift to each member ,I her family from the very banks of the Jordan wa,. ' that of a ibte, into which with the greatest pain and (lifficultv she traced her name as " the last token of a mother's love."

div.head: NATIONALISATION OF THE
div.p: THE NATIONALISATION OF THE
MINES.
MR. KEIR HARDIE'S BILL.

I have seen an advanced copy of Mr. Keir Hardie's Bill dealing with the nationalisation of mines. it is hacked,says the London correspondent of the Manchester " Guardian." by Mr. Clark, Mr. Murray M'Dnnalii, Mr. ' D. Randall, Mr. John Burns, Mr. W. Allan, and Mr. M. ld'Cattan. The preamble sets forth the limited nature of the coal supply and the waste of mineral wealth which private working of the mines is supposed to cause. It la provided that on the first of January, 1895, all mines :Ind minerals within the United Kingdom shall be trans- ferred in fee simple to the Crown and become the pro- perty of the nation. The present owners are to be required to furnish to the Home Secretary a return showing their pecuniary interest in the property, and duly qualified valuers are to be appointed who are to as- certain the present value of mines and minerals,without regard " either to the amount of capital invested or prospect of profits-from the working of the same." On t his basis the owners are to be bought out, the purchase once being paid in Consols. Provision is made for a sinking fund for the redemption of the Consols. A Mining Department with a President is to be created, which would be charged with the regulation of the working cf the mines. There are provisions as to the conditions of employment under the Department, which include the adoption of the eight hours principle.
LOBENGULA.I

Travellers continue to furnish further interesting de- , a!ls of Lobengula. The old gentleman has never ytt so fdr cliegraced himself as to have appeared in the gar- ments of civilisation. He nearly always, however. wears a hat of some description. For a long time hi- wore a top hat, as his Prime Minister (who has visited England) had told him that that was the thing of neauty which" is a joy for ever' among our elite, but finding that it caused no inconsiderable amusement ..mong the white traders and hunters, he discarded it for one of greater comfort sd lesser social ambitions. In wet weather the King geWerally wears galoshes. This is no feeble attempt at a joke, but the plain, unvarnished truth.

div.head: EXAMINER. SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 25, 1893. LADIES' LETTER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER. SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 25, 1893. LADIES' LETTER.

At Nagoyo, in China, a merchant, who is in his 65th year, has just divorced his 26th wife and is about to marry the 27th. He bad resolved when he was young to marry 30 wives, and is delighted that he has now only three more 0 marry to keep his vow. Miss S. J. Clifton late president of the Liverpool La dies' Shorthand Writers' Association, gave an inter- esting account of her typewriting experiences before a meeting held of the association last week. Miss Clifton had been the pioneer of the work of copying in type- writing in Liverpool, having so far back as 1884 estab- lished the first office in that city. Madame Rodriguez, a noted Parisian dresssmaker, died recently in a lunatic asylum. Her fame was great, and she always refused to make dresses for women with poor figures. A certain duchess had often desired to be- come one of her patrons, but Madame Rodriguez invariably said, " When you have shoulders I will dress you.
MY DEAREST NELLIE,

The subject of winter dress has to be seriously considered at the present season for although at the time of writing the weather is still mild, yet a summer costume has the appearanhe of being cold even if it is not so in reality, and somethin g of substantial material and warm colouring seems essential if one wishes to look well and appropri- ately attired. It will be obvious that the modes for the winter are far prettier and more gen erally becoming than those of the past summer. Skirts are neither absurdly wide nor uncomfortably narrow. Sleeves, while still full, are not ex- aggerated and instead of the banded bodice which had to be worn by everybody—tall or short, fat or thin a few months ago, unless fashion was entirely disregarded, all varieties of corsage seem to be equally in vogue, so that you may choose the style most becoming, and yet be quib modish.

Princess Beatrice closely follows all the topical songs, and she always has Chevalier's very latest song seat to her the moment it is published. She has, of course, made the Queen acquainted with them, and the little Prince Alexander of Battenberg is allowed to shout " Knocked 'em in the Old Kent-road " unchecked. After dinner at Balmoral, the Queen frequently listens to a medley of popular airs played by Princess Beatrice, who in all theatrical matters is thoroughly up to date.

New Trimmings. Beading in every form, width, and pattern, is applied to winter dresses, straight and varied, sewn on to the dress or shaped into patterns. Graduated rows of braid are frequently applied to the skirts, and inch wide braid is sometimes carried perpendicularly down the seams. Black on colour is most fashionable; so are shaded braids and embroidered braids, the devices in silk. Jet is not at all likely to be banished. It is every year more beautifully treated, and now is applied in the form and designs used in braiding, as well as in long and import. ant fringes. Crochet has been utilised for tinsel thread trimmings and silk. Jet mingles with gold beads and gold threads. Leather, white and ecru, was liberally employed in Paris trimmings during the spring, and is again imported into England. The cloisonné enamel has inspired some of the newest medireval revivals, but they are too elaborate and costly for ordinary wear. The shot chine and shaded effects have a great element of beauty ; so have the jet fabrics set with brilliants, which on evening gowns flash in the artificial light. All these, however, are combined, when desired, with fur for morning or evening; but fur would seem to be consi- dered incongruous, and there is nothing so warm, and nothing that gives more graceful importance to a dress. It speaks of times of long ago, when men and women• coupled it with rich damask silks, which, with all our machinery, we cannot surpass.—" Cassell's Family Magazine" for November.

A lnng sealskin pelisse, with ciosr-fitting back and double-breasted fronts, full skirt, Russian sable collareLa and cuffs, with head, tail, and claws complete makes a handsome winter costume. It is lined with a rich brocade of purple clematis on' a black satin ground. Another pretty costume is in brown fancy serge, ornamented with fur and waved black braid. It has also a detachable cape for outdoor wear.
A New Dibb.

_ " I'must give you a recipe for a dish, that I thought excellent, though 1 may repeat the warning given by my hostess that it is not one which everybody could digest or would like, as it has more body—shall I say more • star 2'—than most snacks of the kind ; in fact, it would be found a very good substitute for meat by the aver- age meat-eater. Allow an egg for each person, and as much macaroni as you like ; the eggs you boil hard and slice, and the macaroni you boil for twenty minutes,then drop in ccld water, which prevents it turning pasty. Then you drain it again. The fresh is teat, but you can use the bought article; then you must, of course, Cook it until it is done, and that may be from twenty minutes to an hour or more. Next you butter a deep dish, and put in soma of the macaroni and then eggs, seasoning the layers to taste, and distributing the eggs everll37- The top is of macaroni. Then the whole should be made moist, not wet, with some hot milk. Cover the surface with browned crumbs, and stick a morsel of butter here and there, and your dish only wants heating in the oven, and rating at table. The tomato is not always absent from this, snd, as to mushrooms, they turn up every: where. A little sauce or puree of either is spread over the various layers. What do you think of the dish ?" "No doubt it is tamous ; but I will put it to the test with poached eggs in place of the hard ones, and for a change I will serve a cheese sauce with it. What do you say to that ?"—" Cassell's Family Magazine for November.

A red silk evening gown, trimmed with triple rows of lace looks very tasteful. The skirt gradually sloped towards the back • the bodice was quite plain and full, with black face gathered at the square top. It fastened at the back, and the sleeves formed a double puff, divided by a frill of lace. A black moire bodice was out square also, and the satin sleeves had lace falling from them. This gown was trimmed with green and mauve ribbons at the neck, loops of ribbon falling on thai left side on to the moire, and rosettes were also carried up the left side of the skit, which was formed into three pleat l at the back.

The season's hats are large, and the newest are oE silky beaver, trimmed with eo,o..red velvet and quills. A large, pioturesque hat is of tan-coloured velvet, edged with black, and trimmed at one side with a frill of tan-coloured velvet, bows of black satin aad black feathers.

A good example of the mode of the day is seen in a dress of brown smooth-faced cloth, the skirt of which is tiimmed with two very narrow bands of dark brown fur, one placed at the edge of the hem wud the other about four inches above, the bodice having a very long moderately-full basque alit up to within three inches of the waist on each hip, and edged all round and up the openings with fur. The fronts are double-breasted, with a big roll-over collar and lapels of shot blue acid brown velvet edged with fur, the heart-shaped habit shirt or ehemisette visible at the throat being of the cloth. Where the basque joins the bodice, a trifle below the waist-line, a rather thick blue and brown silk cord is sewn, which is finished with a knot and long ends in fronts. This dress would look equally smart, I fancy, in green cloth trimmed with astra- ()llan and shot green and red velvet.

We have been done to death with cape trim- mings, and it is really difficult to tell where the craze is likely to end. Sometimes two or three! surmount the falling sleeves, sometimes there are as many as four lapels ending with capes on the front of coats, dresses, and jackets; the majority are edged with piping, for piping has come back to us with the old-fashioned hoods, which had a great element of beauty and usefulness. It is curious in Paris now to see men and .women alike walking about the streets In wet weather in short dark blue or black waterproof capes, with a pointed hood, which they slip over the head, and this useful adaptation has, without doubt, given rise to the Modulated hood trimmings which appear on many gowns and mantles.

Flounces are in fashion, bat they are often waved. In an evening gown the skirt is of rich brocade, and the frillings of white crepe put on very full. At the hem is a fold of contrasting satin, a charming pale blue, which accords well with .the flowers of the brocade. The bodice is also of satin, the front V-shaped brocade, white crepe forming the flounces over the sleeves and the fullings on the bust. The bodice ends at the waist in a fold of the satin, and is a simple and elegant design, use- ful as a suggestion for renovating last year's gowns, as well as for making up the many new and beautiful silks which are flooding the English market.
Yours lovingly, JENNI 3.
The Armenian bride dons a long veil, and the artist of the village paints boquets of flowers on her neck and shoulders.
Miss Charlotte Dod, the great tennis player, spent time and pains upon the game from A very early age. She lives in Cheshire, and has taken up the golf craze.

Prince Peter Trull« tgkoi, the Russian nobleman, who is painting Mr. Gladstone' portrait, is engaged to be married to a young English girl, Miss Ethel Wright. He panes 6Ft. 41n. in his stockings, and is an unusually handsome man.

A curious story comes from New York of an attempt to poison Miss Maria Tempest by sending her a bouquet of roses steeped in strychnine. Miss Tempest has a habit of chewing rose petals: and noticing a bitter taste, the roses were sent to an analyst, who found strychnine in them. It is suggested it is the work of a jealous understudy. It is also hinted that it may be an adver- tising dodge.

She did not answer him, but clung to him with fate—he was breathing those sacred words, my death•cold hands. wife, over another—an unloved bride. "You would not like to be parted from her," he "Hold my hands clasped closely," the girl said, almost frightened at the intensity of her love. murmured, in gasping terror. "I —I am slipping "Suppose Heaven should take me from you, what away from life—elasp my hands until! all is then ?' over. It will be but a few brief moments. Heaven He never forgot, through all the after years of has been kind to me," whispered the quavering bitter pain, the face she raised to his. voice. "I shall die looking on your face. lam "If we were ever parted from each other, I dying, and I may tell you now how I have loved should go mad," she whispered. "I would not you, she went on with all the unconscious pathos die, for I could not rest in my grave. Oh, Rut- of a little child. "I should never have told you ledge, to lose yoa would be more bitter than this, but I am dying—" death." "Poor Uldene I" he murmured, pityingly. He was touched inexpressibly by the pathos of "Poor child I' her voice and face. He caressed the dark, curly A great wave of sorrow sweeps over his heart, head, and the little, white hands lying clasped in t He holds the little, death-cold hands closer, and his own. . . . . . .

watches the lovely, despairing face that grows whiter and whiter with each struggling breath. The hush grows deeper. There is the silence of death fa the room. The housekeeper buries her head in the white counterpane and sobs bitterly. The consulting doctors look significantly and gravely at each other, and turn their faces away. Slowly the white, heavy-fringed eyelids corn- menced to fall over the dark, wistful, glazed eyes, shutting out the face she had loved so well—only Heaven above knew how welL A great wave of infinity pity filled Rutledge Chester's heart. Poor Uldene I how much she had cared for him ! Ile bent his handsome head over her, and pressed his warm lips to the cold, white clammy ones. It was the first caress and the last he would ever give her in life. She would sink into the sleep of death with that kiss trembling on her lips. " Uldene l—my bride !" he murmurs again, in compassionate pity. But mark the wondrous change that lights up the marble face upon which the cold death-dew stands. That kiss and the sound of the voice she loved so dearly has drawn her soul back from the dark valley of the shadow of death—back to life and the world from which she WOS The tide goes out with a dreary wash, but it does not bear Uldene's soul out with it. The doctors bend forward with a cry of surprise, used as they are to surprises. The fihn breaks slowly away from the eyes that never leave Rutledge Chester's white, handsome, startled face. A faint tinge spread over the clammy brow and the pale lips that Rutledge Chester, in his infinite pity, has pressed with a last good-bye caress. The pulse-beat grows more distinct—the chilled heart flutters ever so faintly. "It is my opinion that your bride will live, Mr. Chester,' whispered the doctor. "Those timely words and that kiss called her back from the grave,' he said, solemnly. Like one in a dream, Rutledge Chester lifts his haggard face. Had he heard aright, or were his senses playing him false? " It is quite true," repeated the doctor, cheer- fully. "I am pleased to tell you that your bride will live." Ut had uot loved her, yet a strange thrill of

_ Poor child! What a world of love she had lavished upon him, all in vain. He would have loved her if he could. But, alas ! love goes where God sends it. And Heaven willed that he should love another, quite as hopelessly as poor Indent) loved him. " Uldeue," he said, thoughtfully, "lam the last one to preach on such subjects; but do you think It wise for any one to become so engrossed in their love as that ? ' "There are some natures that cannot help it," she replied, "and mine is one of them. I could not imagine anything so terrible as losing you. My reason would fail me, like a poor girl's did in a story I once read, and the dreary malheuse where they would take me would never cease echoing with your name. If you died first, Rutledge," she went on, in a sobbing whisper, "I would come and kneel upon your grave, and there my poor heart would break. They would and rm.) lying dead upon your grave. When all that made life worth living was gone, how could I live ?" Rutledge Chester bent his handsome head, and ki:sed the beautiful, quivering red lips in pity too great for words. It was the first and last kiss he ever gave her voluntarily, and the memory of it always lived in Uldene's passionate, undisciplined heart. Her face grew radiant at this unexpected indication of his tenderness. And in that moment the thought was passing through his mind that be might have loved this hapless child in time if his heart had not long since gone out to another. No man's heart is large enough to hold two loves. " When mother returns, and you are strong enough, we will go abroad," he said. " You will like that, Uldene ?" For answer, the dark, curly head nestled against I his shoulder, and she raised those lovely dark eyes, with a beaming light in them, to his face. There was this great charm about Uldene : She possessed, in a most wonderful degree, the gift of fascination. The very touch of those little white hands was a subtle caress. Rutledge felt the charm. He was but human; and, though she was not the darling of his heart— the one he loved and would have chosen for his bride—he could not resist the power of her Wee- tion4 &Id yet the vetrlavishness of the love she

gave tam urea rum. nis pellet had always been that the fair sex should be wooed, and never lose the charm of their delicacy of being wooers. " You will think the matter over, Uldene," he said, as he arose to quit the room, "as to where you wish to go." "We will go anywhere you like, Rutledge," she said. "I can he happy amytrliero—with you." Those were the words he to,‘lt with him from the pink and gold boudoir down to the library. He was too much engrossed in his own thou4hts to hear the commotion in the corridor. A moment later some one turned the knob of the door and flung it open, and raising his head, he .beheld his mother standing on the threshold, and beside her —ah, was be mad or dreaming !—beside her stood Verlie ! He uttered a mighty cry ot raprairous delight as he sprang forward ; then the cry froze on his lips ; his strong arms fell to his side in a convulsive shudder, and he stood in the middle of the floor as if rooted to the spot. In a few, brief words Mrs. Chester explained the accident that had happened to Vedic, as she her- self understood it. Rutledge listened like one

"I have brought her back to you, my boy," said Mrs. Chester, leading Verne up to where Rutledge stood, and placing her little, tremulous hand in his. "She knows how dearly you love her, Rutledge. I have told her all. .I will leave you together," she said archly, "while I go in search of Uldene. What wonderful news this will be to her."

Before Rutledge could find his voice the door was closed softly, and he was alone with Verlie —the one love of his heart—the sweet-faced, blue-eyed darling he loved better than life itself, and who was parted from him now as effectually as though one of them lay in the grave. Verlie could not understand the curious white- ness that overspread his handsome, haggard face. She had pictured so often what her meeting with Rutledge would be like, but never—oh, never— had she pictured anything like this. She was frightened at the fierce, desperate, despairing look in his face. What could it mean? She was frightened and dismayed. He knew what his mother meant when she left him alone with Verlie. She would not stay to see the rapturous lover's greeting between his bashful love and himself. Ah, could she have dreamed of the long story he had to tell Verlie. There was nothing for it but to tell her the whole truth. Yet he longed, with all the longing of his soul, to hear from Verlie' s lips first the acknowledgment —she cared for him. In all the years of his af Ler- life those words would live in his heart. A few words were not much to feed a hungry, yearning heart, but it would be a bitter-sweet thought to him to know Verlie cared for him and that he might have won her if cruel fate had not torn them asunder. .

He knew that he should have resisted the temp- tation to draw from her lips the words. "I love you, Rutledge," when that love could never be realized; but he was only human, and in this hour he was parting from her forever; and he loved her better than life itself. (To be continued.)

MR. HENRY IRVING AND TIIE COLLIE. Mr. Henry Irving was, says "Cassell's Saturday Jour- nal," in Scotland two or three summers ago, and on one of his walks he frequently met a shepherd with a fine collie. He took a fancy to the dog, and a few days be- fore leaving, he said to the Elighlander—"l will give you £5O for your collie." The shepherd seemed sur- prised at the amount offered and was struck with sad- ness, for he was poor and wanted the money,yet he had formed so strong an attachment to the dog that he could not bear the thought of parting with it. After deliberating for a while, he said—" Na, sir, I weel rip tak the feefty pund." " Well, then," said Mr. Irving, "I will give you sixty if you like to bring the dog to ro.! hotel within three days." The man stood looking down at his dog and was silent, and Mr. Irving walked awaY- At the end of three days one of the hotel servants said that a shepherd had called to see Mr. Irving. The Highlander and his dog came in, and the man said that although he did not waat to part with the collietas he wal poor and had a family to support, he could not afford to keep a dog worth £6O, and he had decided to accept the oiler. The poor fellow took the money and thanked Mr. frying. He looked once very hard at the collier which whined, and tried to lick his hand ; then he threw his arm over his eyes and ran out of the room. Mr. Irving -brought the dog to Lomlon,but the rumble of the city and the crowds in the streets seemed to confuSe him. He grew more and more unhappy, and after a few days the great actor began to regret his bargain,for he had only succeeded in making himself, the shepherd, and the dog thoroughly miserable. A few days after his return,Mr.lrving took his dog into Kensington Gardens, and for a moment the poor creature brightened at thee first sight of a few sheep that were grazing under the trees, but soon discovering that they were not his own flock, and that his master was not near, he relapsed into his usual dejection. After this,it was very difficult to get him to take any food, as he soon lost his fine appearance and grew lean, Mr. Irving decided to give him his liberty. So he returned him as a present to tbe Highlander, who afterwards wrote that the dog was so overjoyed to get back home, that he leaped upon his old master's shoulders, and .then ran about the hills to wildly that he (the shepherd) feared for a time that be would go mad.

The great, dark, slumbrous eyes sought his with lock of entreaty piteous to behold. "You are sorry, Rutledge V she gasped, faintly. "No, Uldene," he whispered, with deep feel- ing, "I thank Heaven'your young life has been spared." The doctor touched Rutledge lightly on the arm. "She needs rest' and quiet now. After a good sleep there will be a marked improvement in her condition. I will watch alone by her bedside an hour more."

The occupants of the room rose slowly and quitted the apartments so lately clouded by the brooding shadows of death. ‘Vith slow, unsteady steps, Rutledge Cheater sought the library and shut himself in. Never was a man caught in such a web iv the strauge machinations of fate wedded to one woman, while every pulse-beat of his hart throbbed with love for another. To him the preaeut was full of misery and the future all dark. A prince might have been proud to woo and win boautiful Uldene, with her Wondrous dower of beauty, for his bride. She would have charmed any man with her divine loveliness. Perhaps out of the whole wide world this man who had married her was the only one who could have looked upon her without emotion.

A sense of the cruel wrong that a loveless marriage would be to her came over Rutledge, but It could not be helped. He had often heard and read of the idolatrous love of women, but surely there was never such a fatal, unfortunate, pathetd3 love as that which filled the heart of the beautiful, hapless Uldene. He had given Uldeue his name, but he could never give her his heart. He had none to give. Ilis heart had passed out of his keeping the first moment he had looked into the eyes of Verne. But he must put all thoughts of Verlie away from him now, henceforth and for ever. He arose and took from his writing-desk a little glove, a bit of ribbon and a faded blossom, and laid them sorrowfully on the blazing coals of the grate. A moment more and only the ashes remained. I. "So perish my hopes and my brief dream of love," he said. Yet, even in that moment of bitter despair, he could not find it in his heart to curse the fate that fettered him—until death parted them—to Uldene, whose great, worshipful love won from him the profoundest pity.

" Whenever a railway accident occurs," said a rail- 'way official," people begin to talk of the dangers of travel. They ask themselves which route, or what part of the carriage is the safest, and the timid bid each other a tearful good-bye and purchase an insurance magazine before taking the risk." Occasioually a derailment occurs, yet, these are not the accidents Which figure so largely in making up the year's loss of

The most horrible, heart-rendering and cruel cltas. trophes, however, are those so often resulting from criminal carelessness. Those which by a tittle foresight and care might easily be averted. In travel by rail, there is of course, a bit of danger, but not so much as is involved in the every day move- ments, the pleasure, labours, going and coming of life at home.

The individual hair-breadth escapes; how many we all have. Some of which we may not even bo aware, at least, until the danger is past, and we have just had sur attention called to one, which unless averted, would nertaialy have resulted in loss of life. Ex-Metro. Police, B. Lucas, 1. Eustice Road, Walham Green, Fulliatin, London, writes :—" I was taken with severe pains in the head and across my back, accompained by sickness, Partial loss of sight, swelling of feet, ankles, and legs. Doctors I called failed. A consultation of doctors in One O f the largest London Hospitals gave me up, and sent pie home to die ; gave roe but three weeks to live, diagnosing Bright's Disease. I then commenced taking Warner's Safe Cure. The sickness lessened ; the swell- ing disappeared. I have regained my weight in healthy esh; my eyesight is restored; my cure is complete, ‘nanka to this remedy."

Mr. Caine's bill with regard to advertising among rural scenery proposes to prohibit, under a penalty of £5, the exhibition of any outdoor advertisement in a rural district. It is not to aptly to railway stations or piers and landing-places, or to land on 'which the business advertised is actuallycarried on. It applies equally, however, to advertisements of all sorts in prchibited spots.

One of the richest heirs in the kingdom is dan- gerously ill. The lion. Edward W. B. Portman, the eldest son of Viscount Portman is suffering from typhoid fever at St.G-iles, Salisbury. How remark- ably susceptible the "upper ten" are to this disease. They must inhabit more salubrious dwellings and lead more sanitary lies than the huge majority of the middle class, yet the average mortality must be very much larger in the former than in the latter.

There is a disposition on the part of the Conser- vatives, I hear, to offer terms. A hint has been forthcoming from presumably responsible quarters i that f the Government will drop the poor-law part 9f the bill they can count on getting the third read- in a fortnight. This, however, is a very large if;" and while the Government are prepared to nlale concessions on many ir inor points there is absolutely no indication at present that they are even considering the abandonment of any substan- tial part of the bill.

The Prime Minister has written to Mr. Samuel Woods, M.P. indicating that at present he would prefer not to receive a deputation with reference to the Eight Hours (Mines) Bill, but inviting the hon. gentleman and his.friends to send him a statement Of their reasons for asking for facilities, in order that it may be laid before the Cabinet. The sup- Porters of the bill will consider the Prime Minis- ter's Suggestion. Meanwhile they realise that the Prospect of making further pi ogress with the measure this session is hopeless, but they intend t o take vigorous steps towards pushing it through next year.

. A correspondent states :—" The Ant_ _late are lin good spirits over the last week's debate in the jouse of Commons. It is some time since Anarch- 18m pure and simple has taken such a prominent Place in Parliament, and the length at which the debate was reported in some of tne dailies was re- garded as a fine advertisement for the movement. Mr. Balfour's speech was put down as very satisfac- tory ; to. a class who openly denounce the existence of the wealth autocracy, it is a compliment for an aristocrat of Mr. Balfour's influence to tremble with apprehension at the operation of the move- ment. As for Mr. Aaquith, it Was generally con-

ceded that he understood the subject, and 'puke in the best vein from his point of view. Of course,he is opposed to Anarchism, and he knows that to op- pose them would only increase their numbers. Alto- gether the Anarchists feel kindly disposed toward Mr. Darling for introducing the subj..ct, although his action did waste the time of the House.

"The idea is, when they get up a nieeting or dis- tribute literature, to teach men what they consider to be their degraded and humiliative position in society. After that they leave indivi- duals to work according to their lights. Strangely enough, the man who roused Mr. Darling's appre- hensions, Murdock belongs to the more moderate group of London Anarchists, the men who go by the name of the' Freedom Group.' The advanced isen speak of Murdock end those who think with him as; the philosophers,' as they are opposed to violent measures of the homb-throwing type, and believe, rather, in educating the people un' il they rise in a body and demand their emancipation. Mr. Darling was certainly unfortunate in fixing upon Murdock as the subject of his alarmist speech. But then, was Mr. Darling really alarmed ? "

" They smile, however, at his simplicity in ask- ing Mr. Gladstone whether the London Anarchists and those abroad are working in association. Mr. Balfour's query, too, as to their numbers was re- garded as showing a like ignorance of the subject, for anarchists maintain that they have _absolutely no organisation for purposes of propaganda. They also profess that they themselves have no concep- tion of their numbers. Certainly the leaders are known to each other, but societies of Anarchists do not organise outrages. That is left to individual feeling and individual action. If a man, 1:01' one or two men, contemplated a littl exercise in the way of bomb-throwing they would not take any body of Anarchists into their confidence, but would work en their own responsibility.

div.head: MARRIA.GE OF MR. HAROLD
div.p: MARRIA.GE OF MR. HAROLD
McCORQUODA.LK

An event of considerable interest to the people of Newton-le-Willows took place at Northchurch (Herts.), a few days ago, namely, the celebration of the marriage of Miss Grace Grativille,fourth daugh- ter of Major Beville Granville, J.P. and C.C., of Northehurch, to Mr. Harold McCorquodale, fourth surviving son of Colonel McCorquodale, J.P., DL., 'of Newton-le-Willows, Lancashire. Both of the parties had moved in a wide social circle in the district,and conse- quently the ceremony was witnessed by a numerous and fashionable gathering. The sacrarium and chancel steps at the church displayed a profusion of choice chrysan- themums for the occasion. The decorations were under- taken by the Misses Constable Curtis, with flowers from Charnpneys, Rossway, The Hall, lierlrhamstead, Ash- ' ridge, and Fendley, and from Newbold Revel, Warwick- shire. An .awning was erected over the pathway from the churchyard gate to the porch of the church. The relatives were accommodated in seats under the tower, and immediately in front of the chancel, whilst the whole of the nave was allotted to the invited guests, among whom we noticed the Earl.and Countess Brown - low, Mrs. and the Misses Smith-Dorrien, Mrs. and Miss Constable Curtis, Sir Astley Paston Cooper, Bart., Mr. J. G. and Mrs. Williams, Mr. FL E. G. Craufurd, Miss Barclay, Mrs. E. J. and Miss Pearson, Roy. Fl. T. and Mrs. Wood, Rev. W. Roberts, Mr.W. L. and Mrs. Sutton, Mrs. Lionel Lucas, Mr. Graham Loyd, Mrs. Streatfield Moore, Miss St reatfeild, Mr. Streatfeild, Btc. The cere- mony was timed for two o'clock, and prior to that hour the bridegroorn,accompanied by his brother, Mr. Norman McCorquodale, had taken up his position at the channel steps, whilst the bridesmaids, ten in number, waited the coming of the bride's party at the porch. The brides- maids were the Misses Olive Muriel and Morwenna Gran- ville, sisters of the bride ; Miss McCorquodale, sister of the bridegroom ; Miss Mabel Granville, Miss Compton, and Miss(Finetta Villebois Bathurst,cousins of the bride; Miss Mary McCorquodale, niece of the bridegroom ; and the Misses Sophia and Anna Constable Curtis. They were attired in dresses of white silk with tulle veils, and wreaths of roses and white heather, and each wore as an ornament a gold bangle with moonstone and diamond heart,the gift of the bridegroom. The officiating clergy, who proceeded to the entrance at the approach of the bride, were the Rev. Roger Granville, rector of Bideford, North Devon, uncle of the bride, the Rev. Henry Sher- lock, viear of Celdham, Cambs, brother-in-law of the bridegroom, and the Rev. A. F. Birch, rector of North- church. The bride arrived punctually leaning on the arm of her father, and looked charming in a costume of erhite satin with a wreath of orange blossoms and veil, and wearing di,anond ornaments, including a diamond and sapphire half hoop bangle, the gift of the bride- groom. Mrs. Granville, the mother of the bride, wore a black velvet dress trimmed with helio- trope, and black bonnet with heliotrope feathers. Mrs. McCorquodale wore a black and gold shot velvet ,Cress trimmed with lace, and carried a' rich bouquet of yellow chysanthemums. The whole of the bridal party carried bouquets of choice flowers. The service was fully choral, with the assis- tance of the surpliced choir and the Revs. G. H. Siddans and R. H. Pope (curates), and as the procession filed up the aisle the hymn "The voice that breathed o'er Eden." was sung. On taking up their positions at the chancel steps the ensemble by the grouping ot the wedding party in bright dresses was very effective and pretty. The marriage ceremony proper was impressively performed by the Rev. Roger Granville, and after the singing of the " Deus Misereatur " the Rev. H. Sherlock officiated, whilst the final exhortation was read by the Rev. A. F. Birch. "0 love Divine," 578, A and M, was then sung, and the Benediction was pronounced by the Vicar. The marriage register was signed by the bride and bride- groom, and the chief bridesmaid, Miss Olive Granville, and the best man. As Mr. and Mrs. Harold McCorquo- dale issued from the vestry Mendelssohn's " Wedding March "was played on the organ by Mr. Eric Streatfeild who accompanied the choral service throughout. The completion of the ceremony was also signalized by the peals on the church bells, which continued to rind dur- ing the day. Nearly 200 guests were subsrquently received by Mrs. Granvillie, and the relatives prnsent included Mr. and Mrs. W. Maudsley, Mr. George Gran- ville, Captain Dennis Granville, Lady Charles Paulet, Mrs. Wellesley Pigott,Captain Wellesley and Mrs. Piet Miss Marian Granville, Mrs. Compton, and the Misses Compton, Mrs. Bathurst, Mr. H. Villebois Bathurst, Mrs A Court Pigott, Mr. and Mrs. Edmund Wodehouse, Captain Capel, and Mrs. Wodehouse, Mrs, Fox, Mrs. Frank Wodehouse, Miss Wodehouse, Mrs. Armine Fox, Admiral and Mrs. Fullerton, Mrs. Cochrane, Colonel and Miss Capel, Mrs. de Crespigny ,Colonel and Mrs. McCor- quodale, Mr. and Mrs. G. F. MeCorquodale, Mr. and ' Mrs. A. C. McCorquodale, Mr. Norman McCorquodale, Mr. Stew art McCorquoriale. Mr. and Mrs. Greenshields ' Sir Charles and Lady Hamilton and Miss Hamilton, Mr. and Mrs. Blacklock, Mr. and Mrs. Birley, Mrs. Sherlock, Mrs. Dudgeon. Mr. and Mrs. Harold McCorquodale left by the,4•lB p.m. train from I3erkhamsted Station, to spend their honeymoon at Mr. McCorquodale's shooting box in Argyleshire. The bride's travelling dress was of green cloth with jacket to match, with deep velvet collar, black velvet hat and black feathers. Mr. and Mrs. Mc- Corquodale will take up permanen residence at Park- bury, near St. Albans. It is almost needless to state that the wedding presents were " both valuable and numerous," comprising over two hundred gifts. The bride had been a Sunday school teacher for several years, and the teachers o the Northchurch Sunday school marked the happy occasion by presenting her ' with a copy of Hymns ancient and modern with tunes. The bridegroom was also the recipient of handsome gifts from the firms of Messrs. McCorquodale, Limited, the Liverpool printing and Stationary Company, Limi- ted, and the North Wales Paper Company, Limited. A hunting crop was also presented to Mr. Harold McCor- quodale on the eve of his marriage from the tenants of Rossway and neip„tbouring farms as a token of their esteem and good wishes" with an earnest hope that his union with a young lady so highly respected in the neighbourhood will be blessed with health, happiness, and prosperity." doctrine and polity he appreciated very highly, would do well with a little infusion of the Methodist fervour. Therefore he was not sorry occasionally to .to a Methodist meeting, because when he went back again to his own people,he ought perhaps to convey back a little of their fervour. He should be exceedingly sorry to belong to a Church around which there stood insuperable ecclesiastical hedges, over which it was impossible for the minister to climb. He would not like to belong to a church which however it might boast of its antiquity, was forgetful that the Master said "He that is not against us is on our side." (Applause.) He believed, however, most heartily in the denominational life ot England, as it created a healthy tivalry amongst the churches. Rivalry might be carried to an extreme to become very undesirable, but he believed in having just enough to stimulate each other to good works. He had almost a feeling of envy at the sight of the meeting that night,. because he was bound to confess, that it was al- most impossible to have a meeting like it in Wycliffe for the same object. They were not at all envious at one another's success, but rejoiced in each other's progress and they could strengthen one another in the work of God. He did not think that it was a very favourable time at present to get money, as they had so many claims which were irresistible, but he was glad to gay that at his church the collections for the foreign missions were as good as last year. He supposed that the reason was that these who could afford, gave more liberally than in previous years. He hoped that the same result would be attained that night. The Rev. Owen Watkins, who was stationed in Sout Central Africa for 17 years, next addressed the meeting and gave a most interesting account of his life in that part of the world. He said that be went to Africa as :ninister to the white population of Petermaritzberg at a time when the various missionary societies were pushing forward into the interior of Africa. But the Wesleyan denomination were strangely apathetic, and it was only by his pertinacity that he received permission to go into the " wilderness " to the north. He detailed very graphi- cally his experiences in the Transvaal and among the black population in the interior of South Central Africa. IHe said that civilization without Christianity was a curse to those people. He had found out in his 17 years experience that they were far better without it. Civili- zation must not come first but Christianity, and civiliza- tion must follow in its footsteps. At the end of his address, he appealed for increased subscriptions for the foreign missionary society, and told of his great disap- pointment at not being able to go to the Zambesi owing to the missionary society having to economise their resources. A hearty vote of thanks to the Chairman and the Rev. Owen Watkins was proposed by the Rev. J. G. Bennett, and seconded by Mr. Davey and carried unanimously. It was announced that the collections this year had shown an increase of £5 is. Bd. upon the previous year. The meeting was brought to a close with the pronounc- ing of the benediction.

div.head: WIDNES DISTRESS FUND.
div.p: WIDNES DISTRESS FUND.

The weekly meeting of the Catering Committee of Widnes Distress Relief Committee, wa'S held on Wednesday, under the presidency of Councillor Christie. It was decided to distribute 1,312 hot- pots to-morrow (74unday) and 670 dozen of 41b. loaves with the soup during next week. Accounts amounting to .£246 7s. were passed for payment. The Committee recommended that £5 be granted to Mr. Dauby, clerk to the School Board, for the pur- chase of clogs for the needy children attending the various schools. The meeting of the General Committee was subsequently held under the presidency of Mr. F. Neil. The minutes of the Catering Committee were ap- preved.—Mr. Joseph Morrison, in moving the minutes of the Fina*Cornmitiee said the Committee had decided to ask the subscribers to continue their subscriptions up to and including Saturday, December 2nd. They had received from the commencement £2,557, and had spent £2,194. which left a balance in hand up to Saturday last of £363. Last week the balance was £319. The thanks of the Committee were due to Mr. Ohmy who had sent £9 as the result Of a benefit performance at his circus, and their special thanks were due to the officials of the Cycle Club for the splendid entertainment which they provided on Monday night by their fancy dress ccle ' parade and which realised the splendid sum of £56 13s. 261. He had received the usual subscription from the Tyre Works and £3O had been added to the Widnes fund and the remainder £ll Os. 7d forwarded to St. Helens. E His directors had given him instructions to get the work ' in Widnes started as soon as possible and as they ex- pected a supply of fuel and salt on Monday next. 75 per , cent, of the men would be working full time next week. The minutes were confirmed. It was decided to accept the offer of Gessage's Prize Band to give a second concert in Alexandra Theatre (placed at the disposal of the Com- mittee by Mr. Kiddie) on Sunday evening, December 3rd, tor the benefit of the fund.

div.head: _ SOLDIERS FROZEN TO DEATH.
div.p: _ SOLDIERS FROZEN TO DEATH.
A HORSE GUARD'S BLUNDER.

A military court of enquiry was held on Tuesday, con- cerning the deaths of Privates Rogers and Davis, south Wales Borderers, who perished in a blizzard at ports. down Hill. The coroner's jury found that they died from syncope, produced by exposure to cold, and added a rider protesting against the action of the Horse Guards in stationing in such exposed places as Ports- down forts, troops just brought home from a tropical climate.

div.head: TTTE HEALTH OF THE POPE.
div.p: TTTE HEALTH OF THE POPE.

HIS HOLINESS GRADUALLY SINKING. COLOGNE, THETENDAY.—The " Cologne Gazette "learns from its Rome cprrespondent that although the Pope is net actually ill, his condition is such as to cause the gravest apprehensions in Vatican circles. His Holiness's physician, Dr. Lapponi, observes that the Pope is grad- ually sinking and that the end may come any moment. He doubts, moreover, whether His Holiness will survive the winter.

The new Mayor of Shaftesbury, Mr. W. Whitehead, like his predecessors:is a Wesleyan local preacher and a Liberal. Aberavon this year comes out with a Mayor who wears abuse ribbon. Ile feels a bit lonely. HOUSE EURNISHING.—We notice that Messrs. S. J.War- ing and Sons, Limited, of Manchester, Liverpool, and London, have just opened new premises at the corner of Bing-st. and Deansgate, in the former city, which per- mit of the display in the most elaborate fashion of their comprehensive stock of every requisite for house fur- nishing. A feature of the new showrooms is that all the furniture mmtained therein has been manufactured on the principle of artistic taste, whilst the necessity of construction has in no detail been forgotten. The car- pets are of the most choice description, the bedsteads of special design in harmony with the Sheraton,Louis XV., Louis XVI., and other periods, whilst the Oriental, anti- que, Spanish, Italian, and Turkish embroideries on view form a most unique collection. Every essential to the complete furnishing' of the home may be seen,whilst the range from which to choose is of the widest description. It is important to note that Messrs. Waring take full re- sponsibility for the character and durability of every article in the showrooms around which visitors will be conducted for purposes o'f inspection entirely free from importunity to purchase. Those intending to undertake the furnishing of a house in a most artistic, and at the same time the most useful manner, could hardly do better than pay Messrs. Waxing a visit.

div.head: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES-WARRINGTON.
div.p: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES-WARRINGTON.
THE DOUI3T OF THE HEART.

The Rev. W. H. Drummon4, 8.A., preached the third of his series of sertmns on" Doubting and Believing," on Sunday evening, at Cairo-st., chapel. He took as his subject the doubt of the heart. There was a good congregation, and in addition to the usual musical ser- vices the choir sang an anthem in a creditable manner, and the organist, Mr. J. M. Muir, played, as a volun- tary, 0 rest lathe Lord,"with his well-known taste and skill.

div.head: F.S.A. AT WYCLIFFE CHURCH.
div.p: THE F.S.A. AT WYCLIFFE CHURCH.

There was a very large attendance at the weekly meeting of the P.S.A. in Wycliffe Church on Sunday afternoon. Mr. F. R. Roberts, M.A., was the chairman, and in the course of a short address, he dealt with some of the objections he had heard raised against the P.S. A. movement, contending that although the growth of the movement had been rapid, it had come to stay. Mr. Ackroyd, of Manchester, delivered the address on evil spirits in the world to-day. One of the most fearful evil spirits of the present day, the speaker considered, was that of intoxicating liquor. The boys and girls' refuges in Manchester with which he was connected, were it not for this evil, had no need to exist. The speaker also re- ferred to the evils of the "Sweating system " and gambl- ing, illustrating his remarks by relating some incidents which had come under his own personal observation in Manchester. The musical portion of the service included two solos by Miss F. Booth, and Miss Westgarth. The Rev. J. Yonge, Messrs. G. Wallington and J. Ball also took part in the service.

SERMON TO YOUNG MEN. Wycliffe Church was well filled on Sunday evening, when the Rev. John Yonge preached a special sermon to young men. A good number of young men were present. The rev. gentleman took for his text let Timothy. 4 chapter; 7 to 9th verses, basing his remarks chiefly on the words" Exercise thyself rather unts godliness." Ile said the week which had just passed had been observed by Young Men's Christian Associations in this and ether countries as a week of universal prayer en behalf of young men, and he had received a suggestion from the Warrington Y.M.C.A, that he said speak to young men that night, and he was very glad to accede to the suggestion. Speaking of physical exercise, Mr. Yonge contended that a little was profitable,and was dis- tinctly worth a young man's having, but he did not con- sider it wise to fill as large a part of a young man's leis- ure with physical sxercise as frequently was the case. He also thought that Christian young men were not justified in so exhausting their physical strength on Sat- urday as to be compelled to spend Sunday forenoon in bed, in order to recouperate. Speaking of expenditure in regard to athletics he considered that many spent more money en it than they could afford, remarking that their expenditure for athletics should be among the smallest of their spendings. Bodily exercise not only profited very little, but risked a very great deal, 1

div.head: REV. 13. W. ROBERTS ON GAMBLING.
div.p: THE REV. 13. W. ROBERTS ON GAMBLING.

THE POLICE AND THE WATCH COMMITTEE. At Golborne-street Baptist Chapel on Sunday evening, the Rev. D. W. Roberts preached a sermon on gambling. There was a large cangregation, and in the course of his sermon the preacher, having alluded to various forms of gambling, said there was no necessity to go to Epsom or Newmarket, or even to Liverpool in order to practice the demoralizing eviL It could be done here in Warrington quite as well and as effectively. There were thousands ' who never saw saw a horse race in their lives who were addicted to the evil habit. Then there was the form of commercial gambling. Every day the country was sown with circulars which were direct incentives to gambling. • They penetrated the most unlikly homes I and polluted them. They might in this way be invited upon" reliable information" to buy shares in a mine which did not exist, on the chance of 100 per cent. pro- fit. Let them takeas an example the Liberator Frauds. The directors of that company took their salaries, got deposits on false statements, paid bogus dividends, put money on bogus societies, and probably offered up thanks to God for having enabled them to rob. Illegitimate speculation upon a large scale wss at the root of the commercial ruin, and distress in all quarters of the globe. And under various [corms, in humbler circles, it was responsible for those early departures from honesty, which spoiled many hopeful career, and wrecked many a happy home. How- ever, he did not condemn all brokers, or their trade, be- cause there were many honourable and just and pious men on the Stock Exchange. But while the Exchange was a necessity, it also afforded to unscrupulous men a chance of gambling. To buy stock and pay for it was a perfectly legitimate transaction, but to buy large quan- tities nominally without money to pay for them, in the hope that such stock would rise in value, was gambling. There were classes of commercial speculation which he I characterised as One vast organized fraud—barefaced, thievish, ungarnished fraud. Another form of gambling which he alluded to was that conducted by unscrupulous Life Insarance agents, &c. These, he said, were the evils which the church and public men had to put up with. They were evils which gripped the soul like a demon and blunted every feeling of humanity. They aroused the devil which was in man ; they kindled the fires of hell within his breast. They nursed the rage, de- veloped jealousy, and engendered strife. They swal- lowed up every good and generous instinct ofthe heart; they ate like cancers into the soul and speedily destroyed all that was most noble and God-like in it. Hew long, be asked, were they to stand by and let this vile contagion spread among them? The matter was urgent and admitted of no delay. Some stringent and definite and united action would have to be taken, for many hundreds were on their way to ruin in this town. Gambling was very prevalent in Warrington and was becoming more so every day. There were gambling dens known to the Watch Committee where young men were being ruined by their illegal doings. Here was but one instance,which was an extract of a letter received by him on Oct. Bth, calling his attention to a certain house in, town,where men,women,and boys repaired to bet. The letter stated : " I have a son not 17 who takes all the money he can get hold of, there," and not only that " but steals mine, and all he can get." The Chief Constable knew all about this letter. He had facts in his possession as secretary of the anti-gambling committee of the Social Questions Union, which, if disclosed, would shame the authorities—if they possessed such a virtue as shame. And Warrington would indeed be, in the sight of all right-minded and righteous people, the "black spot on the Mersey." On behalf of the Union he some time ago forwarded a letter to the Mayor, drawing the attention of the Watch Committee to the prevalence of gambling. The letter he received in reply from the Town Clerk, stated : "It is, unfortunately, true that gambling exists to a serious extent, but if you will search the pace reports every week you will find that the police are doing everything in their power to sup- press it." This he contended was false. It was stated by the same authority that "while we may have reason to suspect that gambling takes place in certain houses in the town, there aze many difficulties in the way of effectually dealing with them." What were those diffi- culties which were in the way ? They were difficulties, which if effeatually dealt with would bringcertain mem- bers ef the Town Council before the Bench. They would exclaim "That is an astounding expression." But he could assure them it was true. BEWSEY ROAD WESLEYAN CHAPEL. The annual foreign missionary services in connection with the above chapel were held on Sunday when the Rev. G. D. Mason preached in the morning from the text" And I, if Ibe lifted up will draw all men unto me." In the afternoon, a service for the young was held, which was addressed by the Revs. Owen Watkins, and G. D. Mason, and in the evening the Rev. Owen Watkins preached to a large congregation. On Monday night a public meeting was held in the chapel presided over by Mr. C. E. Parker of Penketh,who was supported by the Revs. J. Yonge, J. Kirtlan and Owen Watkins, and Mr. Winstanley. The Ohs.= an said that it was with great thankful- ness that he saw on the platform their truly beloved superintendent (the Rev. J. Kirtlan). That was the fir-t occasion since his severe illness that he (the chair- man) had had the pleasure of meeting him,and he would be expressing the joy he knew they all felt in knowing that he was so far restored to health and strength again that he was going to address the meeting. Their wishes end prayers went out to him that his preserved life would long be preserved to his church and to his family for many years. (Applause.) The Rev. J. Kirtlan next gave the annual report. He expressed his pleasure at seeing Mr. Parker in the chair. He was much moved at the way the chairman had spoken of him. ,Be felt that he would never get out of the debt which ie owed to the friends of this circuit as well as to the friends out of his own church, for their prayers during the most critical period of his life. He felt that niAit that he must acknowledge before God's people his indebtedness to the Christian people of this town and neighbourhood. He felt that his life had been given back to him with increased • responsibility. In the report there were a number of items which would be of intPrest. There had been an increase of 57 chapels during the year,six additional missionaries, and 65 more catechists, and there were 231 new members in the churches. There had been several new conferences formed in various parts of the world which worked very well. The income of the foreign missionary department for the year 1892 had be-m £124,654 12s. 4e., and the expenditure £124,745 133, id. leaving a deficit* of sol Os. 4d. which made the total debt of the department 3E21,521 18s. 11d. The ladies missionary committee had also expended £9.000 during the year towards which the Liverpool district (of which Warrington forms a part), had contributed £937 91. 10d., which was a very good proportion. The ordinary income for the foreien mis- sions for the Liverpool district had been £7,207 95.„ being an increase of £3B upon the previous year. In addition to this there had been legacies atnountiog to £1,839 N. 6d., which made the total increase £l.OBl is. 71. The total income for Warrington had been £lO2. The Chairman briefly addressed the meeting express- ing his deep sympathy with foreign Missions, and hoped that the good work might go on. The Rev. J. Yonge said that he was always glad to go to a Methodist meeting, because when it was cold out- side It was sure to be warm inside. (Langhter.) He sometimes felt that the congregationallats, whose

div.head: IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.
div.p: IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.

-- MONDAY. In the House of Commons on Monday evening, Mr. MACDONA questioned the President of the Board of Trade regaroing a statement which had been published that there are 400 fl ,ating wrecks in the Gulf Stream con- stituting a serious danger to navigation. Mr. MUNDIALLA I said the Board of Trade had no such information in their possession. But the question of the removal of derelict ships from ocean routes was one of the 'natters consid- ered at the Maritime Conference held at Washington, and the recommendations of that Conference were being carefully considered. Sir U. KAY-SHUTTLEWORTH informed Sir E. A. Bartlett that all the ten battleships provided for under the Naval Defence Act would be completed early in 1894. 'rhe House again went into Committee on the Local Goveriment Bill. Mr.H. Fowler's amendment providing that there should be a parish council for every parish with a population of 200 or upwards was carried by 203 to 134. Mr. Fowtsa moved another amendment that an order of the County Council might provide, if the parish meeting consented, for establishing a Parish Council in a rural parish having a population less than 200, and also provide for grouping a parish with some neighbouring parish or parishes under a common Parish Council with the consent of the parish meeting. The right hon, gentleman accepted an amendment moved by Mr. FIENEAGE adding words to the effect that a parish with a population of 100 and upwards might establish a Parish Council quite independent of the County Council I3ut where a parish had a population of less than 100 the County Council should determine whether it should have a Parish Council or not; and, thus amend, the Government amendment was agreed to. After further discussion clause 1 was passed, and some amendments to clause 2 were also disposed of. TUESDAY. In the House of Commons on Tuesday evening, Mr. H rnmi ASQUIT, replying to a question as to the cettal of several persons to prison at Stroud for non-payment of fines imposed under the Vaccination Acts—in some cases second fines,—said he regretted the state of the law on the subject, and the Government had introduced a bill to alter it ; but if he were to remit the penalties he should be in fact repealing an Act of Parliament. Mr. LABOUCHERE put a series of questions about Matabeleland and the Chartered Company, and was in- formed by Mr. Buxton that her Majesty's Government would net consent to any measure which they did not consider just and reasonable, and that every endeavour was being made to open up friendly communications with Lobengula with a view to bringing hostilities to a speedy and satisfactory end. Mr. ACLAND, in answer to Mr. W. APLaren, said the recognition of mixed classes in evening schools rested with the Education Department and not with the inspectors. The House again went into Committee on the Local Government Bill. Mr. W. WLAREN moved an amend- ment to include married women ratepayers among the persons entitled to vote for Parish Councils. Mr. H. FOWLER said he intended at the proper time to insert a new cause removing altogether the disqualification of married women in respect of local government elections. Mr. A. J. BALFOUR said if this was done it would make it impossible in the figure to keep those women off the Parliamentary register, and Mr. CHAMBERLAIN said he should certainly oppose the extension of the franchise to women in municipal elections. Mr. M'Latuts's amend- ment was then withdrawn. Mr. COURTNEY moved an amendment to give effect to the cumulative system of voting. The amendment was strongly opposed by the Government and was rejected by 186 to 114.

div.head: WEDNESDAY.
div.p: WEDNESDAY.

The House of Commons again went into Committee on the Local Government Bill on Wednesday. To the pro- posal that the proceedings of every parish meeting should begin not earlier than six or later than eight o'clock in the evening Sir It. Paget moved an amend- ment that the proceedings should begin at such a time as the parish meeting itself should decide. The amend- ment was rejected by 219 to 106. Clause 2 was still under discussion when the hour for adjournment arrived.

div.head: THURSDAY.
div.p: THURSDAY.

In the House of Commons on Thursday evening Sir E. Grey, in answer to Sir E. A. Bartlett said Her Majesty's Minister and the senior naval officer at Rio de Janerio were acting in concert with the representatives of other naval Powers for the protectien of the lives and property of foreigners. Mr. MUNDELLA, replying to a question, made a state- ment about the havoc caused on our coasts by the recent gales. The Board of Trade, he said, had received re- turns showing a loss of 237 lives, and additional returns were coming in hourly. The number of persons re- ported to have been saved was 508-105 of these by life- boats—and the Royal National .Lifeboat Institution claimed that 102 lives had been saved in addition to these of which the Board of Trade had returns. The right hon gentleman added that the Lifeboat Institution was managed better than any other institution of a similar character. Mr. Foltwooo questioned the Home Secretary about the action taken by the prosecuting counsel in the Liver- pool tobacco frauds case, and was informed that neither the Director of Public Prosecutions nor any of his agents had any knowledge of the case. In reply to Mr. Labouchere, Mr. GLADSTONE said the Government intended to carry into effect in the spirit in which it was adopted the resolutien of the House in regard to the county magistracy, but the method of doing so must be in accordance with the machinery at the disposal of the gxecutive. On the order for the third reading of the Employers' Liability Bill, Mr. CHAMBERLAIN said that when the bill passed employers would insure, and the result would be to get rid of whatever inducement of self-interest there now was to take precautions against accidents. If the Government would not face and settle the question of compensation for all classes of accidents, they might have left the free force A voluntary arrangements fair play. Mr. Asquith defended tlae measure in a speech of some length. Is the subsequent debate Mr. MATHER expressed hearty approval of the bill, which was eventu- ally read a third time amid cheers. •
