div.head: SHIP CANAL NAVVY. 1 Alßs. S. A. ALLEN'S
div.p: THE SHIP CANAL NAVVY. 1 Alßs. S. A. ALLEN'S
SOME INTERESTING DETAILS.

The army of navvies on the canal is now all but disbanded. One small brigade is left, and that i,t be presently dissolved. In small companies, the 20,000 men have for months been scattering them- selves over the face of the country. With bundle ia hand, the sum of his belongings, the navvy tramps from place to place—the pioneer of our civilisation. Living almost in a wilderness, he makes for us our railways, canals, reservoirs, and harbours of refuge. It would not be quite correct to say that the army which has made for Manches- ter its gateway to the sea wilt depart in full strength. There are many wounded soldiers whom it is neseseary to leave behind. Some of those who have fallen have crept back to their old homes, it may be in remote country districts ; but perhaps the larger number will be established in the poor houses of Lancashire and Cheshire. Before the last files of the able-bodied make their way abroad over the land it may be well to speak of the navvy as we have found him during the last six years. In this long period he has found a temporary home in the towns and villages along the thirty-five miles of canal. Where town or village was not at hand colonies of wooden huts have sprung up for his accommodation on marsh or field. The coming of the navvy was looked forward to in many a quiet Cheshire community with undisguised dread. It was thought to mean disturbance and restlessness where hitherto life had been very placid. In the larger centres, like Warrington and Runcorn, there was also a measure of fear. There was even a call for a strengthened force of police. But apprehensions were soon calmed. The navvies quietly established themselves and took kindly to the new conditions. Now that their exodus is all but complete, the villagers and towns- people who received them are not without feelings of regret. Once the sort of natural barrier which exists between the navvy and the ordinary member of society was broken by contact it was found that behind a rough exterior and a somewhat surly manner various good qualitiea were hidden. The industry of the man is con- tinuous ; there is no bone of idleness in him. He is net, take the average of the class, a drunkard or roysterer. His independeace may sometimes have the look of defi- ance and even aggression, but it is really a trait which those who minister to the navvy regard as one of the most promising features in his character. The sincerity may be downright and rather brutal, but it may be made to tell for good. .

The navvy ha'S often very much of the gentleman about him. While the canal was making many ladies visited the scene of operations. If one were near a muddy place the odds were great but that, in a care- less sort of way, the labourer threw a plank over the soft ground. There was not the grace in his action that Sir Walter Raleigh threw over a famous historical per- formance, nor would the same good fortune attend it, but the good willeand true gentleness were there. The missionary and the harbourer of the navvy tell of many acts of kindness on his part. The men are ever ready to help each other. If a penniless comrade, looking for work, appears among them, his appeal, though it may be unspoken, is never in vain. A levy is made to supply him with immediate relief, and if it is at all possible the " ganger "takes him in the ranks. Should a poar man be maimed or killed—as but too often happens—an in- stant and substantial collection for anyone who may be dependent upon him is set on foot. Some day our knowledge of the common language of these men may be improved. It is broad and rather eourse,and smacks of the soil. It would be interesting to have a collection of some of the names by which the men know each other. In some of the villages on the hills which form the Yorkshire border Edwin Waugh tells us that many people are unknown, even among their neighbours, by their surnames. In Roby's " Traditions " a woman is mentioned for whom it would be useless to inquire for her proper name, though anyone in Whitworth village could have instantly directed you to " Susy o' Jem's o' Fairoff's, at th' top o' th' Rake." So among the navvies but with las complexity of designation, individuals are met with whose surnames have almost dropped into oblivion by disuse. They are only to be distinguished by an epithet descriptive of some personal peculiarity or of the part of the country from which they came. There is " Gloucester Joe" and " Cheshire Tom there is a tall man that is " sten " and the short-thick- set man that is" nobble." The familiarity of appella- tion is carried even further. The constant visitor is described on the same principle, and tho head of the Navvy Mission is content to be called, in an affectionate way, the " Parson Slasher" or the " l'arson Ganger." An artificial light much used at nights on the canal is commonly called the " Lucy Jane "—the derivation, no doubt, being from lucigen. The members of the Navvy Mission have a good deal to say to the credit of the men which cannot here be put down. Mrilolliday, at the Latchford centre, says it is delightful to work among them. They are, in nearly every case, civil and obliging. They receive him on pleasant terms of equality and friendliness. In the dinner hour and at night he often reads to them, it may be a mission letter from Mrs. Garnett, a passage from the Bible, or a chapter from an entertaining work Among the younger generation of navvies there are many who have had an elementary education and can read for themselves, but the older bands are for the most part quite illiterate. The Navvy. Mission, it should he said, established centres of work at some fourteen points on the canal route. Mission halls and schools were built, and a minister was appointed to each place. The Mis- sion is in connection with the Church of England, but as it was recognised that men of all denominations were drawn to the works, a combination serviee was provided in which all, as far as possible, might find something that they were used to. A shortened form of Church service was used', and the prayers were extemporary. As the canal has been completed from point to point and the navvies have made their departure the number of missionaries has been lessened, and to-day there are only seven on the line of works. First the mission hall at Eastham was closed, then that at Ellesmere Port, and so on till the canal was carried as far as Saltport. In the same way, the staff was reduced between Manchester and Latchford. By the end of another month the work of the Mission between Manchester and Liverpool may have come altogether to an end. The fact has alreadJ been mentioned that the Hon. and Rev. Robert Grim- ton, a son of the Earl of Verulam, has had the superin- tendence of the Mission. Mr. Grimston can speak, ' perhaps better than anybody else, of the navvy in all his aspects and of the good in him which stands lout. We have referred to the great number of accidents which have happened during the construction of the canal. With sad frequency the death of one man after another has been chronicled. Many have been cut off in the flower of their prime. A very . much larger number have been crippled, and will never see service again. It would be hard very often to say whether the latter have not the worse fate. This is the price which has unfor- tunately to be paid for all great undertakings of the character. It has been a very common thing to see on the canal men who were short of either a arm or leg. The duty given to these maimed people, who grew in number as the canal did in size,was to look to the sema- phore signals on the overland railway,—to attend to the points, and do other things requiring no great activity. The canal is made, and one wonders how these men will fare in the future. They can no longer tramp abroad as of old, and it is to be feared their outlook is but sad. Mr. T. A. Walker, the original contractor, established three hospital centres for the wounded. One was at Ellesmere Port, the second at Latchford, and the third at Barton. For the part of the canal nearer Manchester the Royal Infirmary served. If an accident happened, not a moment was lost in conveying the sufferer to the nearest of these three points. A long and peculiar whistle denoted to everyone on the line that an engine was bound for the hospital,and immediately the railway was cleared of all obstruction. At each hospital there was a resident surgeon, with a proper nursing staff, and nothing that the best skill could accomplish was'wanting. The hospitals at Barton and Ellesmere Port have been long closed, for near those points the work of the navvies has ceased. But Latchford, during the past few months, has been a busy centre. •In the long cutting, operations have been hastened on by work night and day. Payment has had to be made for the quick progress, and Mr. Walker, the resident surgeon, has had his time pretty fully occupied' in attending to the patients. There are 24 beds in. the hospitals, and a couple of days ago 18 of them were oc- cupiet). Some of the cases may serve as a sample of the vast roll of injured during the past six years. One man fifty or sixty years old, had lost the sight of one eye, if not o: both, through a blasting operation. He is bad.ly hurt in other ways, and will never be able to work agam. Two men had been run over by a waggon, and a third crushed by a steam navvy. In these eases amputations would be necessary. The other cases were mostly those of fracture caused by waggons and the fall of poles and planks. Several people had suffered burns from the lucigen light. One patient who entered the hospital tell from the high-level bridge at Latchford to the bank below, a distance of about 40ft. His skull and thigh were fractured, but after being off work for a few weeks he is now getting quite well. The Latchford Hospital is a bright and cheerful place, with the glow of warm fires reflected in its pinewood roof. The patients have every kindly attention, and those of them who are on a fair way to recovery beguile the hours in looking at picture- books, or, if they can, by reading simple stories.— "Manchester Guardian."

THE COAL STOPPAGE.
REMOVAL OF THE LIVERPOOL POLICE FROM ST.
HELENS.

The Liverpool police stationed in St. Helens during the last month left for Liverpool at 2.40 on Monday after- noon, their services not being required further. The cost to St. Helens during their stay has been about £l,lOO. THE REPORTED HITCH AT R. EVANS AND CO.'S

div.head: COLLIERIES.
div.p: COLLIERIES.

It has been officially stated at the head offices of Messrs. Richard Evans and Co., that nothing in the nature of a hitch had occurred at their Golborne pit or any other pit belonging to the company, and that the report that a deputation had waited upon the general manager with regard to the employment of union men was not correct. Instructions had been given to all the pit managers that all the old hands must be found work. Everything was going on smoothly, and practically the whole of the men formerly employed had been taken on. Only about one hundred men out of the 4,000 employes of the fir:n now remain idle, and work will be found for these as soon as possible. TERMS OF THE SETTLEMENT.

The following is the official statement of the terms of settlement arrived at last Friday : Terms of settlement of the coal dispute agreed upon between representatives of the Federated Coalowners' and of the Miners' Federation of Great Britain, at a con- ference at the Foreign Office on Friday, Novemberl.7th, 1893, Lord Rosebery, K.G., in the chair. 1. That a board of conciliation he constituted forth- with, to last over the year at least, consisting of an equal number ot coalotvners' and miners' representatives —l4 each. They shall, before the first meeting, endea- vour to elect a chairman from outside, and should they fail, will ask the Speaker of the House of Commons to nominate one, the chairman to have the casting vote. That the board, when constituted, shall have power to determine from timo to time the rate of wages on and from February 1, 1894, the first meeting to be on Wed- nesday, December 13, 1893, at the Westminster Palace Hotel.

2. That the men resume work at once at the old rate of wages until February 1, 1894. It is agreed that all collieries, so .far as practicable, be re-opened for work forthwith, and that, as far as practicable, no impedi- ment be placed in the way of a return of the men to work. _

We, the undersigned, chairman and secretaries of the Federated Coalowners and of the Miners' Federation of Great Britain,on behalf of those represented at this con- ference, agree to the above terms of settlement of the present coal dispute. Signed on behalf cf the coalowners— A. M. CHAMBERS, Chairman. Tnomes RATCLIFFE Ewa, Secretary. On behalf of the Miners' Federation— BENJAMIN PICKARD, Chairman. Tuoates ASHTON, Secretary. ROSEBERY, Chairman of the Conference. H. LLEWELLYN SMITH, Secretary of the Conference. POOR RELIEF AND THE PRICE OF COAL.

The Bourne (Lincolnshire) Board of Guardians on Thursday aecided to grant outdoor paupers fid. per week extra because of the high p-ice of coal. HOW THE COL STRIKE AFFECTED RAILWAYS. Mr. Webb. locomotive superintendent of the London and North-Western Railway, speaking at Crewe. on Wednesday night, said their eueines had run 1,000.000 miles less during the past three months on account of the coal strike. To 11-ep Crewe works going they re- qiiired 5000 tons of coal every day. They decided to reduce the hours of work rather than discharge the men. Through the collier's strike twenty millions of money had been stopped circulating.

div.head: SHIP CANAL.
div.p: THE SHIP CANAL.
TIIE COMPLETION OF THE CANAL.

The" Morning Post," referring to the approaching opening of the Manchester Ship Canal, says :—The citizens of these flourishing localities are confident that • hey have made a profitable investment of about £10,000,000 in the undertAking. but whether they will get the eight per cent, or eleven per cent, which the most sanguine have been anticipating remains to be proved. Certainly no stone has been left unturned to secure as much trade as possible for the venture. Already a Glasgow firm has announced a direct line of steamers , between th. Clyde and Manchester, to commence rim- ming from Glasgow on Doc-mher 30 and from Manchester a few days after. The Cotton Spinners' Association have intimated to their American correspondents that in future preference will be given to cotton which has been brought through to the capital of the cotton indus- try without transhipment, and in accordance with this intimation large steamers are receiving cargo at New Orleans for conveyance direct to the new English sea- port. It is evident that the Manchester merchants are determined upon 'exerting their influence in favour of making the canal in every way a success, and it will be hoped there is no disappointment in store for them. Naturally the port of Liverpool must stiller more or less severely as a result of the diverting of one of its most important branches of trade to another channel, but the loss will probably be mere than counterbalanced by an accession of other business through the greater ease ' with which ships can reach the docks, as the serious obs struction at the Mersey Bar is now being successfully removed. THE FORMAL OPENING OF THE CANAL. The Chairman of the Canal Company (Lord Egerton) writes that it is not the intention of the Ship Canal Com- pany to have an official opening on January 1, but at some future time, probably after Easter, when the weather is likely to be more favourable. FLOODING THE CANAL AT RUNCORN. The work of filling the Ship Canal between Old Quay Runcorn, and Latchford was commenced on Monday morning. At ten o'clock in the presence of Mr. E. D. Jones, the agent, and Mr. H. W. Aber- nethy, the engineer, the sluice.at the Old Quay was opened and water began to flow into the canal cut- ting. The mechanical arrangements to allow the inflow of water are very simple. Through the dam, which separates the tilled portion of the Canal from the empty clunnel, has been placed a wooden shoot, one foot below water level. This shoot measures six feet hiF,M and four feet broad, and within it is fixed a door which can be easily raised and lowered so that the flow of water can be regulated. To break the fall of the water and save the bed of the Canal, what is technically known as a timber apron has been placed in position,and by this contrivance the water is diverted as over a slop- ing platform and is carried forward without any violent rush. When the shoot is epened to its fullest extent, a vast volume of water is admitted, but it was only open tn an extent of twelve inches on Monday morning, but as the tides rise, more water will be admitted. It is ex- pected that with the water admitted at Old Quay at Randal's sluice at Latchford and by the various streams en route, the water in the Canal will be raised from 18 inches to two feet per day, and at the end of a fortnight the requisite depth of 26 feet will have been attained. When this is accomplished the dams at Runcorn and Latchford will be removed by dredgers and then these will be no obstacles from Eastham to Manchester.

div.head: STRIKE OF SCOTCII MINERS.
div.p: STRIKE OF SCOTCII MINERS.

Most of the men employed in the Lanarkshire it came out on strike on Thursday, the masters having refused to give them an advance in wages. The miners contended that inasmuch as Scotch coal had gone up in Price they were entitled to an additional shilling per day. THE EXAMINER.
SATURDAY. NOVEMBER 25. 1893.
Sentences THERE have, t his week, been two

at or three cases at Liverpool Liverpool Assmes. Assizes which are fairly open to a little public comment. Two of the cases sprang from the neighbouring colliery village of Haydock. In one instance a man was charged with /saving stabbed his wife with a knife with intent to mur- der. He pleaded guilty of unlawful wounding and Mr. Justice Day, who said he always treated the "real working man" with indulgence, simply bound the prisoner over to come up for judgment when called upon. This was a merciful sentence, anti no doubt the judge took into account the man's previous good character, and the pleadings of the mnch-inj tired but forgiving wife. In the other case from HaYdock, seven young, but real workingmen " were concerned. These young miners were charged with having "riotously assembled with other people in order to dieturb the public peace." The " riot it may at once be said, was not on the largest or most destructive scale. Its importance was mainly derived from the fact that it was one of the results of the coal Took-out. In other circumstances, it would, as likely as not, have been described as a" broach of the peace." The prosecution certainly did not display any vindictiveness, and the prosecuting barrister admitted that the men had not been previously convicted. But Mr. JUSTICE DAY seemed to think that this was a much more serious offence than the other, or, perhaps, lie thinks that a locked-out workman is not a " real working- man." Whatever might be the reason, he, at all events, committed these seven men to gaol for three months hard labour—a penalty which did not err on the side of leniency. These two cases form a suggestive contrast. We believe that notwithstanding tilt decision of the judge, nine- teen out of every twenty persons will consider that the stabbing of a wife with a knife is at least as serioue an offence as unlawful assembling at a time of great public excitement. The other mat- ter.to which reference may be made is the whole- sale resort to flogging in cases of robbery with violence. According to the "Liverpool Daily Post there have been twelve of th3so cases at the Assizes, and in eleven the lash has been ordered. This seems a falling back to the old idea of brutal punishment with a vengeance. Whht is the object to be served? The "Daily Post" denies that there has been any revival of outrages in Lserpool ; the police reports for the last three I years, in fact, show a diminution of stabbing and I

wounding crimes, Therefore, those sentences cannot be intended as an eieeptional deterrent to meet an exceptional emergency. If they are meant to reform the individuals flogged, the exputtation is not supported by criminal history. A man ean not go through such an ordeal without being still further degraded and embittered against all laws, human and divine. We noticed a few days ago a protest in a London newspaper against the "flogging sentences" of another judge in another part of Englani. It is to be hoped that the julges, or some of them, are not adopting this brutalising remedy of set purpose. The laws for many years past have been gradually human- ised, and it would be a pity if these judges rovited any further than is absolutely necessary,. old and discredited punishments. •

AT' a time when Mr. R. lean- Some Remarkable rorer, the member for Warring- ures. ton, and other Tories are doing their best to impede and mutilate the Employers' Liability Bill, it is desirable that people should keep in mind the great need that there is for such a Bill " Labour's Death Roll " was the title of a lecture given in London this week by Mr. John Bunms, M.P., and the figures which are quoted in that lecture tell a tale which is as startling as it is pathetic. Labour and industry have, as Mr. BURNS said, during the last fifty years, sent more people to their graves, to hospitals, and to beds of suffering than any war which has taken place during the same period. Of Lancashire miners alone there have, in thirty years,. been no fewer than 31,466 killed outright, while the yearly list of accidents reaches a stupendous total. In South Wales 280 out of every thousand meet with more or less serious accidents in the year; and in Cleveland one out of eight was away from work an average of three weeks through injuries re- ceived. In connection with other industries, the London Hospital deals with as many as 36,000' accidents in one year; and at the Poplar Hospital, which is situated near the slaughtar-houses, ac- cidents were admitted at the rate of three per hour per day. In the mill-sawyers trade 397 men out of 2,900, or ten per cent.,were away from work for twenty-six weeks in one year, through acci- dents. Amongst brick-makers eight per cent., and amongst steel-workers seven per cent. were away for the same period from similar causes. Coming still nearer home, Mr. Bram says:—" On the Manchester Ship Canal there have been 130 fatal accidents, 1,300 non-fatal, and 166 men perma- nently disabled. In most cases these men were engaged by sub- contractors, who had hitherto escaped • liability ; but thanks to the clause respecting these gentry, which had been intcoduced into the Bill, that would not be the case in the future." With regard to the rail- ways, there had, in the eighteen years from 1874 to 1893, been 12,000 killed and 160,000 injured. In seven years 1,220 out of 14,000 shunters and brakesmen were killed, and 11,690 injured on all the railways, which means that eighty per cent of these workmen can look forward to being killed or severely injured in seven years. These are not the men, Mr. Burns contends, who ask for" con- tracting out." "It is the station-masters of whom one out of 1,738 is killed and one in 293 injured— not the shunters of whom in 1892 one in 164 was killed and one in sixteen injured." That there is a very distinct value to workmen in protective legislation is shown by the case of the sailors. In 1882 one out of every fifty-nine sailors was lost, but by 1889 the proportion had decreased to i one in 126. And, then, as to contracting out, the member for Battersea quoted figures to show that , on railways where the men were contracted- out, the accidents were most numerous. In fact, Mr. Burns's lecture was brimful of cogent arguments in support of "the Bill, the whole Bill, and nothing but the Bill,"and a strong indict- ment of the policy of those whose desire to , strangle or emasculate it is only too evident.
WE are now told that the Mats- The Idatabele belo war is practically at an end. War.

The regiments of native warriors have been completely broken up and demora:ised, and it is not expected that King LOBENGULA can for long avoid capture. This African chieftain is a man of huge proportions, and, when travelling, he has to be dragged about in a wagon. From the latest information it appears that a few of the king's more faithful foil( wers have yoked them- selves to the vehicle, and thus taken the place of the cattle which have been lost. Under such cir- cumstances LOBENGULA'S flight can not be a very expeditious one, and it may, one should think, be taken for granted that he will be rapidly overtaken by the pursuing party. The invasion of Matabeleland promoted by Mr. RHODES and his chartered company will then be crowned with complete success. On the whole, this latest episode in South African "develop- ment" will form a suggestive incident in the his- tory of this latter part of the nineteenth century. It is another proof of the aphorism that history repeats itself, for, it may be said to be in some of its circumstances and in its degree, a sort of squa- lid repetition of the Norman Conquest of Eng- land. Mr. RHODES fills the place of Duke WILLIAM with the added and unromantic elements of the company promoter and dividend hunter. Recruits were drawn to the standard of the Con- queror by lavish promises of loot and land, and so they were to those of Mr. RHODES. Judging by a question asked in Parliament by Mr. LABOII- CHERE, on Tuesday evening, the men, or many of them, who have composed the little army which invaded the country of the Matabale were each promised a large slice of land, fifteen mining claims, five alluvial claims, and a share in the loot. On the whole, therefore, we do not seem to show so much improvement upon the ethics of the eleventh century as might have beer. expected— at all events,in regard to the appropriation of other People's land. Of course, there are some people who say that this latest invasion has been under- taken in order to extend the benefits of civilisa- tion and Christianity. The Norman DUKE did not make any special protestations of that kind. At the same time he was under no suspicion of acting in the interests of a chartered company of specu- lators.

The chair was taken by the l'resident of the club, Mr. James Taylor, and several Warrington artistes took part in the con- cert. Mr. J. Haynes delighted the audience with his songs and character sketches, and was de- servedly encored. Mr. and Mrs. IL H. Pearson were also very successful. The other art iites Messrs. J. Suillow,J. Wood were most efficient accompan- ists, and the proceedings were brought to a close with a nigger sketch, entitled "The Black Doc- tor," in which Messrs. S. Lloyd, A. Priestner and A. , Dixon very ably took the respective parts.

WIDNES CHURCH INSTITUT& At the weekly meeting in St. Paul's Parochial Room, there was a parliamentary debate. The Government introduced a Local Veto Bill and succeeded in carrying the measure by a majority of one.

THE WIDNES DISTRESS FUND. For the benefit of the fund a match between Runcorn and Widnes Football Clubs was played on the ground of the latter on Thursday afternoon in the presence of 2,000 spectators. Neither teams were representative, but an interesting game ended in a draw neither side scoring. PAROCHIAL CHURCH CONFERENCE AT HALTON. The third annual parochial Church conference was held in the Library, Halton, on Wednesday evening, the Vicar (Rev. G. D. Wray) in the chair. There was a large attendance.—The Vicar referred to the Parish Councils Bill, and showed in which way it might affect the interests of the church as originally drawn. The following resolution was proposed by Mr. F. Latham, and seconded by Mr. W. H. Thomason : "That this church parochial conference, of the parish of Halton, Cheshire, while cordially accepting the principle of local self-government as contained in the first part of the Local Government (England and Wales) Bill, is yet ef opinion that no parish should cease to exist as a civil parish, without it own consent ; and further that clauses 5,6, 13, and 58 require amendment in the more careful definition of • affairs of the Church' ecclesias- tical charities ' and parochial charities 'and that copies of this resolution be sent to Messrs. H. H. Fowler and J. T. Brunner." This was carried unanimously. Mr. Latham then dealt with the question" How can we best extend our church's usefulness " and a discussion ensued. JOSEPH PRITCHARD, Watchmaker and Jeweller, 51, High- at., Iluncorn.—ildvt. RUNCORN SONS OF TEMPERANCE. At the fortnightly meeting of the above order, on Saturday night,a paper was read by Mr. Thomas J.Holt, on 'The opening of museums, art galleries, and read- ing rooms on Sunday." The subject was ably dealt with by the essayist. He held that so I.mg as public- houses were opened on Sunday, it would be an advan- tage to have art galleries and museums open for the public, as it would be a counter-attraction. There was also much to refine and elevate in works of art. After the paper there was an interesting discussion for and against, by the following members : Messrs. Daniel His- brown, David Smith, Edward Key, Samuel Temperley, Thomas ';oolre,and Samuel Henderson. It was held that it would be a desecration of the Sunday, and that it should be boldly resisted,as it was the first step to Sun- day shop opening, Sunday theatres, and a Continental Sunday. If they gave up the outworks, the citadel would soon fall. If they took away a man's Sabbath, his relivion would soon come to nothing. A day of rest was needed for the body.as well as for the mind. A vote of thanks was passed to Mr. Holt for his paper. 'The chair was occupied by Mr. James Johnson.

ROMAN CATHOLICS AND THE EDUCATION RATE. On Friday, in the House of Commons, Mr. Robert Pierpoint, the member for Warrington presented a petition from over 200 Roman Catholics of Et. Mary's Latchford, praying that the Education Rate be made universal,and that it be distributed in due proportion to every public elementary school whose efficiency in secular instruction shall satisfy the Education Department—proper facilities being afforded for securing the right disbursement of the money paid over from the rates, while the Catholio management of their schools shall remain intact. BY AN OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDENT.

In no town was the newi of the termination of the coal struggle received with more joy than in the Chemical centre •of Widnes. Upwards of 4,000 , persons have been thrown idle through the dispute and great privation and suffering have been experienced by many families. The relief committv formed by the Mayor has accomplished a good work at a very moderate cost,and although the strike is at an end they will have to continue their self sacrific- ing labours far at least another ten days or a fort- night. Yesterday operations were resumed at a number of the works and Mr. J. Morrison, general manager of the United Akali, Company for Widnes district, states that on Monday 75 per cent of the men will have commenced work again. In Runcorn also the termination of the strike was hailed with great satisfaction. The local industries have not suffered to the same extent as those of the sister town, but the price of coal has become almost pro- bibitive and householders have had a difficulty in keeping the fire alight. The relief committee organised by Mr. S. Taylor, is dealing ,with the existent distress.

The great event of the near tuture will be the opening of the Manchester Ship Canal. Water is being admitted into the last section of the canal cutting at the rate of about two feet per day and there will be an unbroken stretch of water from Bastham to Manchester early in December. Run- corn people hope to benefit largely from the under- taking, and that before many years are past deep water docks will replace the present lay-by. The canal has certainly been of great benefit to trades- men during its construction and now it is com- pleted, Runcorn Bridge is expected to be a formid- able and even impossible barrier to many large ships, which will, perforce have to discharge at Runcorn and have the goods transhipped to Man- chester. Local interests will thus be benefitted.

Considering the bad times the Bethesda Bazaar was a very successful affair. It was a source of general regret that Mr. Brunner, MX., could not be present, but the cause was still more regrettable. Mr. Taylor occupied his place and performed the opening ceremony in characteristic fashion and he gave an effective reply to some of the denouncers of the bazaar. Since I last wrote Mr. T. Speakman has had a relapse, but, it is pleasing to note, that he is again , progressing favourably.
DEATH AND FUNERAL OF MR. WM. HARTLAND, OF WIDNES.

At the ripe old age of 82, Mr. Wm. Hartland, one of the most respected men in Widnes, passed away on Monday. He had been ailing for several years, but was not confined to his bed until nine weeks ago. He started his career as et- young man with the firm of Messrs. W. Gossage and Sons, and he became manager of the works, a position which he retained for 40 years. He was one of the pioneers of Wesleyan Methodism in VVidnes, and for fifty years was a locni preacher, class leader, circuit steward, and held other offices. It was mainly through his exertions that Hart- land Chapel was built, and it was giveip his name in his honour. The firm of Messrs. Gossage gave a donation of £1,500 towards the cost as a token of their esteem for an old and respected servant. For five years he was a member of Widnes School Ward. His mortal remains , were committed to the grave at Widnes Parish Church, lon Thursday afternoon, amid every token of respect. The coffin was borne on the shoulders of nephews and grandsons, and in the procession, besides a large number of relatives, were the Mayor (Alderman F. H. Gossage), Rev. F. Silcox, Rev.J. Preston, Alderman H. S. Timmis, J.P., Messrs. W. W. Gossage, J.P., A. Carey, R. Cook, A. Thorp, J. Jackson, 13. Brown, D. Lewis, F. J. Poole, D. J. Brookes, T. Smith. J. Williams, S. B. Stringer, S., Robinson, A.Case, J. Williamson, H. Rushton, T.Baxter G. H. Denby, W. Clarke, J. Stead, J.Flewitt, J.Hews M. Johnson, F. Lawrinson, T. Ormryde, J. Briggs, T. Whitby, J. Whitby, A. J. Loines, J, Hough, J. B. Lee. The service in the church was con- ducted by the Revs. W. Hodgson and W. Stan- ton Jones. The Vicar delivered a brief address. That day, he said, they were laying to rest one who was highly respected in Widnes as a straightforward busi- ness man and consistent Christian, one who had let his light shine before men, and brought light across the dark waters to many poor souls. They laid him to rest in the sure hope of the resurrection of life. Yes, de- parted saints were taken to live with Christ in Paradise, in a state of perfect joy. The mourners could think of their dear departed brother as being in " Abraham's bosom." and consequently in the Lord. At the con- clusion, the hymn " For ever with the Lord " was sung, the Rev. W. Stanton Jones presiding at the organ, The solemn service at the gaveside was read by the Vicar, and was concluded by the singing "Safe in the arms of Jesus.
THE RESUMPTION OF WORK.

The news that the coal crisis had been termi- nated was greeted with unmistakable signs of re- lief in Warrington. It has been calculated that for the past ten weeks there has been more than 6.000 persons in Warrington alone, dependent for their sustenance upon the Relief Committees dispensa- ions. Tile committee's task is now, fortunately, drawing to a close, and the ladies and gentlemen of whom it has been composed may rest assured ' that their charitable labours have been genuinely and extensively appreciated by those who have received timely assistance in their distress. Of the money contributed there is at present .£667 195.4.1. in the hands of the committee. The usual relief will be granted from this sum next week, and any balance which may remain will be haneted over td the Ladies' Commi tee for special use. All of the ironworks re-commenced operations d tir- ing the early part of the week. But the employ- ment of hands has had to be regulated by the un- certain supply of coal. At Hallam and Bewsey forges sufficient coal has been obtained to enable the employment of about one half of the men. Work is now in full swing at Whitecross, Monks Hall and Co., and at Sankey Wire Mills.

CoNCERT IN AID OF THE DISTRESS FUND. The usual concert in the Co-operative Hall on Saturday evening, promoted by the B.Q. Union, was in aid of the local distress fund. Admission was free, but during the evening a collection was taken. Councillor Henry Roberts occupied the chair, and in a few introductory remarks said it was a very pleasant duty to take the chair at a concert, and that duty was made a great deal more pleasant when the object of the concert was a good one. The concert that night was for as good an object as it was possible for them to subscrib,. to. Up to the previous day a Very heavy cloud had hung for sixteen weeks over all sections of the community. Every branch of trade and commerce was suffering from the coal strike. Thanks, however, to the interventiou of a man whom he tnightdescribe perhaps without offending anybody's susceptibilities as one of the greatest states- men of the age—he referred to Mr. Gladatone— (applause)—thanks to his intervention and the able and wise counsels of Lord Rosebery.2-(applause) —the great coal capitalists on the one hand and ti.e immense army of miners on the other, as represented through their ceders, met together, and in the course of a few hours settled a dispute which had been waged for so long. (Applause.) He knew he was echoing the sentiments of every man, woman, and child there that night when by said that they were devoutly thankful that this terri- ble condition of things had come to an eno so satisfac- torily. (Applause.) In reading the report of the con- ference one could not help being struck by the fact that there had been a little concession on both sides. The most valuable result of the conference was the fact that a Conciliation Board was to be established, and that, it was hoped, would prevent for many years to come a repetition ofianything, like the coal strike. (Applause.) They were glad to know that on Monday the whole of the colliers in England, Scotland and Wales would resume work. Whether the.cause of the colliers was right or wrong one could not help admiring the courage with which they had fought the battle. (Hear, hear.) They most not overlook the fact that while the coal strike was at an end the distress consequent upon it would not end so speedily. He was afraid that during the whole of the winter the result of the strike would be felt in Warrington. Many hundreds of families who had hitherto been in receipt of good wages had, during the enforced stoppage of work, to live upon their savings, and in some cases, having no savings, they had to live upon the charity of the public. They had suffered to such an extent that it would take many months to retrieve their loss ; and lie hoped the people of Warring- ton would not allow their subscriptions to cease at once because the colliers and theScnal ()wows had ceased to struggle any longer about the question of wages. He hoped that all who were interested in the town would not allow those who were not so fortunately placed as themselves to suffer any more than could be avoided dur- ing the winter that was coining upon them. (Applause.) The programme was pleasantly varied, and passed off most successfully. The artistes were Mr. and Mrs. R. H. Pearson, Mr. Walter Woods, Mr. P:g. Bate, Mr. J. S. Haynes, and Mr. Taylor, P.C.M. " Light in the dark-- ness " by Mrs. Pearson was in every way a success, and she received an encore. A similar honour was accorded to her for her excellent rendition of the song" Children asleep." The instrumental selections by Mr. R.H, Pear- son (violin) and Mr. Walter Woods (pianoforte) were well rendered, and were received with emphatic ap- plause and recalls, The first item was " Saltarella" (German), and in the second part of the programme " Andante Religioso " (Thome) and Dance (German), Mr. P. T. Bate is a baritone of some merit, and he was loudly applauded for his singing of" To-morrow will he Friday Mr.J.S.Haynes gave a comic song,entitled"The Waiter" and was rewarded with an encore. Mr. Tay- lor, P.C.M., also received an encore for his song, "Time Schoolmaster," and in addition contributed a recitation " The Lifeboat." A vote of thanks was passed to the Chairman, on the propositien of the Rev. J. W. Varley. The following ladies had charge of the refreshment de- partment :—Mrs. Varley, Mrs. S. 11. Stringer, Miss Laverock, Mrs. Bennison, Mrs. Adams, and Miss Hunt.

THE NEW REFUSE DESTRUCTOR AT ' LONGFORD. IMPORTANT TESTS. On Thursday, two representatives from the Leeds Coi poration visited the Longford works, and made prolonged tests upon the working of the' new ref iisb destructor Which has been erected there, 'and pa- tented by Mr. Deas, the engineer, and Councillor Beaman. A oeputation from Stockport also visited theworka onTbursdaY,for a similar purpose. To-day the members of the Sanitary Inspector's Association are to send a deputation to view the destructor. Enquiries are being received from all parts of the country and further deptstations are expected. The Corporation of Leeds has always held a pro- minent place in matters appertaining to engineer- ing and sanitary development. In • common with other corporations their attention had• been drawn to the imvrovements that had been'Ootight about by Mr. Dees, at the Longford DeOyand on Thursday they deputed two well-known tid ex- perienced engineers to make an independent and - thorough test of the destructor. The object of the test was to ascertain the capabilities of the furnace in burning town refuse, and the steam producing 'power of the refuse. The 24 hours consecutive test is usually adoptea in these circumstances and it was the one that the Leeds engineers adopted on this occasion. The test began at 12 noon on Thurs- day, and was continued uninterruptedly for the ' 24 consecutive hours ill noon yesterday. Mr. Deas and Councillor Beaman were present along with the engineers during the whole time. On the comple- tion of the test it was found that the destructor had burned 23 tons, 18 cwts. of refuse, unscreened and as delivered from the town carts,in the 24 hours. The average quantity consumed per day in the destructors oh 20 of the principal towns in Eng- land is only 74 tons perilay, which is not one third of the quantity that was shown to be the daily con- sumption in Warrington. The destructor evapo- rated 1.141bs of water to every pound of refuse, and the horse power was indicated at 127. The percen- tage of clinker was 27, which is very much less than the residuum of other furnaces. The temperature of the excaping gases in the combus- tion chamber was 2,000 degrees Fah. The report will be submitted to the Leeds Corporation by the engineers in a few days. This test was not applied to the sanitary improvements in regard to the decrease of the smell which is also a feature of the destructor. The elevator which is another feature also continues to work satisfactory

----- SOCIETY OF FRTENDS.—On Sunday afternoon, at the request of Ellen Robinson, a minister of the Society of Friends, a service was held in their meeting house at Penketh. All persons who were not nonneted with any congregation were specially invited to be present. There was a good attendance.

DISTRESS FUND.—The scheme for providing work for the unemployed flatmen, &c., a hint of which was given in our last issue, luts resulted in a subscription list being opened to pay men who are now engaged in planting I trees, &c., on the Recreation Ground. This work has long wanted doing, and a more fitting occasion could not have been seized. The gentleman who has had to do I with the formulation ot thir. good scheme is Mr. .1. lington, who has also collected the subscriptions. The response tc his appeal has been most generous, the amount collected being over £2O. MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT ASSOCIATION,—The weekly meeting of the above Association was held on Wednes- day night in the Wesleyan school, Mr. G. Randles in the chair. Mr. J. Gandy, of Warrington, delivered an address on the " Labour Question." In the course of his addrees he gave a list of many grievances which the working-class held themselves to he under, and gave his ideas as to the means of lessening those grievances, lie entered upon a brief resume of the great advances the working class had aesieved in comparison with that of 50 years ago, and expressed his opinion that much of the misery and distress was caused by the drunk Illness and improvidence of a great portion of the working-men. He also thought education would do much for them. Over production and competition were also causes of much importance in the cutting down of workmen's wages. At thecouclusion of the address the members were invited to discuss the question, and the following did so Messrs. White, Peers, Houghton, Rathbun Furness, Handles, and Parker. Mr. Gaudy 4 replied and the discussion closed.

LECTURE ON HANDEL. On Wednesday evening a lecture was delivered by the Rev. Elward Moore. of Warrington, in the Friends' School, Penketh on "The life and work of Handel." By the courteous invitation of the Superintendent, Mr. Albert Pollard, 8.A., the lecture room of the school was well filled With a select audience. The musical illustra Cons were supplied by Mr. R. H. Pearson (let violin), Mr. Edward Moore (2nd violin), Mr. R. N. Foster (viola), Mr. Henry Bond (violoncello), Mrs. Varley, and Mr. W. 11. Payton (pianoforte). The vocal selections were ren- dered by Mrs. Farley and Mr. Joseph M. Bate. Mrs. I Pearson. who was Also to sing, was called away from home by the illness of a relative. Mr. Moore first gave ' a brief sketch of the early life of Handel, *hewing how ' the difficulties in the way of his musical career were I overcome, and pointing out that it was the severity and toil of his early technical studies that laid the foundation 1 of a great and honourable career. Having described his adventure respecting the organist's daughter of Lubeck. and his duel with Mattheson, Handers continental travels, and his attachment to the court of the Elector of ' Brunswick were mentioned. In connection with his life in England,the opera "Rinaldo" was alluded to,and then the famous" Largo" was played. The reconciliation of Handel to King George I was illustrated hy two pieces of the " Water Music " played by Mrs. Varley. 'I hen the lecturer indicated some of Handel's notable contemporaries, and the " Harmonious Blacksmith " was cleverly placed by Mr. W. H. Payton. This was followed by Handel's violin Sonata in A, played by Mr. Pearson. It received such an enthusiastic en- core that Mr. Pearson repeated the last movement. Then Mr. Moore dealt with Handel's brave struggle against the ignorance end prejudice of his time, remarking that Handel presented the spectacle of a clear far.seeing I mind, manfully striving against what he knew to be falqe and perishable. Handel's visit to Oxford was de. I scribed, and his further attempts to win the favour of the people by " Italian opera." " Softly sweet in Lydian measure," was sung by Mr. Bate, with violon- cello obligato by Mr. Bond., and was muchsenjored. After dealing with Handel's failures in respect to opera, Mr. Moore cause to the great branch of Oratorio with which Flanders nameis for ever associated. " Saul," and" Israel in Egypt" were bath described It was mentioned as an example of the taste of the time, that airs from the operas had to be sung between he num- bers of" Israel," td get an audience at all. A full de- scription of the " Messiah" folk-need, illustrated by "Comfort ye," by Mr. Rate ;the "Pastoral symphony," and "He was despiser," by Mrs. Farley. "Samson," "Judas Maceatieue,” and other oratorios were men- tioned. Handers, blindness was illustrated by " Total Eclipse." from Samson. which was well rendered by Mr. Bate. Several amusing anecdotes were told about pan- del's relations with his singers and orchestra. Anac• count of his death, and a brief slce'cli of his character concluded the lecture. A vote of thanks brought to a close a very enjoyable. evening..

div.head: REV. ARTHUR MURSELL AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: THE REV. ARTHUR MURSELL AT WARRINGTON.

The Rev. Arthur llursell, of London, the popular preacher and lecturer, visited Warrington on Tues- day. In the afternoon at Bold-street Schools, he preached on the subject : " A sermon from a shop window." Ile selected for his text the words "And if thou sell ought unto thy neighbour, or buyest ought out of thy neighbour's hand, ye shall not oppress one another." (Leviticus xxv. 14). In the course of his remarks he alluded to the eight hours question, and said that they should treat men as men, not as trades- men, der,ks, porters, or what not. Time should be allowed for recreation, devotion, self-culture. These were parts of life and elements of work, elements with- out which there was very little life or manhood possible. A man would be a better shoprnan if society gave him a little more time to be a man. Cabined, cribbed, con- fined, he went to his slavery and looked upon a customer as a natural prey to be fooled or robbed or duped as best he could. If he smiled, it was a sham smile' a mere muscular twitching of the face. If lie said " Good morn- ing," he did it without knowing what the morning was, and his politeness was a clause in his indentures,an item of his contract with his employer, and no sign of his good will. But some might say : We don't want his good will. When Igoto a shop Igo for ribbons, tea, or for turnips, and not sentiment." IS'ell if they went for that only, they ought to be ashamed of themselves. If a ribbon was not part of the festoon of common brother- hood it was worth its price at 1111. a yard. If the tea did not carry with it the genius of a social meal it was gooseberry and not a meal, and if the turnip did not savour of a garden, then it was a decayed and a rotten comestible. It was only as sentiment was admitted in- to all their intercourse that true social growth would thrive. They needed to learn the first principles or axioms of brotherhood. The preacher instanced Lon- don cabmen, who had to have tea every afternoon on the splashboard. Was that, he asked, the 19th century theory of the development of the race and the periecca- bility of man ? If those who discussed these questions over their turtle and port at the City Guildhall would bring faces and hearts as well as figures into their cal- culations there would be a chance of reform. He did not know what the percentage of the London tramway companies paid their shareholders by making their em- ployes work 14 hours a day, but if it was five, ten or 15 per cent., they should he content with less, and give their servants eight hours daily at a fart. wage. But greed was at the bottom of all. People dined on divi- dends and yet made their brothers take their meals on splash boards.

The Rev. A. Mursell, delivered a lecture in the evening at the Bold-street Wesleyan schoolroom upon Lord Tennyson. There was a fairattendance. and the chair was occupied by Mr. R. Garnett, J.P. The chairman in the course of a short address, said that at the present time there was too great a tendency to indulge in light litera- ture. He urged his hearers to study good books which were available. There was no doubt that if the books in the library were examined, books which were the most thumbed would not be the best books, but rather the reverse. He regretted this state of things, and hoped to see an improve- ment.—Mr. Mursell said that the poet was not born bin flamed into existence in Lincolnshire on the sth April, 1809. His first school was borne, and his first tutor was his father. He wrote " The lover's tale " in 1828, hut it was by "In Menaorian " that Tennyson attaine I the height of his fame. At tie time he wrote thin poem materialism was rampant in the land, but Tennyson rebuked the doubters with his golden lyre, and quieted the fears of many christian hearts. Tenny-on's faith syn of a very high character to judge from his poems. He was very aver-e to notoriet),and would adopt all sorts of precautions to keep himself retired from public gaze. In this respect he was the reverse of Longfellow. ! There were no doubt physical cau-,es for this, such as short sightedness, but when the stiffness was broken through, Tennyson was an excellent com- panion. The lecture was listened ts with very great attention by the audience, and a hearty vote of thanks was accorded the lecturer and chairman, on the motion of the'Rev. G. D. Mason, seconded by Mr. W. Silcock. The meeting closed with the pro- nouncing of the Benediction.

LABOURS. The weeklj• meeting of the above committee was held yesterday in the Town Dail, the Mayor (Alderman E. Greenell) in the chair. Mr. F. Monks gave the weekly statement which showed that 23,980 pints of soup had been distributed during the week against 23,640 last week • 28,553 lbs of bread against 28,502 last week ; and 1,273 lbs of sugar and ozs of tea and 1,208 jars of jim. The expenditure had been £2Ol 4s. Bd. against £lB7 ss. 23. last week. This increased expenditure was due to the additional sugar given away. The total amount of subscriptions was £2.438 7s. 4d., expenditure £1770 83.. which left a balance of £667 193. 4d. The amount received for this week from Warrington was £45 83. sd. and the amount as the result of the special appeal was £239 us. 9J. The weely subscriptions had been discontinued, Po that the total amount received this week was £284 18s. 2d. £B5O 93.3d.had been received as the result of the appeal made to outsiders, and the total local subscriptions were £1,787 18s. id. _ .

The Mayor moved that the relief be discon- tinued on Monday December 2nd—Mr. F. Monks seconded.—The Rev. E. C. E. Carleton asked if that resolution applied to the sick people.- -Mr. Monks said that those cases would be under the care of the ladies committee which would be requested to continue its labours for a little time longer.—The Rev. E. C. E. Carleton thought that the committee might go on for another week. They hal £6OO to expend. It was rather too precipitant to stop in a week. fie wouli like to see the relief stopped .gradually.—The Rev. John Yonge was of the same opinion. He thought another week should be given.—Mr. Monks said that the relief was for the men in distress from the want of cod. The men had been at work for some days. So far as his works were concerned, his men got to work on Tuesday night. Pearson and Knowles also started some part of their works on the same night. Pressure had been put upon the coal proprietors to supply a quantity of coal so that the works could be started. The men would receive wafges on Saturday by means 'if" subs" No man who was out of work now would be out of work for want of coal. He thought that the recommendation of the executive committee to terminate the relief on Saturday week would be in the interests of all. Out of tha £6OO in hand, there would be about £3OO expended next week, so that there would not be a large balance. It was not proposed that the ladies' committee should finish their work, and it was desirable that somethimg should be left for them to draw upon.—The Rev. E. C. E. Carleton said that there would still be distress iii the t wi'n and lie moved that the relief he given another week.—The Rev. J. Yonge sectreded.—The Rev. Owen Watkins said that facts came before the executive committee which warranted them In recommending that the relief should come to an end on Saturday week. He hoped that the executive com- inittee would be supPorted.—The Rev. J. Yonge said that if the executive committee were in possession of any reason for doing so, why did they not tell the com- mittee thos- reasons ? He felt very strongly disposed to divide the committee upon the question. It would be rather an unkind thing to close the relief in the way the executive committee recommended.—Mr. Monks said that the committee could not afford to keep on another week, and thought it wouid he a great mistake if the amendment were earried.—Father flennelly supported the executive committee, and the amendment was at length withdrawn and the resolution carried unani- mously. The Mayor proposed that a cwt of coal be given to each family receiving relief.--The Rev. Owen Watkins seconded.—Mr. F. Monks said that the executive coin- mittee had already given the coal away to be in time for the week end. He hoped the general consinittee would agree to it.—The resolution was carried unanimously. The Mayor propesed that £2O be given to the Warring ton Charity Organization Society cm account of the extraordinary demand upon the fund of the society during the coal di4 ute.—Ttie Rev. E. C. E. Carleton seconded and spoke in eulogistic terms of the society and of Mrs. Ellison the secretary.—The resolution was carried. Mr. Monks said net M.-Executive Committee contem- plated publishing a report or the work of the Relief Corn- inittee and sending a copy to the subscribers whe had ! fio generously contribbted to the funds. This concluded the business of the melting.

div.head: MYSTERIOUS DEATH OF A BOLD FAME IL
div.p: MYSTERIOUS DEATH OF A BOLD FAME IL

-- Yesterday afternoon Mr. S. Brighouse held an inquest at the Clock Face Inn, Clock lace, near St. Helens, on the body of Thomas Whitfield, farmer, of Union Bank Farm, Warrington-road, Bold, who died suddenly on Tuesday last. Superintendent Keigh- ley watched the proceedings on behalf of the police. —Mary Ann Whitfield, the widow, said the deceased was 62 years of age. Ile went to bed at eight o'clock on Monday night in good ,health. Nobody PI ep t. with him. Next mozning at eight o'clock, she found her nDsiband lying in bed with his eyes shut, but alive. Between ten and eleven she was in the kitchen, when she heard a noise in the bedroom awl going there, found her husband lying across the led in an no- conseious state. She sent a neighbour for Dr. O'Neil. of Farnwort h. The doctor, on arriving, at 11-20, ordered a mustard plaster to be placed on her Mishand's neck and hot oven shelves were placed to his feet. At one o'clock he died. Dr. O'Neil refused to give a death certificate.—The Coroner : About three years ago did ' your hus- band receive some wounds on his head and go t 9 Dr. O'Neil's; to have them dressed?— Witness : , Yes, he did receive some wounds. We had had some words.—The Coroner: Wait a mo- ment. After consultation with Superintendent Keigbley and Dr. O'Neil, the Coroner said, " I don't think we ought to ask you anything further now. You had better sign your name to what you have already Paid."—The witness did so, and the --Coroner said that there were ru- mours in the district that the wounds had been caused by Mrs. Whitfield. lle, would not suggest that these wounds had caused death, and the doc- tor would not he able to give a decision without making a post mortAn examination, and he therefore authorised him to make one. The inquest was ad- journed until Tuesday next.

TIIR RRCRNT. GALE. Very little damage was done in Warrington and its neighbourhood, by the violent gale which swept over the country during Saturday and Sunday. Slates were blown off various houses, and the gable ends of number of buildings were damaged. In the suburbs slight danrige was done to 'various plantations.
DR. GUEST GORNALL ON SANITATION.

, AN INTERESTING PAPER. : The second meeting of the Warrington Literary and Philosophical Society for the session 1893-4 was held in the Museum lecture room, on Monday evening, the chair being occupied by the Rev. L. J. T. Darwall. president. There was an average attendance of members and friends. The Rev. W. if. Drummond, 8.A.,801d-st.,Mr. T. E. Gib- son, Museum-street, and Mr. W. E. Atkin, Bold- street, wore elected members of the society, (luring. ' the evening. The paper for the evening was one upon Sanitation given by Dr. Guest Gornall, M.A.,, M.B. (Cantab.) After a few introductory remarks by the Chairman; . Dr. J. GUEST GOIINALL, proceeded to read his paper on "Sanitation, ancient and moderp." He observed that down to the etid of the Stuarttimes the sanitary interests of the cemrnunity rested upon a basis of knowledge that, was the common property of the doctors and the laity. Though medicine as a science could nct be timid with truth to have existed before the present century,its beginnings were to be recognised in the Changes of the 17th, when the new spirit or inquiry and of close ob- 'servation of natural phenomena was productive of such men as Harvey, their first great physiologist, and of Sydenham, the father of modera physic, whose teach- hogs set his successors on the'road'to a snore exact study, of the symptoms and treatment of diseases. They could not follow the conrse 'of the new and start- ling increase of knowledge in all directions, but confine , themselves to the subject of disease prevention, in which, it became increasingly evident during the 18th centetry that the medical profession -coeld be of !immense service to mankind. ' It was a . remarkable fact, and one to be ' proud of, that British practitioners then took the lead of the world in that great work, but it would be a matter of equal regret if the restrictions upon investigation _which now obtained, enabled; as they seemed to ,'be doing, their Continental neighbburs to gain all the'gleiry of modern improvements both in knowledge , and 'in erne, „ -e practice. The misguided persons who objected to ere' experimentation on animals were indeed blind to the ' experiments which nature herself was hourly performing on human beings. The iBth century was productive of many works of immense value to mankind, but perhaps none greater than those associated with the names of the men who deservedly ranked as the fathers of British . _ ..ce ge, sanitation. To these Dr. Gerrie!l referred, as well as to the Mee for the past four ,the new philanthropy; to the rise of humenity in British other ' ' • 4itics. It would take too long to discuss the origin of to 1: a momentous change in the whole idea of principles of I6c overnment that I ad been productive of modem sanita- ton. It might be tee .t the factors that had been chiefly' Credited with the transformation, religious in the early part, political in the latter pare of the 18th century, represented but concomitant features in the evolution of the race, but the fact remained that during that period a I previously unknewn activity was manifested in measures for the material benefit of mankind, in erecting hospitals and refuges for various classes of destitute and afflicted persons, and efforts for reforming and reclaiming the ivicious and criminal, and for educating children of the poor began to be put forth on an unwonted scale. It *Mild be tedious to follow in detail the long struggle by which sanitariens gained their ends—a struggle against, opposing interests, pecuniary and sentimental, backed up by the economic doctrine of unlimited competition: that discouraged any intervention in industrial, concerns. The reign of her Majesty opened without any law of direct sanitary intention upon the Statute Book, ' except the old useless Quarantine Act, though the Poor Law of 1834 was des; tined to have important consequences: 'lt was on the initiative, and largely under the direction of the late Sir Edwin Chadwick, secretary of the first Poor Lave Commission, that inquiries into the sanitary conditiore of the people were held about 1839-40 and subsequent years. The conclusions then arrived at, and the recom- mendations made therewith, were powerful in shaping the policy of subsequent administrations. One of time results of greatest importance was the establishment of the Central Board of Health in 1848, the powers of which transferred in 1858 to the Privy Council were vested in the Local Government Board in 1872. They need not follow the fortunes of theseearlier experinlents in State medicine, record the difficulties in face of which they were carriecLand the errors of judgement that well. nigh proved fatal to a policy so beneficial in Its ulti- mate results. The chief" bone of centention "of those early days was the still present, perhaps insoluble ques- tion of centralization or decentralization of authority. It was a matter of history that the centralization policy pursued at first,retarded greatly the progress of sanitary improvement. The Government once proposed to man- age the cemeteriee themselves, and to engage in the general business of an undertaker. It was true that at that date the education or disinterestedness of local authorities were not such as made them eminently cap- able of responsibility in sanitary matters, and many People conscious of the enormous evils to be•rectified sighed after a beneficent despotism. But the prevalent feeling against centralization was undoubted, and even yet. At a well-known st4tesman amid the other day, . We prefer to misgovern ourselves a little to being better I governed by other people." The disastrous cholera epi- demics were powerful in arousing public interest in ' hygienic Measures. The enormous Mortality they ten- sioned and the fear they Inspired did much to arouse the attention of the more influential classes to matters need- in-, reform, while the labours of such men as Kingsley did much to drive home the lesson% that the more favoured had same responsibility for the physical well- being of the poor. The results in the way of organiza- tion they all knew. One of the latest changes, the es- tablishment of County Councils, bade fair by the influ- ence of moral suasion, often more powerful °than com- pulsion, to keep many of their sanitary authori- ties up to the mink. At every stage there had been compromise between what ought to be or might be, and what had been at the moment possible, and in compromise was the very stability of English Institutions. Progress was slow, nor even were all' that satntarians aimed at accomplished, were those who would receive the boon capable of benefiting by it. But let them look at some actual achievements. Allowing both for commercial proeperty and educational advance san:tation itself was to be credited with striking results Mr. Gornall compared the death rates per 1,000 of three successive periods of ten years in proof of the assertion, and in concluding an interesting and able paper he said the Public Health Act of 1872, subsequently amplified in 1875. first inaugurated the present general system of health authorities with their medical officers, and payed the way for other beneficel measures, such as the Com- pulsory notification of disease. Year by year since then the decline in the death rate had peen gradual and con- tinuous. Let them look forward a little. Some present, must in their own experience have seen striking changes In Warrington, must have seen the old open drains dis- appear, and what was once a town so fever-stricken as to form the subject of a Government enquiry became comparatively healthy. But that much remained to I 3 done was evident to every one. The science of, the cause and prevention of diseases was being added to every day. Let them hope that local patriotism would not lag behind in its eagerness to apply improved methods. ' Let them, too, hope that in the future men of business ability and leisure weuld not be deterred by the spread of democracy from taking their due share in local ad- ministration, due because they shared in its benefits. (Applause.) A discussion upon the paper followed. After which a hearty vote of thanks was passed to the lecturer.

THINGS BEARD AND SOW , t t 4. AT WATVIIINGTON...:-- . , 1,, "Shop Door Theft." Thie has now become a very familiar heading in connection with the police re- ports, and to all appearance% these shop door thefts are increasing at an alarming rate. A case of this description heard at the Borough Court on Satur- day furnished an opportunity to the magistrates and their clerk to make some timely remarks. The clerk had been noticing the kind of hooks in use-at 'present by tradesmen to hang their goods outside, eind remarked that it was a very easy matter for a ~in mon to filch articles without being detected, and e suggested that the "fish hook" head should be +Used. The presiding magistrate (Alderman Burgess), however, was stronger on the point, and considered that the time had come when parties exhibiting ' goods in such a way as to be a temptation to needy or dishonest people should tit punibhed. Id -- -Vithout in any way wishing to excuse the mak practises of these shop door pilferers, I think the magistratea and the police are fairly entitled to ask ' tradesmen to take all reasonable precautions against these petty larcenies. Whether the "fish hook" proposal of the magistrates' clerk would be feasible and effective or not, I, of course, do not venture an opinion.

• A very successful meeting in aid of Foreign mis- sions was held at the Bewsey-road Chapel on Mon- day night, both in regard to the numbers present and financially. The financial success is rather surprising considering the bad times that Warring- ton has gone through lately, and the amount of ! subscriptions which have been required by, and re- ceived by, the relief committee. In spite of this 1 the collection at Bewsey-road this year has amounted to more than last year. This, taken in conjunction with the almost equally satisfactory result of the foreign missionary services at Wycliffe Church, proves that the interest in foreign missions has not decreased, but 18 as great as ever it was. ,The collection also proves, I think, that when people once get into the habit of giving as has been - mouths it becomes like
Jr habits ; they get used to giving, anti perhaps, like it.

The police appear to be often the subject of mis- take on the part of the pugilistic portion of the community, to judge from the remarks oi the Chief Constable, on Monday, at the Police Court. The occasion of his remarks was the cots.) of 'a ma *ho was brought up for bringing hi a fist in violen4on- tact with P.C. Turner's nose. The man as an eikuse ' said that it was not Turner's nose that he wished to " punch," but another man's, and that he hit, the nose of the man in blue in mistake for the other man's nasai organ. The Chief Constable said that very often constables were struck in mistake for some one else, and that if the persons apologised they were allowed to go. It seems to me, however, a strange thing that a man cannot distinguieb be- tween the policeman with his distinctive at and buttons, and a civilian. There is; perhaps. another explanation for some of these " Mistakes," which the genial and forgNving "Chief" overlooked: It may be sometimes tho tight that when the" bobby" is busily engaged, with some one else that that is a favourable opportunity of having "a go" at him, and of course it As quite ' accidental?'

A correspondent writes :—I witnessed a very curious scene, on Wednesday morning. It occurred in the fish market. My attention was attracted by seeing a large crowd of people surrounding a person who, from the pattern of his clothes,and his fashion of wearing them, was evidently from the country. It was quite evident, however, that these charac- teristics were not the attraction ; the tact was the fellow was copiously and bitterly crying. I,was just in time to hear one-of the bystanders, ask " Why, what's the matter old chap ?" But th,e,only answer was another outburst of tears. SOine one else tried, and was only succe +slut in elinfOng afresh outburst of mingled tears and sobs. Presently a stout woman with a market ba,ket in one hand and a stick of celery in the other,snothingly queried " Billy, what's the matter, lad." And then the ruins of the following confession were picked out from a chaos of sobs and tears " her." Everybody started in and asked if it was hit here he had lost, to which general question he answered " Naw its me gurl." A great many people jeered the poor fellow at this public demonstration of an I unusual weakness, and several factory girls endea- voured to build up a joke upon the affair by approaching the man and asking" Well. won't I do instead ?'' But the flow of his grief did not abate. How long this simple son of the soil would have gone on weoping it is hard to say, had not a personal friend of his made a timely arrival, and after gath- ering that" Mary had gone whoam with another fellow," conveyed the jilted one to a neighbouring house of refreshment. I gathered that when he emerged some two hours later he was indulging in fugitive flights of eloquence upon the fickleness of woman—as well as fugitive flights about the Street

I am told that not a few Warrington tradesmen are disposed to endorse the protest—or is it a la- ment ?—of a Liverpool tradesman which as ap- peared in a daily contemporary. This tradesman seems to have serious apprehensions as to the bazaar season which is now upon us, for he safe: —" To many of our tradesmen the bazaar season is nothing less than a 'reign of terror.' Not only is the tradesman expected to contribute goods or cash to the bazaar at his own place of worship, but to every one in his neighbourhood, no matter how he differs from the promoters in doctrine. No sooner is a date fixed for a bazaar than the unfortunate tradesman is bored to death for • something for our bazaar.' It would astonish sone of your readers to see the number of applications that some tradesmen re- ceive in the course of a week. lam of opinion that few tradesmen think they get their religion at a cheap rate, ' without money and without price.'" Ile will not admit the argument that a trades- man need not give unless he likes, for, he says, cus- tomers must not be lost in these days of severe com- petition. There is no doubt a good deal of truth in what this tradesman says. But, for my part, Ido not see any remedy—unless, of course, tradesnien follow the modern fashion and combine amongst themselves to form a protective association—an " Anti-Bazaar League" or a " Nothing-for-Nothing Federation."

A new pastor has at length been chosen to fill the ministerial vacancy at Hill Cliffe Baptist Chapel, caused by the lamented death of Rev. S. Kenworthy. The Rev. J. S. Hughes, formerly of Bacup, was welcomed with much enthusiasm by a meeting ot the congregation on Thursday evening, and much active work is expected of him in his new sphere of labour. Ile is n native of Cefm, Wales, and is a capital speaker. In coming to Hill Cliff, Mr. Hughes has connected himself with one of the oldest landmarks in the history of the sect. The present chapel itself was erected in the year 1688, and the first notable Baptist of Hill Cliffs was Roger Holland, who was burned at the stake by Bonner as an infidel. The first minister was Thomas Howe who died in 1695. A few years after this, 90 history claims, the little chapel on the hill Intro- duced the tenets of its creed into Liverpool, where they were planted for the first time. Several very notable ministers afterwards made the C'Thoel the centre of their labours, and indeed Mr. Hughes hay the satisfaction of knowing that upon him has fallen tile mantle of such men as John McGowan, the author of the "Dialogue of Devils," and several other notable preachers.

It certainly can- not be-to the credit of a town like Warrington with a population of over 52,000. that within its borders, there does not exist a hall for this purpose capable of holding a thousand persons. div.head: COMMON LOT.
div.p: THE COMMON LOT.

However differently situated as rcgards social posi- tion, or separated as regaids location, it is the common lot of all sorts and conditions of mvn to be liable to various ailments and diseases. All men under these circumstances are, to a certain extent;—placed on the saute footing. "A fellow-feeling makes us wondrous kind," and nothing interests a sick man more than to hear the experience of others who have suffered from the same complaint as himself. Now, though the names of vari- ous forms of disease are legion, in this country people are subject, more or less, to one of the following form of ailment. 1. Disease of the Digestive organs, such as Indigestion, Ylatul.nce, Headaches, Dyspepsia, Heartburn,

Drowsiness, Palpitation, &c. _ _ 2. Diseases of Liver, such as Billiousness, Jaundice, Depressed Spirits, Impure Blood, Melancholy, &c. 3. Nervous Diseases, such as Fainting Fits, Neuralgia, Despondency, Nervousness, Nerve Pains, General Weakness, &c. 4. Diseases ot the Respiratory Organs, such as Com- mon Colds, Asthma, Bronchitis, Spitting of Blood, Shortness of Breath, &c. Strictly speaking, all these ailments have a common origin.
