div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES,
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES,

TRAVELLING WITHOUT A RAILWAY TICKET. William Pigot, an ironworker, was charged at the Borough Court, on Tuesday, with travelling on the L. and N.-W. Railway from Crewe to Warrington without paying the fare, and further charged with obstructing a ticket collector named Williams in the execution of his duty. Mr. Williams, ticket collector, said about 5.20 on Monday night, on the arrival of the Crewe train, he asked the defendant for his ticket, but he would not pro- duce one, and went on his way outside. He (witness) followed him, and brought him back. The defehdant then said he had been on the platform to see some friends off, but he could not produce a platform ticket. He then ran up Parker-street, but was caught. When brought back he offered to pay the fare from Crewe,and said he had fallen asleep in the carriage. Another rail- way employe deposed that the defendant at first dis- tinctly denied coming by train, and refused to pay any fare, or give up a platform ticket, and attempted to get away. He was under the influence of drink. Detective Ede also gave evidence. Defendant was fined 103. including Costa. HITTING THE WRONG PERSON. Patrick Hannon, 60, John-street, was charged at the Warrington Borough Court on Monday, with assaulting P.C. Turner in Winwick-street on Saturday night, and also with doing wilful damage to a cell to the extent of 12s. 6d., the previous evening.—Mr. Browne defended. —P.C. Turner said that there was a disturbance outside a fried fish shop on Saturday night, and on his going there, the prisoner without any provocation, struck witness on the nose, making it bleed.—P.C. Baxendale said that when prisoner was brought to the police- station, he was put into a new cell, and during the night he broke a water closet, and also a ventilator.—Mr. Browne said that P.C. Turner's brother had had a dis- pute with another man on Saturday night, and prisoner who was a friend of his, intended to strike the man, but in mistake struck the constable. He did not deny doing the damage in the cells.—The Chief Constable said that very often constables were struck in mistake, but if they apologised they were let off. There was, however, no excuse for the damage done to the cell.—The magistrates fined prisoner 15s. including COM. THEFT FROM THE FOOTBALL PAVILION. At the Warrington Borough Court on Saturday, Jos. Doherty, and John Bartlett, were brought up on remand charged with breaking and entering the shop of John Birchall, and stealing three pairs of clogs value 8?. 6d., and were further charged with entering the pavilion of the Warrington Football Club, and stealing therefrom a football jersey, and one pair of pants. Prisoners pleaded guilty to both charges. Evidence against the prisoners in reference to the first theft was given on the previous Wednesday, and was reported in our last issue. The Chief Constable repeated the evidence, and said, that, after stealing the clogs, the prisoners went to the football pavilion, in Wilderspool-road, and entered it. They took one jersey and a pair of pants. The pavilion was seen safe by Thomas Barnes, on Saturday night, but he found it open on Monday morning. It was as- certained that the prisoners had sold the stolen articles at a second-hand clothes shop, for 10d. They pleaded guilty when charged, and said they broke the windows with stones, to get in. The tnagistratescommitted each prisomer to jail far one month on the first charge, and one month on the second charge, to run consecutively. SHOP DOOR TEMPTATIONS. • • •

-- On Saturday at the Borough Court, a ship canal labourer, living at 38, Leicester-st., was charged with stealing from the shop door of Messrs. Wainwright, 4, Buttermark,t-st„ the previous day, one pair of men's boots, value 7s. 6d. The prisoner pleaded guilty. The statement of the Chief Constable showed that the pair of boots stolen were hanging outside the shop tat Messrs. Wainwright's. At 520, the prisoner went into Morton's pawnshop, and offered for pledge a pair of boots, stating that he had bought them at the " Clock " for Si. 10d. As the price 74. 6d. was marked on the boots, a consta- ble was sent for, and the prisoner was locked up. From inquiries made by Inspector Spinks, and P. C. Loxham, it was found that the boots had been stolen from Messrs Wainwright's shop aoor, but the boots had not been missed until the police had brought them to the shop. Inspector Spinks gave the man a good character, and said the man's wife and family were in a destitute con- dition. The Clerk (Mr. White) said he was noticing the hooks on which the boots were hung,and the boots could be very easily taken. The hooks required to have a catch similar to a fish hook. The chairman (Mr. Bur- gess) said that time had quite come when parties exhibi- ting goods in such a way as to be a temptation,should be punished for so doing. The prisoner would be dis- charged with a conviction recorded against him.

div.head: MIN olt CASES.
div.p: MIN olt CASES.
WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT.
SAIIIRDAY.—Before Mr. John Burgess (in the chair), and
Mr. L. Voise—x.

„. DRIJNX:AND DISORDRRLY.—Mary Ann Ryan, whose husband is undergoing two months imprisonment for assaulting her, was charged with being drunk and dis- orderly in Bridge-st., the previous afternoon. P.C. Loxham proved the case. She was discharged on the understanding that she went into Father Nugent's home.
MONDAY. —Before Mr. F. Monica (chairman) Alderman Harrison, Councillor Roberts, Mr. T. Bircball, Mr. S. Wright, Mr. J. W. Hayward. MAILING lila Crimcg...—Mark Burke, 4. Pye's Yard,was

. „ charged with stealing from the shop of Edgar V. Morton, Winwicit-street, on :Saturday evening, a man's tweed trousers valued 7s. ed. Defendant pleaded guilty. The evidence showed. that a woman named Chesters saw . .

-.---__ _ prisoner walking in front of Morton's shop on Saturday night in a suspicious manner. After a short time he went into the doorway and deliberately had his pick of several trousers and then took one and made off along Foundry-street. The woman gave the alarm, and the prisoner was caught immediately :ifterwards and taken to the police station. The magistrates committed prisoner to gaol for one month. AssAutr ON A WIFE.---Joseph Daviue was bound over for six months for assaulting his wife in Brick-street on Saturday night. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—Janies Edmund, 17, Tur- ner-street ; Edward Griffin, Morris Yard ; Mary Burns, 13, Old-road ;were each fined for this offence. CHIMNEY ON Prim—Charles wainwright, 151, Mersey- street was fined ls. for this offence. BLOCKING THE STREET.—Patrick Burke, 3, Naylor-st. was fined 55., for allowing his cart to remain longer than necessary in Winwick-street on the llth jut. UNJUST SCALES—Jonathan Broadhurst, 57, Bostock- st.' Bernard Percival, 36, Aikin-street, and Philip Woods 3, Collin-street, were each fined for contravention of the Weights and Measures Act. Trespay.—Before Mr. R. Garnett (chairman), and Mr. E. J. Guest.

_ Farm LABOURERS IN TROUBLE.—James Maguire, and Patrick Riley were charged with stealing from the shop of Catherine Gibbons, 65, Mersey-St., a man's cord vest value as. 6cl.—Mr. Hunt (chief constable) stated that tha prisoners were farm labourers, and came from Lymm, the previous day. The two went into Mrs. Gibbons' shop to buy a vest, but they said they were toa dear for them, and after the prisrmers had left the shop, Mrs. Gibbons missed a vest. Information was given to the police, and P.C. Bell SAW the two men standing near Mersey-st., a new vest being worn by Maguire. They

.• A DESERTER.—Andrew Noon, Golborne, was charged with being a deserter from the Ist Battalion Lancashire Fusiliers, on the 15th November. P.C. Simpson appre- hended the prisoner at his mother's house that morning. Prisoner pleaded guilty, and was reoanded to Strange. ways Gaol to await an escort. THEFT FROM A RAILWAY STATION.—Harry Riley, who had been apprehended the previous day on coming out of jail after undergoing 12 months' imprisonment, was charged with having sometime between the 3rd and 4th November, 1892, feloniously stolen a silver lever watch, silver chain and pendant from a van lying at the New- ton-le-Willows railway station, the property of James , Coop. The complainant stated that the van was deli- vered to the railway company on the 3rd November, 1892, and it was left in their charge. The following morning he went to the station to see if the van had gone to Darwen, and found a railway employe loading the same, and perceived that the van padlock had been taken and the bolt shined. He complained to the station master, and on examining the van he found the ' watch, chain,and pendant missing.—The station master corroborated as to the van being left in his charge, and seeing it off to Darwen.—Charles Henry Flopwood,pawn- broker's assistant to Mr. Makin, Bolton, stated that on the 11th November, 1892, a man came into the shop about 1-30, and offered in pledge a silver albert and silver medal. He gave him 35., and the man gave the name of Harry Riley.—P.C.Green deposed to apprehend- ing the prisoner, and on searching him he found the watch produced, and a pawn ticket relating to the pledging of the silver albert. He charged him with breaking in a van about the 14th November, 1892, and stealing the articles named value £2, the property of Thomas Coop. Prisoner replied "1 am very sorry for having done it. I was out of work at the time,and went to look for some money at the van, but not finding any, took those things."Prisonerasked to be treated leniently. He was remanded to the Liverpool Quarter Sessions.
LYMM PETTY SESSIONS. FRIDAY.7Before Mr. T. P. Norris (chairman), Messrs.
C. Lister, W. Lone, and Dr.' Brabazon..

DRONE AND DISORDERLY. John Flynn, labourer, Lymm, appeared in court drunk to answer a charge of being drunk at Lymm, on the 13th October. He was sent to gaol for seven days without the option of a fine, Mr. Lister strongly commenting on the defendant's con- duct,—Joseph IVinstanley and John Robert Wilson were dismissed on a charge of being drunk and disorderly at Lyrnm on the 11th inst. CHARGE OF TRESPASSING.—A COMPRONISE.—Thomas Middleton, a gamekeeper, was charged with having on the 30th October trespassed on certain land in the occu- pation of Thomas Hulme, the elder. Mr. Fletcher so- licitor, appeared for the prosecution, and Mr. Hawkins, solicitor, for the defence. Mr. Fletcher stated that Col. Legh was the owner of land on which the alleged tres- pass was supposed to have taken place. The land in question was bounded by a road called Dobelane, or Green-lane, and was the boundary line be- tween High Legh and Mere. On Monday the 30th Ootober, a keeper named Waight who was in charge of Colonel Legh's land, heard shots, and on going to )ob-lane he saw a dog of the defendant's was working in Mr. Hulmes fences, and soon afterwards a pheasant was seen to arise from his land, and whilst standing in Dob's-lane, near Mr. Hulme's fences, the defendant was seen to shoot it, and the dog afterwards went for it.and took it to the defendant. Mr. Fletcher contended that the defendant was trespassing in-as-much as the defen- dant shot the pheasant on that half of the road abutting Colonel Legh's land. The defendant was keeper of the land on the opposite side of the road. Evidence in sup- port of Mr PI eteher's statement was given by Walter Waight, gamekeeper, Mr. Tunstall of High Legh, Mr. Hawkins for the defence contended that the road was included in the estate opposite Col. Legh's on which the defendant was game-keeper, and that it was marked an the ordnance maps as such, and was repaired by them The two solicitors after a consultation, decided to withdraw the case on the read deing made a buffer one. and not to belong to either party.

div.p: were apprehended, and Mrs. Gibbons identified the vest 1 as her property.—Mrs. Gibbons and P.C. Bell g-ive cor- roborative evidence.—Maguire was fined 10s. and costs, and Riley was discharged. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—For this offence in Rose Yard, Joseph Ellison was fined and Thomas Brown f. r the same offence in Doltnan's-lane. was _fined ss. and costs.

div.head: WEDNESDAY.—Before Messrs. J. Fairclough (chairman),
div.p: WEDNESDAY.—Before Messrs. J. Fairclough (chairman),

J. Geddes and J. H. Fleming. A CAB HawEa IN TROUBLE.—Martin Gordon, a cab driver,was charged with stealing from the Norton Arms, Latchford, on Monday, a carriage rug, value 103., the property of Thos. Percival, farmer, Moss Side. Cheshire. The prisoner had been a cab driver for a short time for Mr. Connor, but had been discharged. On Monday a sale was going on at the Norton Arms, to which, Mr. Percival came with his horse and trap. He left his rug strapped to the trap but when the sale was over, he missed it, and the matter was reported to the police. Prisoner had been seen about the yard of the Norton Arms during the afternoon, and the next morning, Detective Monaghan discovered that a man answering the description of prisoner had been offering a rug for sale at a posting establishment. During the afternoon prisoner was met by Monaghan who took him into cus- tody and after a little demur, he said that he had bought the rug for a man on Warrington bridge for Is. The rug was afterwards found in prisoner '8 house. Prisoner was committed for seven days' hard labour. FRlDAY.—Before Mr. j. White (chairman), Aldermen Harrison and Wright, and Messrs. W. Pierpoint and J. W. Hayward. DanNa am) DISORDERLY..--JOhil Shields, Dial-street, who made his 44th appearance, was dismissed with a caution for this offence. BREACH OF THE noway ACT.—John and Joseph Wilkinson, fustian cutters,Longford-street,were charged that on the 1711 October, they employed a female named Louisa Lonan over seven work days without having a certificate from the doctor of her fitness to work—Mr. C. W. Shaw, H. M. Inspector of Factories, said that the defendants were summoned because they had not pro- cured a certificate from a surgeon. The surgeon in War- rington was Dr. White, whom they were required to send for, to get a certificate within seven days alter the engagement of a girl.—The defendant said that it was quite an oversight that a certificate had not been pro- cured. Dr. White usually came in the afternoon, but when the girl with four others should have been examined he was on his holidays and his assistant came in the morning when the girl was at school, and the matter was forgotten. He bad since obtained the neces- sary certificate—The magistrates fined defendants ss. and costs. CRUELTY TO A lloasz.—Thomas Bates, Longford- se reel, was charged with working a horse while in an unfit state on November the 11th and James Wilkin- son, was charged with causing it to be so worked—ln- bpector Luff, it.S.P.C.A, said that on November llth, he was in Winwick-street and saw Bates driving a mare attached to a cart containing aerated water. The mare was very lame, and on examining it he found that it was suffering from strained tendons and its leg was very hot and swollen. Bates took the horse home and witness discovered that Wilkinson was present when the mare was taken out—P.C. Jones corroborated, but Wilkinson assented that it was quite fit when it was taken cat.— The case against Bates was dismissed,but Wilkinson was fined 103. and costs.
RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS. Moxpe Y. —Before Mr. James Reynolds, and Mr. Alfred
Thomas.

STREET OBSTRUCTION. red -e-rick Wakefield and John Watson, youths, were summoned for obstructing the footpath in Heath-road on Sunday the 12th inst. Ordered to pay the costs. DISMISSED.—Joseph Jones, Penketh-lane, was sum- moned for a-saulting Emily Skidmore,of the same place. A row commenced on Wednesday about the complain- ant's clothes line, and it was alleged defendant struck at her but missed her. Tho case was dismissed. BREACH OF THE PEACE—Harry Lydrake, a young man was summoned for co:nmitting a breach of the peace by fighting, and he was ordered to pay the costs 7s. ed. ASSAULT ON THE POLICE.—Hiram Richards, a middle aged man,was charged with being drunk and disorderly Mill-st., on the 17th inst., and with also assaulting P.C.'s Beckett and Davies. At half-past eleven the prisoner and a woman were quarrelling, and as they would not desist they were apprehended. The prisoner became very violent. He threw Beclott to the ground, and kicked him, and when Davies came to the aid of his comrade he also kicked him. He was brought to the police station after a severe struggle.—The prisoner was fined in aotal of 255. or in default twenty-one days' hard labour. _ . .
AN UNFOELTUNATE.—AIice Flampson, an unfortunate, was sentenced to a month's hard labour in default of not paying a fine of 40s. far being guilty of disorderly con- duct.
WARRINGTON OCCASIONAL COURT. WEDNESDAY. —Before Mr. James Tinsley.

V4OIIANCY.—A young' man named John Slater, of nm settled A bode, wascharr,ed with begging.—Defendant, who had been previously convicted 21 times for various offences, was sent to gaol for seven days with hard labour.

Tuarrs OF TlMBER.—Bridget Cunningham, Nelgon-st., was charged with Stealing a log Of timber from Golding Davies' works. valued at Is. P.C. McGuinnis deposed that he met di fondant coming from the works in ques- tion carrying the timber produced. Defendant said she had no coal to make a tire. Lawrinson, foreman joiner at the works, said the manager did not want to press the case. Fined Zs. 6d.—Two other women, named Johannah Quinn, Peel-et.. and Mary Mahan, Water-st., were also chatged with steating a quantity of timber from Hutchinson's works, and valued at Ed. Defendants pleaded guilty, Alderman Timmis said the Bench sym- pathized with at( in in their distress, but they should not leave the paT hs of rectitude. As there were so many complaints about stealing, a fine of 2.5. 6d. would be inflicted.

Thomas Stone, 18, Dennett-street, was charged at the Warrington Borough Court on Monday, with being drunk and disorderly in Bennett-street, on the 11th inst. This case had been remanded from the preceding Mon- day, owing to charges of illusage against the police, which necessitated defendant's removal to the Infirmary. Mr. A. Browne defended. P.C. Turner said that about 11.35 on the 11th inst. he was on duty in company with P.C. Newey in Winwick-st., when they heard a disturb- ance going on in Dennott-street. They went there and saw a crowd of people. Mrs. Stone, the wife of defend- ant at once came to them and complained of her husband ill-using her. While they were in the street, the defend- ant came rushing out of the house with his coat and vest off, and threatened to kill witness. Witness told him to go into the house. He commenced showing his fists, however, and struck witness on the side of the head. Witness then took him in custody but he pulled him into the house. When in the house he caught witness by the throat and they both fell clown to the ground. P.C. Newey now came to witness's assistance and after a struggle, during which Mrs. Stone kicked her husband, they dragged defendant out of the house, and then put the snaps on him. When in Dallam-lane, he promised to go along quietly and said that he had had too much whiskey. He begged that the snaps should be taken off, and hoped that there would be no charge of assault brought against him. The snaps were thereupon taken off, and he walked quietly to the police-station. He made no complaint of ill-usage at the police-station.— P.C. Newey corroborated the last witness's statement.— In cross-examination, both officers denied that they either jumped on defendant or struck him. They only dragged him to the door of his house.—lnspector Spinks said that on Sunday, the day following the disturbance, the defendant was bailed out, and made no complaint at the time. On the following morning, witness heard that defendant was in the Infirmary.—Mrs. Blackburne also corroborated the officer's statement.—ln cross-examina- tion witness said that defendant was "about half and half drunk."—Mr. Browne contended that the charge of being drunk and disorderly fell to the ground even from Mrs. Blackburne's evidence. He was perfectly able to take care of himself. He would call three witnesses who saw P.C. Newey jump upon defendant and also kneel upon his side.—Edward Dower denied that Stone ever came into the street, before lie was brought out by the officers, or that he assaulted the officers at all, but he saw P.C. Turner strike defendant in the chest, when defendant was trying to push him oet of the house.-- Kate Dower gave similar evidence.—Ann Stone, defend- ant's wife, said that her husband came into the house on the 11th inst., and because his supper was not ready he knocked the table over. Witness thereupon called him a•' drunken brute," and he then knocked her out into the street. Her screams brought the officers on the scene. They came to the house and her husband asked whether any of his family had sent far them They replied that no one had, and he then told them that "outside was the place for them," and attempted to push them out. Turner, however, struck him, and the officer came into the parlour where Stone was knocked to the ground and Newey commenced jumping on him while Turner put the hand cuffs upon him. They then ' dragged him into the street, and took him to the police- station.—ln cross-examination by Mr. Hunt, she raid that there had been a bother with sctne soldiers during which they had threatened to beat her husband. When the officers had her husband down on the floor in the parlour, she " pushed " him on the shin with her slipper. —Elizabeth Stone gave corroborative evidence and also said that Newey beat her father with a short black stick. —Robert Stone supported this statement.—Thomas Stone, the defendant. was next sworn. He said that on the day in question, he had had a quantity of drink, but could control himself. He was vexed when he found that his supper:was'not ready and in the course of a few words with his wife, he threw her out into the street. The officers came up upon hearing her screaming, and after a struggle in the parlour during which they illused him, they took him into costody. He denied that he struck the police. He did not make any complaint at the police-station because he did nor think that his injuries were so severe. After he was bailed out, how- ever, he was drily able to walk to the " Cross Keys," when a cab had to be brought, and when he arrived home, he had to be assisted to bed. Dr. Brooks who was called in, advised him t) go to the Infirmary where he remained until last Saturday.—The magis- trates by a majority inflicted a fine of 53. including costs, and the Chairman said that the maeistiates were of opinion that insinuations against the police should not be made unless they could be proved.—Mr. Browne, very warmly, said that as he had three witnesses to prove the charge it was very wrong to say that they were mere insinuations.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, NOVEMBLR 25, 1893.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, NOVEMBLR 25, 1893.

AN UNGRATEFUL GIRL.—A girl named Harriet Walker no fixed abode, was brought up charged with stealing Si. 3d. from a house in Midwood-st.—Mrs. Burns, Mid- wood-st., stated that on Thursday night defendant came to her house ; and as she was in a destitute condition witness took her in out of charity. On the following morning she gave the girl ss. 3d. to redeem some clothes from the pawnbroker's, but she did not return, and wit- ness did not see her again until she was in custody. A further charge of stealing a basket of shrimps, &c.valued at 63. was preferred against defendant.—Sarah /Lan Lomax, Bank-st., stated that on the 7th of November, defendant came to her father's house, and asked to be all-wed to sell shrimps. A basket containing six quarts was given her to sell, but she never returned with the money or basket.—Defendant, who pleaded guilty on this charge also, was sentenced to seven days' imprison- ment on each charge.—Superintendent Keighley prom- ised that he would see the police min missionary about the girl when she came out of gaol.
rush, and t3ok play into the visitors' quarters, when Lawton, a Warrington forward had to retire. From loose

play Thornton got over but the referee ruled against him. Towards the interval Warrington again attacked, and a rush by the forwards took the ball over the lines, it finally going dead. Half-time arrived with- out any score. With a strong wind'at their backs, the home team expected to have matters all their own way, and in this they were not disappointed, for with the exception of a good run by Lawless Warrington were never really dangerous. As the result of a fins effort Isherwood scored, and the same player followed suit a few minutes later. Page also scored, and Tobin con- verted. Thornton put in some good work for Warring- ton, who retired beaten by 1 goal 2 tries to nil.

Sr. HELENS RECREATION V. WIGAN.-At St. Helens on Saturday. The weather was bitterly cold, and the wind was blowing a perfect hurricane down the field towards Boundary-road. Wigan were short of Trow, Seddon, Winstanley, and Hnsworth, and the Recs, were without Ellison and Fildes. Wigan, having won the toss, de- cided to play with the wind. Seddon started, and Wigan soon got the ball to the Recs.' goal, and Holding attempted to drop at goal, hut the ball went outside,and a minor resulted. From the kick off the Recs. gradually worked play to the centre, but Mitchel neutralised any improvement made by the Recs, with a good kick, and Gill saved under the posts. The Recs. played remark- ably well against the wind. Molyneux made a good run to the centre, and the position was further improved by Hughes. but nothing but minors had been scored at half time. In the second half Seddon dropped a goal, and St. Helens won by a drop goal to nil.

Sr. HELBSTS V. rIIEBROMC—PIayed at St. Helens. The Saints were short of Sudlow, Foulkes, Little, Brown,and Brownhill, and Tuebrook of Holmes, Goss, and Hughes. Cross won the toss, and played with a strong gale. In a couple of minutes M'Lees scored for the Saints, Trainor failing at the place. The homesters, with the aid of the wind, again worked down, and Jones scored, tne kick at goal being again futile. Football et any sort was almost impossible with the gale blowing. The visitors made an attack from a pass from Appleton. ' Doherty scored for the Saints, but no goal resulted. The home team continued to press. Score at half time *— St. Helens, 3 tries ; Tuebrook nil. In the second half Trainer, Cross, and Doherty scored for St. Helens, and Cross placed two goals ; while Hewitt scored an unim- proved try for Tuebrook. Final result ;—St. Helens, 2 goals, 5 tries ; Tuebrook, 1 try.

WARRINGTON ST. MARY'S V. PEMBERTON RECREATION. On Saturday St. Mary's journeyed to Pemberton. Pem- berton started the ball, but were soon compelled to de- fend, which they did in fine style until Sanders got pos- session and dashed away, and passed to Berry, who out- ran his opponents and scored under the posts, the kick at goal being charged down. On restarting Pemberton tried hard to equalise, but the Saints' defence was too strong, and at half-ticne the score stood St. Mary's, one try ; Pemberton nil. On tnrning round, the home team having the wind, the visitors were several times called upon to relieve, but the- forwards keeping the ball at their feet soon reversed matters, and had hard lines for scoring, Welsby being tackled on the line. Darkness coming on made the game of a scrambling nature, and on the whistle sounding for time St. Mary's retired the winners by one try to nil. .1 BARTON V. WIDNES.—The meeting of these teams at Barton on Saturday was expected to draw a record gate, but the weather prevented many from attend- ing. In the first half the home team had considerably the best ot matters, Kilner and Benyon being decidedly unlucky in. not scoring, the former having the ball kicked from under trim when dropping. However, He- witt scored soon atter,Quigley failing at goal. Halftime: Barton one try to nothing. Resuming both sides pressed, Barton did most, Johnson, Millar, and Willis being dan- gerous. Widnes had their turn, and just on the call of time, from a splendid passing movement, Clarke scored, though the ball was palpably passed forward twice. Re- sult—a draw', each side scoring a try. Millar, Quigley, Benyon, Johnson, Berry, Worthington, Hewitt, Clarke, Brennan, Forster, Whelan, and Wynn were conspicuous for their respective sides. STOCKTON EIEATII V. WALKER'S BREWERY.ThiS match was played before a large number of spectators at Stockton Heath. The visitors were assisted by Carey and Mason, whilst the hoinesters were minus Smith and Glover. Stockton Heath had the best play throughout, and were victorious by one goal two tries, to one try.

div.head: SERIOUS CHARGE AGAINST THE
div.p: SERIOUS CHARGE AGAINST THE
POLICE.
ST. HELENS TOWN COUNCIL. THE MANAGEMENT OF THE CEMETERIES.
IiEW TAYLOR PARK.

The first meeting of the Parks, Markets, tt,pd Cemeteries Committee of the St. Helens Corporation was held on Wednesday. Councillor H. Martin, who was re-elected chairman, referred to the taking over of the Burial Board. He said it was a matter of satisfaction that the Burial Board had performed their duties exceedingly well, in fact that they had handed over the cemetery with only a very small debt resting on it. It would be necessary t ) en- large the cemetery before long. The single interment portion and the Roman Catholic portion would only last about two years, but, with additional land purchased on that side, the cemetery would last for twenty years. , He (the chairman) thought he would mention the mat- ter, and thus give them time to consider it.—The Town Clerk said there were many matters requiring attention, 1 and the cemetery management wanted putting on 4 permanent basis, particularly under the altered circum- stances with regard to sextons. He suggested that a special meeting be held at the cemetery, for the purpose of going into all the matters.—lt was agreed to hold such a meeting at half-past three o'clock on Tuesday next. A communication was read from the Local Govern- ment Board, enclosing a letter from Mr. Thomas Glover, secretary of the St. Helens Trades Council, and asking for the observations of the committee thereon. The letter signed by Mr. Glover asked what were the pre- scribed conditions required by the Town Council, as if the Trades Council did not know what the conditions were, it might be impossible to comply. The matters re- fers to the holdings of meetings in the public parks.— The Town Clark (Mr. Teeves), explained that the bye- laws stated that no meetings should be held in the parks, but there was a proviso that the Corporation might grant leave for a meeting, in accordance with such other con- ditions as the) might think fit to prescribe, and then anybody taking part in such meeting should not be con- sidered to have infringed the bye-laws—The Chairman said the minute explained itself, and he did not see what 'could be objected to in it. The committee did not see their way to propose any further alteration. It was decided to erect a red granite tablet at the toll- bar entrance to the new Taylor Park, with an inscrip- tion recording the name of Mr. S. Taylor as a donor,and the date of the deed of the gift.—The Town Clerk stated that he had written to owners of property abutting on the park who had made entrances to it, requiring them to block up such entrances. As oily one had replied,he suggested that the committee erect an iron unclimbable fence along the front cf such doors.—This w4s agreed

div.head: MANAGEMENT OF TUE FIRE BRIGADE.
div.p: MANAGEMENT OF TUE FIRE BRIGADE.

Mr. James Hatton asked who was going to pay the expenses of the horse which had its back injured while galloping to a recent fire at Greenbank Alkali Works. It would have to he kept in the stables for an unknown tlme.—The Town Clerk said the ratepayers would have to pay.—Mr. Hatton asked, if the horse had been killed, who would have paid.—The Town Clerk repeated : The ratepayers.—Mr.Chadwick wanted to know who was to blame for the accident.—The Town Clerk said Chief Constable Wood had just taken charge of the fire bri- gade, and he had issued a definite order that hQrses driven to fires must only go at a trot through the town where the streets were narrow and the turnings sharp. As a sub-committee were inquiring into the whole mat- ter, it would be idle for the committee to discuss the matter further. The Town Clerk reported that the Local Govern- ment Board had sanctioned the borrowing of £l,OBO for tho erection of cottages at the Boundary-road depot.

div.head: ELEMENTARY EDUCATION.
div.p: ELEMENTARY EDUCATION.

Mr. T. Dutton, superintendent, repnrted to the St. Helens Corporation Schovl Attendance Committee on Wednesday, that during the past month 229 lists, giving the names f 3,665 irregular scholars, had been received from the schools, as against 173 and 2,613 respectively in the corresponding month last year. There had been brought up for investig,tion 292 oases, against 224. The number of scholars on the rolls was given as 15,125, against 14,102 ; and the average attendance was 12.904, against 12,076. showing an all-round percentage of 85, against 86.
Edison is a very mod Prate sleeper, and has stated as his opinion that in the future ma will learn to do with no sleep at all or neat to none.

The open date which Warrington had on their card for Saturday was filled by an engagement with Blackley. The boisterous gale of wind, which blew had the effect of both marring the game and reducing the "gate." The total number of spectators was not more than 1,000. The local team had draws considerably from the A team to fill vacancies made by absentees. Jolley and " Smack " Bate, a course, were away assisting the County. Blackley had what is known in the vernacular as their " scratch "team. They were also fortunate in winning the" toss," and chose the pavilon goal as their end of defence and were assisted by the strong wind. At the outset Warrington introduced a considerable amount of dash into their play and for a time drove the opposing forces dangerously near to their line. How- ever, this did not last long. Blacirley's three quarters, especially Cooper, saw that it was high time they took advantage of the high gusts of wind which swept the field like promiscuous hurricanes. So they took every opportunity of putting in flying kicks with the result that play was soon in dangerous proximity to Warring- ton's goal line. Clarke, John Bate, and Bailey made an attempt to elude this impending danger by a very spirited series of passes. But again the alert three- quarters on " the other side" made dangerous shoots at goal, and had it not been for the prompt attention which the ball always received at the hands of Heesom, Blackley had assuredly have boasted a higher score than they secured. Warrington became very eager to give their scorer a little employment ; but their eagerness was only productive of a penalty kick in favour of their opponents, who failed to make much use of it. Burton who had been selected for trial from a junior team, hereabouts showed some excellent form anti con- veyed play into the visitors domain with the skill of an old veteran. Turner, Donohue. and Ranches all took advantage of this favourable position and made individual efforts to score. But bad luck frustrated each attempt. Before Warrington were repelled, how- ever, Burton distinguished himself again by notch- ing a minor. Give and take play followed for some time, and no signs of scoring were given by either team, with the result that the spectators began to feel their warm enthusiasm being gradually chilled by the bitterlY cold wind, and lack of encouraging play. By and by, how- ever, Turner, /lampoon, Evans, Taylor and Bate made a combined rush and soon had play at the pavilion end again. In vain did the opposing three-quarters endea- vour to transpose the oval ; they, were too closely taken care of to introduce even a promiscuous " flying" kick, whilst their passing, as it was felicitously put, was " but passing poor." A period of careful, dogged play followed, broken by a few individual attempts. And then, just as the spectators were resuming their cry of discontent—" play up lads "—Potts accepted a pass from Bate, and in the twinkling of an eye, had shot the oval over the bar and granted the scorer the joy of marking four points. Blackley, however, did not allow their ill-fortune to have any connection with their play. They worked away manfully and soon their efforts were rewarded, by Haigh scoring a try, which was not im- proved. The restart—after the lemon period—was characterised by some smart play displayed by Burton, who wasiassisted in his endeavours by Potts. The latter, ' in a few moments performed a feat which brought down upon him a perfect ovation of applause—from the specta- tors—not the Blackley players. He took up a pass at half way, and with aispiendid dash, soon cleared the whole of the opposing combination and then qu'etly trotted up to the line, and " placed." Turner failed to do any- thing with the kick. Fine give and take play followed, but no further scoring was indulged in by either team. So that at the conclusion of the game the results were : Warrington, one goal and a try (seven points), Blackley, one try (three points). The teams :—Warrington; Heesom, back; Burton, Evans, and Potts, threQ-quarters ; Clark and Bate (cap- tain), half backs ; Turner, Taylor, Berry, Donohue, Bandies, Bailey, Hampson, Phillips, and Forster, for- wards. Black-ley : Arrowsmith, back ; Atkinson, Cooper and Ashton, three-quarters ; C. Howarth and Oswald, half backs ; J. Howarth, Haslam, Isherwood, Cook, Taylor, Lund, Johnson and Haigh, forwards. Re- teree : Mr. J. Iligson, Salford.

RUNCORN V. SALE.—These teams met on the Irwell-lane enclosure, Runcorn, on Saturday, before a meagre gate. Neither team was fully represented, but Runcorn were the worst sufferers. There was a perfeet hurricane blowing, and the game was a complete fiasco, a more miserable exhibition never being seen on the Runcorn ground. In fact the match ought to have been aban- doned, as anything like accurate play was impossible. The following are the players :—Runcorn : Butterworth, full back; E. J. Morris, T. Warder, W. Faulkner, and T. Robinson, three-quarter backs; J. Faulkner and G. Robinson, half-backs; Reece, H. Farmer, J. Stubbs, A. Taylor, G. Moores, T. Antrobus, A. Clarke, forwards. Sale: E. Gardiner, full back ; E. A. Smith, R. Sawyer, J. Braithwaite and J. Cookson, three-quarter backs; R. S. Thorpe and H. Parrott, half backs; J. H. Taylor, R. H. Boote, J. Haigh, H. Harvey, S. Harvey, E. Harvey, A. Leicester, H. Maddock, forwards. The game was divided into four quarters. Reece started for Runcorn and Cookson replied. G. Robinson started a passing movement, but little advantage was gained, as the wind made the ball very erratic, and several easy chances were missed. Sale defended well, and the first quarter WAS reached without any score. On the re-start play was taken to the Sale quarters, where off-side play by Parrott caused his side to be penalized, but only a minor accrued from the kick. Haigh showed up prominently for Sale, and dribbled well on two occasions, but he was badly supported. The remaining portidn of the second quarter was very monotonous: only on one occasion was any interest aroused, when some pretty short passing was indulged in by the Runcorn backs, but Morris just failed to reach the ball, and an easy opening was missed. Neither side had scored at half time. Early on in the second half Warder and J. Faulkner each contributed pretty runs, and as the result of a passing movement Morris scored near the corner flag, but the kick failed. This was the only major point, and the game ended— Runcorn 1 try 8 minors, Sale 2 Minors. WARRINGTON 2ND V.LEIGII SHAN/ROC/IN.—The Warring- ton 2nd journeyed to Leigh to fulfil their engagement with the South East Lancashire Cup holders, who could boast of an unbeaten record. Warrington won the toss, and took advantage of the strong wind. Tobin kicked off, and a lofty punt by Chapman saw Shovelton grassed with the ball in his possession, Thornton got the ball away nicely, and looked like scoring till Murphy stayed his progress. The home forwards now came witit a

WARRINGTON ST. ELPHIN'S v. CHESTER COLLE GE.— Keen interest was aroused in this match, which took place on the College ground, Chester. A boisterous gale , was blowing when Howarth started the ball on its tra- vels for the College, Forbes checking when the home team seemed likely to score. Taylor and Hatton then broke away on the left, Tickell shooting into Scott's hands. Wright and Gunn raced away on the right, but being so closely attended by Cook, Gunn could not get his shot in. Anthony did a bit of good work agaimt Wright, Gunn making a good attetnpt to screw in. As- sisted by the wind,the College men were now constantly on the attack, Jones having an anxious time of it, Col- ley eventually clearing. Hickinbottom and Radford got through the College half back line, but Neville was handy and repulsed the invaders. The game for some time was carried on in neutral territory, but at length Howarth broke away and 8114 into Jones's hands, who threw clear, Horseley receiving, and some fine play was shown by the College right, Horsley defeating Jones with a high shot. This success put the home team on good terms with themselves. Horsley and Taylor could do little against Anthony and Cook, and Anthony neatly robbing Taylor, raced off and succeeded in equalizing. Midfield play followed. Half time score : St. Elphin's, , one goal ; Chester College, one goal. On the re-start Hatton and Taylor passed well, Taylor shooting wide. A fine exhibition of the triangular play was shown by Anthony, Hatton. and Taylor, which was loudly ap- plauded by the students, Taylor notching the second point for the Saints. Final result : St. Elphin's, two goals ; Chester College. one goal. WARRINGTON T. MELLING.—This fixture was brought off on Saturday on the Cricket Ground at Arpley, in boisterous weather. Warrington were minus the services of Clarke and Linnaker, and the visitors were without their goal keeper, Spinks (Warrington) filling the vac- ancy. Melling won the toss, and elected to play with the wind,which was blowing strongly towards the old pavi- lion. The visitors almost immediately broke away, but good play by Francomb and Philips averted danger. Reid was neatly robbed, and the visiting forwards bore down on the home goal, a sharp shot defeating Forrest. The home team now played with energy, and Connor got through a good amount of work.. Eventually the left wing broke away, and Dendy passing to Fennelly, that player followed up a neat dribble with an excellent screw shot, the visitors' custodian having no chance whatever. The visitors again pressed, and a number of unproductive corners followed, the whole of the home backs playing with rare dash against big odds. Mather was particularly conspicuous at this point, his tackling and kicking being quite sound. Shortly before half time the visitors put on a second point from a scrimmage. Half-time score—Melling, two goals; Warrington, one. In the second half Warrington reversed matters and the final scores were :—Warrington, four goals; two.

PADOATE RESERVE V. WARRINGTON POST OFFICR.—This match was played at Padgate on Saturday, in a gale of wind. Padgato kicked off and the Post Office faced the wind. Play was even for the first few minutes. Padgate rushed up and were very near scoring but the wind carried the ball over. Owing to the gale, the teams crossed over at the end of fifteen minutes. On the restart Padgate again broke away and a corner resulted. In attempting to clear the corner kick Goodfellow headed through his own goal thus giving Padgate their first goal. The Post Office now made a determined effort with the aid of the wind to draw level, but their efforts were in vain. Bennett cleared well for Padgate and after some neat passing Dakin notched the second for Padgate. Half time score : Padgate twe, Post Office nil. 'towards the close of the second half, with the wind in their favour, the Post Office forwards pressed continuously. Their efforts were successful, as from a nice bit of combination, Cox scored. From the kick off nadgate made a strong effort to score, but the rush came to nought. Gardiner obtaining possession rushed up and passing to Hallows, that ',layer drew the scores level by a good shot. No more scoring was done before the call of time.

WARRINGTON ASSOCIATION RESERVE V. MELLING RESERVIL.—The Warrington team played with only eight men, and fully expected their unbeaten record would be broken. During the Ent half they had the advant- age of a strong wind, and scored twice by Ogden and Mather. In the second half they were content to defend their goal, and were only beaten twice, the match end- ing in a draw. R. Smith, the cricket captain, played a grand game in goal, and some of his saves were mar- vellous. The whole team are to be congratulated on their plucky play against such heavy odds.

WHALLEY RANGE V. GUAPPENHALL,—ThiS match took place in a regular blizzard on the ground of the former, two thirty-fives being played. Both teams were fully represented. From the bully,Grappenhall pressed hard. and in fact had the best of the game Lhroughout. Shortly after the commencement, Carter for Grappenhall put the ball through, a performance which he shortly after- wards repeated. Whalley Range made spasmodic rushes to the visitors' goal, but were quickly repulsed, though they managed just before half-time to score their •nly goal, the game then standing Grappenhall two goals— both of which were scored by Carter, who played a ratt- ling good game throughout—Whalley Range, one goal. Upon resuming play Grappenhall again pressed hard, awl the home defence was sorely tried by the visitors' forwards, who, in spite of the miserable weather,played a splendid combinatlon game. Grappenhall only added one more goal, two being disallowed on the plea of "offside," The visitors' defence was very good, and they showed up in their old style when the ball hapl.ened to come their way. Altogether it was a pleasant,though damp game, and ended in an easy victory for Grappen- hall by three goals to one. For Grappenhall, Carter, Owen, Burrows, Knowles, and Wicks played thorough hockey.

Age does not wither, nor custom stale the popu- larity of bazaars as a means of raising money, for religious and philanthropic purposes. Toe power of Bethesda Church had recourse to this method on three days this week for the purpose of obtaining a sum of £3OO. On Sunday September 13th 1891, the church with the exception of the outside shell, was destroyed by fire, and the reconstruction and re- novation involved an expenditure of £2,100. The stam of £1,900, including the insurance money, was obtained, leaving a balance of £2OO still wanting, A further £lOO is also needed to complete the restoration. 'Therefore the bazaar was held in the expection of raising £3OO. The bazaar which was held in the schoolroom had been arranged by Messrs. Wilkinson and Son, of Liverpool, to represent a street in the Normandy town cf St. Maio, and the result was pleasing and effective. The opening ceremony on Wednesday afternoon should have been performed by Mr. J. T. Brunner M P., but that gentleman was unable to attend througn illness and Mr. Samuel Taylor, the respected chairman of the Board of Commissioners, kindly officiated instead. Besides the stallholders. attired in various gay and becoming cos- tumes, there were present the Rovs J. Simpson, R. •G. Hughes (Widnes) Craddock (Frodshain) J. Rulford Williams (Presbyterian) Messrs. James Simpson; J. R. Frith, James Handley J.P., T. Handley, W. Handley, W. H. Chadwick, Joseph Litter tic. After a hymns had been sung and prayer offered by Mr. Hughes, Mr. W. Handley chairman of the bazaar committee, explained that the money obtained from the Insurance Company, and the money raised at the re-opening services, did not meet all the expenditure which was found necessary. The whole of the property was put in a thorough state of repair. The congregation were also put individually to considerable expense in replacing books and cushions which had either been destroyed or rendered useless by the fire. Something like £lOO was raised at the re-open- ing services, the books and cushions must have cost a futher £lOO, so that it was deemed advisable to leave the provision of the remainder of the money needed, until a more favourable opportunity. Therefore a sum of £2OO was borrowed for twelve months and that time had nearly expired. In order to keep faith in this matter the ladies suggested a bazaar,and as the previous experience of bazaars at Bethesda had been pleasant and the results highly succe:stul the suggestion was willingly accepted. They wished to raise £3OO for the purpose or clearing off the debt and carrying out of the things which were almost essentially necessary, and as they were assured there were more than £3OO of stuff they hoped to raise that sum, although the times were not so favourable as they had hoped for when the bazaar was first mooted, Mr. Brunner, who had undertaken to open the bazaar was not able to be present. They had an intimation last week that his Parliamentary duties would prevent him from attending, but this was fol- lowed by a note on Tuesday, stating that he had taken ill on Saturday, and the doctor had forbidden him to leave the house. So on his behalf Mrs. Brunner kindly enclosed a cheque for £2o—(applause)—and to show her own sympathy she had sent a cheque for £5. Mr. William Hayes had sent £2O as a m•mento of his friend- ship with Mr. Tomkinson to whom they were indebted for the building of Bethesda Chapel some 60 years ago. Mr. E. H. Moss, J.P.. of Middlewich, had sent £5, and Dr. Robinson, son of their first minister had contributed a similar amount. Mr. Joseph Vettlin had sent a sovereign, a reminder of his visit there severs years ago. so that they had now in hand casts to the amount of £56.

Mr. Taylor, who was cordially greeted, said after the I full explanation of Mr. Handley there was not much left I for him to say with regard to the opening of the bazaar. When he visited the chapel after its restoration he was greatly pleased; he considered it one of the prettiest chape!s that he had seen for a very long time (ap- plause) and when he heard of the effort that was being made to clear off the debt he was not surprised, because he felt sure that the people would not sit in that beauti- ful chapel week after week without having that burden removed. (Hear, hear.) From what he saw around him in that beautiful decorated room and the state of goods both useful and ornamental, he was confident that at the close of the bazaar on Friday their anticipations would be fully realised. Some people had an objection to bazaars, but he had not; he was very fond of bazaars. (Applause.) Some people talked about bazaars being fleecing concerns, but it was his opinion that if they were not fleeced they would go away dissatisfied (laugh- ter) and there was not one out of ten who did not go there for that purpose (laughter) but they knew an Englishman would have his privilege—he would pay and grumble. The ladies however would not care about a grumble if they could only get people to buy, which, he felt sure, would be the case in that bazaar. His experience had been that people would give so much more through a bazaar than they would directly. Besides in connection with a place of worship bazaa.rs have a tendency to bring the people happily and amicably together. They went to church or chapel I moved to their friends, and away they went, but when they got everybody takitg a deep interest in work of ' this kind, it must have a good effect afterwards. (Applause.) No one would be better pleased than Mr. I Simpsen at the great interest and determination devoted to getting up that bazaar. It would have a lasting effect. Mr. Taylor then formally declared the bazaar open amid applause. On behalf of the Committee the Rev. J. Simpson then presented Mr. Taylor scith a beautifully illuminated handbook of the bazaar, as a memento of his visit. Mr. W. H. Chadwick then moved a hearty vote of thanks to Mr. Taylor for his valuable services, and in eulogistic terms spoke of Mr. Taylor's generosity, genial- ity and his readiness at all times to lielpthe necessitous. —Mr. Taylor, briefly made his acknowledgements and handed in a Bank of England note for £5 as his contri- bution towards the funds.

The ladies then commenced the sale of their wares. The stalls were in charge of the following ladies :--No. 1 Mrs. Turner, Mrs. Johnson, Mrs. Acksrley, Mrs. Powell, and Mrs. Radcliffe ; Misses, Lvdiate Slade, Johnson, Rogers and Unsworth. No. 2, Mrs. T. Handley, Mrs. Cameron, Mrs. Walton, Mrs. Littler, and Mrs.. Cart- wright ; Misses E. Riley, E. Handley, and M. Handley. No. 3, Miss Rob, assisted by the Misses Riley, Crhaghall, Heatherington, Hesford, Stone, Senior, Bell, &c. No. 4, Mrs. Forrester and Misses Forrester. Speakman, Camerin and A. Johnson. Firmer stall Misses Speakman, L. Chadwick, Heaton and Lunt. Refreshments : Mesdames Boyle, Dobson, Reed, and Temple, and the Misses Littler, Chadwick aud Richardson. There were numerous en- tertainments for the amusement of the visitors,and they I were repeated each evening, under the direction of Mr. C. LcCouteur, a select concert party rendered selections of music. There were musical entertainments in charac- ter under the superintendence of Misses E. Ainsworth, L. Johnson, and Mr. W. Ainsworth; and a humorous character sketch hy the celebrated Funnious, entitled " April Fools." The village minstrels gave performances under the conductorship of " Charley Bones, M.P." There was also an Indian jungle, provided with shoot- ing galleries, &c. The second days' proceecings commenced at two p.m., on Thursday, when Mr. Arthur Rigby, of Froditiam, performed the opening ceremony. Mr. T. Handley said Mr. Thomas Rigby, J.P., C.A., had promised to under- take that duty. but Was unable to do so through illness, and his son had come to take his place. They were glad to see a worthy son following in the footsteps of a worthy sirs. The amount taken at the stalls on the previous day was £B5 10s. 4d., which added to subscriptions amounting to £56 is. made a total of £146 is. 4d.—Mr. Rigby after expressing the hope that the last two days of the bazaar would equal the success of the first day, and that the ladies would be rewarded for their patience and perseverance, declared the bazaar open. Mr. T. Handley handed Mr. Rigby' an illuminated copy of the hand tuyik to the bazaar and proposed a vote of thanks to him for his services. He referred to Mr. Rigby's father's connection with Bethesda 20 years ago, and t 3 the service be had rendered to congregationalism by establishing a place at Frodshatn.—The motion was carried.—Mr. Rigby made a donation of £5 and Mr. A. Fletcher of Northwich, of one guinea.
RUPTURE CURED.—S J. SHERMAN, Hernia Specialist, 64, Chancery-lane, London, sends his book on rupture poet free. Branch Chambers, 26, Manchester.—Advt.

THE ATTEMPTED WIFE MURDER AT
HAYDOCK.

A LENIENT SENTENCE. Martin King (50), collier, was indicted at the Liver- pool Assizes, this week, for having at Havdock, on the 14th ult., feloniously wounded Bliztbeth King, his wife, by stabbing her with a knife with intent to murder. Mr. Cottingham prosecuted, and Mr. Collingwood Hope F defended. On the day in question prisoner and his wife were together in a public-house, and in the evening, the wife, with two wounds on her throat and her hands cut, was found lying on the highway. Prisoner's cap and knife were found near to where she lay. —Mr. Hope said 1 that prisoner would plead guilty to unlawful wwnding. He said that he must have forgotten himself t..) have assaulted his wife in that way. They had been married twenty-seven years, and there were eight children of the marriage. There had been no complaint as to the way prisoner had treated his wife. The wife was 'called,and stated that prisoner had always been a good husband and father. His Lordship (Justice Day) said that, having regard to prisoner's good character and the nature of the cir- cumstances of the offence, and the application made on his behalf by his (prisoner's) wife, he would bind him over to come up for judgment when called upon. Pri- soner was of good character as a working man, and he (the judge) always treated the real working man with i ndulgence.

div.head: VOLUNTEER PRIZE _DISTRIBUTION AT
div.p: VOLUNTEER PRIZE _DISTRIBUTION AT
ST. HELENS.

The annual presentation of prizes to the 2nd Volunteer Battalion South Lancashire Regiment, took place in the Volunteer hail, St. llelens,on Thursday night. In the absence of the Mayor (Captain A. Sinclair), through indisposition, the chair was taken by the Deputy-Mayor (Mr. F. It. Dixon- Nuttall). There was a crowded attendance. Colonel W. W. Pilkington, the commanding officer, speaking of the battalion, said its strength was 806, the same as last year, and 193 recruits joined during the year-19 more than in the previous year. (Applause.) The battalion won at Bisley £122 in cash, four badges and crosses, Corporal Preston being ninth in the final stage of the "Queen's," and Lieutenant White was also in the 100. At the county meeting at Altcar the battalion won £65 and one badge. Corporal Norbury shot in the English Twenty team in the international match at Glasgow and won £l6 and a badge. The total prizes won away from home were £214, five badges and crosses. They won their annual match with the Ist Liverpool by 82 points. In the match at Altcar recently between Lanca- shire and Yorkshire two, or three of their men com- peted, and Pi ivate T: A. Lockie, St. Helens, was the highest scorer on either side. The prizes to be presented that night consisted of the sum of £5O given by Col. Gamble, £35 given by the field officers and officers, £5 by Captain Sinclair (mayor), and £25 by other friends of the battalion. Those figures did not include the Beecham Challenge Cup, value over 100 guineas, which was won outright last year by Corporal Norbury. Messrs. Ireecham generously purchased the cup from Norbury, and again presented it to the battalion for competition, with the altered and more stringent condi- tion that in future it must be won four times in succes- sion, or six times in all. (Applause.)—An illuminated address and a purse containiog £l5O were then presented to the late Sergeant-Major Tyson, who retired after 16 years' service a few weeks ago.—The Chairman next distributed the prizes. He warmly commended the volunteer movement.

THE DESTITUTION AT ST. HELENS. ORGANISED lIELP FROM LIVERPOOL. On Monday, in the Town Hall, Liverpool, under the presidency of Mr. James Samuelson, a meeting was held with the object of devising means towards the relief of St: Helens workpeople who for some weeks to come, and until the works with which they are connected are in full operation, will be unable to obtain employment. The attendance in- cluded the Lord mayor (the Right Hon. W. B. Bowriog), Mr. John Henderson, Mr. Sampson, city coroner, and Mr. P. J. King the secretary. Mr. Henderson, at the request ot the chairman, gavel an account of a visit paid by them to St. Helens on Sat- ' urday. They were met at the station by Mr. King and , Mr. Swift, and went to the relief committee-room.where they saw Messrs. Forrest and Massey and Dr. Bellew. In the course of conversation with regard to the distress at St. Helens, which all admitted to be of a very exten- sive character, some doubt was expressed as to whether the Mayor of St. Helens might not resent interference• on the part of Liverpool men. The Mayor, however, afterwards met them in a very friendly spirit. He thought that the efforts of the United Alkali Company to relieve those connected with their -win works, added to the relief administered by the Charity Organisation was quite sufficient to meet the distress. During the first ten or eleven weeks of the strike they had had 119 application for relief,and had relieved sixty-nine. That struck him (Mr. Henderson) and the others as being a very small proportion of those likely to require assis- tance, and they felt bound to point out to him that there seemed to be still room for relief to a large number of people who would not be touched by the Charity Organisation ; indeed, they had themselves had evidence of some hundreds of women and children being in want. They parted with the Mayor on good terms,their visit hay- ing relieved him of any idea of uncalled for interference. With regard to the action of the Alkali Committee, it was very creditable to them that they had endeavoured to meet the distress as regarded their own employees. At first their relief took rather the form of giving repay- able advances ; but afterwards, when the effects of the strike became more acute, they found this would not do, and they very generously enlarged their views, and he was told they were spending as much as £l5O in re- lief to their own workers. Of course, there were some 2,000 or 3,000 people unconnected with the Alkali Com- pany's works, so that there was still, and would be for some weeks, a very large relief field. They were told that it would still be three or four weeks before the ; works stopped through want of coal were in full opera. • tion. The visits they paid to people reported to hem distress showed a mass of abject poierty.—The Chair- ' man, in supplementing this information, said there were four relief organisations in existence at St. Helens—the United Alkali Company's Committee, the Charity Or- ganisation, Mr. King's, and the Salvation Army. There had been from 3,500 to 5,000 connected with the glass, copper, and other works thrown out of employment. It was very largely due to Mr. King's activity that addi- tional relief was administered, because, in addition to what he had raised, others were spurred on to help.—Mr. Sampson thought the committee should confine their efforts to the relief of those thrown out e.f work through no fault of their own, because there was likely to be a great deal of distress in Liverpool during the present winter.—The Chairman and Mr. Henderson replied that this was the intention. Beside, the coal miners were al- ready working .—Mr. King, in reply to questions, In- formed the meeting that about £142 had come into his hands, and there was about £2O left towards the corning week. About £lOO a week would be wanted for the next three or four weeks.—The Lord Mayor said he had just had a deputation complaining that the relief was not given impartially, and he was very glad to be in- formed that this was not the case, as he assurcd the de- putation of the committee's intention to observe strict impartiality as to creed, nationality, and polities.—The Chairman added that, from the investigation he had made a•nong the people on Saturday, he telt convinced that distress was being relieved impattially, and that there had not been the slightest favouritism. He thought that if Liverpool contributed from £3O to £4O a week during the next three or four weeks they would have done all that was expected of them. Mr. King was afterwards, on the chairman's suggestion, author- ised to draw up an advertisement, making an appeal for subscriptions. The proceedings then terminated.

div.head: DEATH FROM EATING TINNED CORNED BEEF.
div.p: DEATH FROM EATING TINNED CORNED BEEF.

An adjourned inquest was held on Tuesday at Macs- bury, near Oswestry, on the body or Amy Mulla.rd, Ave years, who died on the 12th inst. from the effects of ' eating tinned corned beef.—The coroner read a letter from Mr. T. P. Blunt, the county analyst, stating that he could not find any poison either in the meat or in the child's stomach. The microscope revealed numer- ous organisms in the meat, and there was no doubt it had undergone some fermentative change, though the sr.sell and tasto were wholesome. The importance of only eating tinned foods when freshly opened could not be too strongly impressed on those using them. When such foods were opened some time poisonous properties seemed to be acquired without the accompaniment, necessarily of such putrefactive change as would appeal to the smell or taste. Dr. O. Leslie, Oswestry, who had made a post-mortem examinationtexpressed the opinion that death resulted from the mechanical irritation caused ioy the fermentation of the beef. The jury re- turned a N4trdict accordingly.

div.head: HAYDOCK " RIOTS."
div.p: THE HAYDOCK " RIOTS."

SEVER 4: SENTENCES. At the Liverpool Assizss, on Wednesday, before Justice Day, Frank Barrett, Peter Mitchell, Patrick O'Donnell, John lisnealy, John Caulfield, Joseph Lynch, and Thomas Flynn, all young colliers, were charged with rioting at Ilaydock on the 21st Octo- ber, and also with assaulting and resisting the police in the execution of their duty. On being formally charged, all the prisoners pleaded guilty to rioting. Mr. Swift, who appeared for the prosecution, said he thought the ends of justice would be met by the pro- secution accepting the plea of guilty of rioting which had been taken, and not proceeding on the second count in the indictment—that of assaulting the police. Mr. llorridge, who appeared for the prisoners, said he ' had taken a great responsibility in advising the prisoners to take the course they had. They were all working- men who had heretofore bore irreproachable character.. and they had now left their work in order to take th, it trial. On the day in question there was a considera ISS disturbance at the colliery, and the prisoners were nu e or less taking part in the disturbance. Therefore he dh., not think it was his duty to try and shake the evidence of the police. Except in the moments of folly and ex- citement, prisoners were quite incapable of committing such offences of which they were charged. They were not a premeditated body of men who had assembled with the intention of rioting. There was a row in the street, and when the police came prisoners foolishly resisted them. His Lordship: According to the evidence the rioters hurled stones at the polica.—Mr. Horridge : My friend Mr. Swift does not intend to offer evidence as to the assault.—His Lordship: I was careful in saying that the " rioters" hurled stones. The word "rioters" is in the evidence.—Mr. florridge : It was a time of great excite- ment, which is now passed.—His Lordship: The times of great excitement are times when law and order must be enforced.—Mr. Horridge : Prisoners are men who are not law-breakers, and nobody regrets more than they do now.—His Lordship: I have no doubt they regret it now. —Mr. florridge : They are real workmen, and have steady woik, and have left off to take their trial, and I hope your lordship will take that into consideration. They are not men of the criminal class.—His Lordship: Riots are not usually committed by habitual criminals. but by violent persons.—Mr. Swift: The prosecution don't know anything against the prisoners previously. His Lordship, in passing sentence, said they had been well advised to plead guilty to this charge. lie was sorry that it was his duty to punish, and punish severely, , men against whose character nothing was known ex- cept this. But it was absolutely necessary, having re- gard to the great prevalence of riot and disturbance which had characterised the country during the last few months, and the lawlessness shown to exist, and which had rendered necessary the employment of very large bodies of the public forces in suppressing it, that per- sons found guilty in ,a cosrt of justice of this offence should receive exemplary punishment. This was neces- sary in the interests of everyts dy concerned in the wel- fare of the country ; and who was not concerned in the welfare of the country, and who was not dependent upon the welfare of the country for his living? Every man I was interested in the welfare of the country whatever he I was, and it was absolutely necessary that punishment should be inflicted on all persons found guilty of lawless- ness of this descript,on. In this case the riot was got up for the purpose of intimidating and punishing in a brutal manner men who were desirous of doing neces- -1 sary work for their class, and prisoners inspired them with terror by their conduct, and wrecked an unfor- tunate man's house. It was shocking that honest men desirous of maintaining their wives and children and of preventing their employers' property being destroyed through the pits'being flooded should be molested in broad daylight by a lot of ruffians gathered together. Prisoners must have known that their conduct was criminal in the highest degree, was most dangerous to society, to the persons they attacked, and to the whole community. Ile was sorry to have to pass such a sen- tence upon them, but it was necessary for the c4minon good that such persons should be punished and made to understand that the law was still strong enough to pro- tect society against outrages of this description, however powerful men might be when they banded themselves together to create disturbances and inflict injury. Each of the prisoners must be itnpiisoned and kept to hard labour for three months. As soon as the sentence was announced several women in court, evidently related to the accused gave unmis- takable indications of grief.

As to Dean hicNeile, Ikr A. 117 it as a matter of fact that what I stated of him, vi : that he told his people from the pulpit not to et Arsoy Catholics, or to have dealings with them, becaus .5, as he said, "as they are idolators," is true, and if 'sfr. And, furthermore, let me say that it was through the actions and teaching of this " Apostle of Charity," this preacher of the Crucified that in the daily advertisements for many years after, there appeared the stereotypedaddendunk "No Irish need apply."—Yours, &es, , • J. C. DALTON. Warrington, Voir. 20, no. COUNCILLOR ROBERTS AND THE ELECTION OF ALDERMEN. Slr,—Mr. W. H. Brook (the late Town Clerk) has written to the papers to say that he ruled that discussion in regard to the election of an alderman was illegal and oat ot order. Mr. Brooks' letter is certainly a surprise. If he had referred to the published reports of the Council meeting held July 2nd, 1889, before rushing into print, he would , never have written such a letter. Let use I refresh his' memory by quoting the following extracts from the report in question. - - After the Mayor (Alderman Sutton) had that the next business was the election of an alderman, the following question was put by - "Alderman Joseph Davies.—Will you allow tile, Mr_ Mayor, to ask the Town Clerk if it is usual, proper, or necessary for a member to propose any one for the post of alderman) ? "The Town Clerk.—The proper course is to hand in the voting papers." Further on— Councillor John Platt said: "Much as I respect the Town Clerk! don't think his advice is in accordarce with what is usual in Warrington, certainly not in other towns. The Mayor.—" I don't object one bit ; you may go on discussing the thing as long as you like. Councillor Platt.—" I don't ask for your indulgence; I stand here in pursuance of a right which I possess when a matter is brought before the Council, to give my reasons or otherwise," &c. The Mayor.—" I was simply explaining; I don't object to anyone speaking. Councillor Platt.—"l don't suppose you would, and I dor t think the Council has get to the stage when we should apply the closure. The Town Clerk.—" It is not a ease of moving and seconding; I am not saying a word about any speeches. I simply wish you to understand that in the election of aldermen there is no nominating and no seconding, but that each member of the Council can fill up his voting paper as he thinks fit. Alderman Crosfield.—" If there is no one nominated and no one sesonded, does it follow that a member of the Council is debarred from making any remarks la chooses ? The Town Clerk.—" No, I should think not. After this preliminary discussion upon the question of order, an exhaustive debate upon the merits of the can- didates (Messrs. Francomb and Greening) followed, and then the vote was taken. On this occasion, at any rate, Mr. Brook did not advise that discussion was " illegal and out of Order," his statement to the contrary notwith- ing. On the 9th November, in the same year, the triennial election of aldermen tcok place, and Mr. Brook, aos Town Clerk, was again present. If upon the previous- occasion Mr. Brook in his desire to avoid a further angry, controversy permitted that to be dose which he now i says was " illegal and out of order," why did he on this occasion allOsv, , unquestioned a repetition of such " illegal "procedure? Along discussion took place upon the merits of two of the candidates, in whictr very hard things were said about the conduct of the Tory party in ignoring for the third time the 18 years services of the late Mr. Greening, and giving preference to a gentleman greatly his junior in all respects. Facts require a good deal of explaining away, and I leave it to the exceptional , ability 4 Mr. Brook to reconcile his opinions and action in 1889 with the opinions he expressed in the letter referred to. The question involved in this controversy is a most Important one, and I do not think the people of Warring- ton are content to see one of the most important func- tions of their Town Council reduced to the level of a sham and a farce, and a man foisted upon the town in the position of alderman as to whose fitness therefor at least 90 per cent, of the intelligent and respectahle rate- payers Of the town would utter an emphatic and indig- nant nogative,—yoursi fso.i

div.head: "THE DRINK TRiFFIC."
div.p: "THE DRINK TRiFFIC."

Sir,—You will, I think, allow me a line or two inyonr I valuable columns, in order to put Mr. Storey on the track of fair play, and unprejudiced opinion. In the beginning of his letter he regrets tnat I ever escaped being a drunkard, and consequently a disgrace to myself and family. This is, perhaps, in his eyes, a very righteous thought, and, as I do not see the correctness of his reasonings, it must come to pass that I shall be a "boozer." Mr. Storey insists that a man cannot take a glass of alcoholic liquor without being ruined bady and soul. Then, I say, that there ate 20,000,000 people in this kingdom in that pitiable state. Supposing out of forty million people, half of them at the most are teeto- tallers, infants, and the like; then on these islands we have half of our population in a state of idiocy ! How terrible As to calling drunkards fools, and being pitiless as to the future, I must remain so. In this race of life we must rush on, assisting the halt, the maim, the blind, and the helpless. Carl we, I ask, over-burden ourselves with those beings who, regardless of our warnings, drink deeply of the cup of pleasure, and lie on the road- side embracing the beloved barrel? My name must re- main-for the present " Neuter," and I assure Mr. R. Storey that lam not so lucky as to have interest in any brewery; but I and many others can tell him that the total abstainms hurt their cause mortally by this cease- less and useless shrieking and railing at the brewers.Mant look ou,but few stop to help the cause. My suggestion is; if the evil of intoxicants is in great, put the trade in the hands of the Government ; and instead of licensing the publicans, license the drinkers.—Yours truly. NEUTER.

• -- POLE MICAL AMENITIES. When Foulke-, and Dalton a " fall " must try And bite their thumbs, they know not why. "Hudit.ras," up to date. Sir,—lt is a pity both the doughty champions of their own religious ideal, who have been girding at each ether in your columns for the last week or two, cannot be brought to see that it would be better to shake hands and agree—to differ. _ . . . .

Of ii-ourse they are both right—especially Mr. Foulkes. If there be any truth in history it is an undoubted fact that the Catholic Church has persecuted Protestants. Quite so. While one is in the mud the other is in the I mire—especially Mr. Foulkes. If history can be at all relied upon the Protestants have persecuted the Catho- lics wheu they had the power. Even the much-perse- cuted Puritans of the "Mayflower "started the game of persecution as soon as they got the chance. And as it has been so it. will be. The power to do evil carries with it the temptation to do it. The lesson history teaches us is to trust no corporation, institution,or body of men with the power of persecution for opinion. I would not trust the Church of England of to-day with the power possessed by the Church of Rome 400 years ago. There straining power which to-day holds the Church ot England back from thg perpetration of these erinies upon its opponents, is the rationalism with which it is shot through and through.
