"HOME RCLE AND THE PHOTESTA.NT MINORITY." Sir,—Mr. Foulkes will kindly pardon me for pointing out, that he has hopelessly strayed away from his sub- ject. My original letter to you was to illustrate by example that the Catholics of Ireland under a Home Rule Goy, ernment would not persecute their Protistant fellow countrymen. The examples I adduced were those set by Catholic nationx at the present time, which (as I wrote' you then). said Catholic nations da not now persecute anyone for conscience sake, and also that no office in the state is forbidden to any person on account of his religion. I also pointed out the example given by Lord Baltimore and tits. fellow Catholics in Maryland, and pointtd a iporal from all this,viz. ; that Protestant states, who do'even to this day persecute Catholics in one form or other should follow these examples set them by Catholic nations. Then your correspondent comes forth and asserts that my true account of the positiaa of Pro- testants under antholic - is false—and how does he
, powers it—b launchi

proceed to prove _ ia unch ng forth eplenetic attacks on the Catholic religion and bringing up the oft-exploded tale about the Pope and the massacre of St. Bartholomew &e.— But I am not desirous of following Mr. Foulkes wherever he may chose to lead me—not that I am afraid of this redoubtable champion of evangelical principies— ahem ! But just this my verbose friend from the, bills of Frodsham (in your private ear)—l mean o stick to the point Which you are evading, by bringing up "the Vati- can Decrees," by the (1.0. M. wh9,however.much tmay admire aS a statesman, I think very poorly of as a Theo- logian. I may also add that the " Glories of Mary" have nothing to do with the question we are at present debating, which is that Catholics at the present time are . _ . .
more tolerant than Protestants, and by tolerance I mean

that they do not persecute Protestants, whilst Protes- , ants do persecute CatOclics,and withhold certain offices in the State from them on account of their religion. I am not now discussing whether it is right that Cath- olics should hold positions of eminence in the State on account of the false ideas which some people hold of their religion, but I am contending that it is a fact that Catholics at the present time do not withhold any right from Protestants on account of their religion nor are they likely to do so if Home Rule is conceded to Ireland. That is my point. Mr. Foulkes has a different idea of tolerance. He thinks Catholics intolerant because they look upon their religion as a better one than the Protes- tant religion, as he says, quoting Professor Gilmartin, of Maynootk," And the more one loves religious truths," (as distinct from error of course) " and the spiritual interests of our neighbour, the 'more must we seek, within the limits of justice and prudence, to stamp out heterodoxy." If, then, this is Mr. Foulkes' idea of intol- erance, viz. : that it is intolerant to think your religion (which in the case of the Catholic is only natural because hi religion was made by Christ and not by Luther) bet- s ter than any other, and also that to strive to spread that religion around you by every means that are 's just and prudent "—if this is intolerance,—then why in the name of common-sense does Mr. Foulkes put himself to so much trouble to put down Popery! I am sorry to have to say this of Mr. Foulkes but it is nevertheless true, that he, like many other earnest men, are very often misled by being contented with the garbled- quotations of such discreditable writers as Jewel and Blackenev. TILE COAL DISPUTE. Sir,—We can now congratulate ourselves that the coal Crisis is over at last,. although the evils it has worked will be remembed for a long time to come, and it will take months to put the working people's homes in the same condition as they were before the lock out. Some have died for the want of food, and in some cases hunger has wrought irreparable injuries to the health of the sur- vivors. The great coal owners and middlemen have made A few millions pf pounds, and " Cyruro " has lost £2O, and so he considers he must take sides with the sweating masters by cnampioning them through the Press. Strikes are very inconveme'i and a very brutal way to get, .-redress, but,- unfortunately, sometimes they beconullinevitable.. it our mechanic i And.aus colliers and sailors had the making of the laws that govern them they would likely have made them so that they could lawfuby prevent blacklegs from interfering in their quarrels witlythe capitalists. Let a man wh is not a lawfully appointed,member of the Bar step up into our Police Court to'plead a case and see how long he will be allowed to speak! Nay, let a debt collector head his request for prompt payment in a style that in anyway would lead people to surmise he was a solicitor, and the Law Association will be on his track, and he will be brought up for practising without a license and fined or Imprisoned. You see, Mr. Peers, the' lawyers made the laws p suit themselves, and they have a remedy against blacklegs; they can stop them without cracking their skulls. But easy, John, the time is coming for the sailors,and no doubt for all the workingmen. By and by no man will be shipped on a British ship as able seaman unless he has done four years hefore the mast. No man 'ought to be allowed down the mines as a collier unless he had first qualified from his youth and been a drawer iand passed a certain examination, to show that he could take care of his and other npen's lives when engaged in his dangerous occupation. We have a good many quali- fied engine drivers idlelor the want of employment.and we have men attending to steam machinery who do not understand their work. Those men are in danger of their livos and limbs, and are also a danger to others, as well as depriving better qualified men of the living they are entitled to, simply because it suits the sweating employers to employ the nurnbilkulls so as to get the work done cheap. When we get more labour representa- tives and the workers make the laws these things will be altered without cracking skulls; until then let not John Peers raise iredless cries of intimidation. There were no knobsticks worth talkie.' about, and it redounds to the credit of the three hundred thousand coal pit hands that they were all Men true to the core,though they were tried by all kinds of unfair means, they stood firm and, thank God, they have won the day. Cymro would have us believe he is a friend of the col- liers. All I can say is—it is really a case of God pro- tect the colliers from their friend. It is acknowledged on all hands by the employers that 2s. is about the aver- age paid for mining a ton of coals, and Cymro is of opinion that 63. per ton is little enough for the railway company to carry the coals 200 miles. To talco 30 wagons of 7 tons each that distance it will take three men seven hours, or yeu may say ten hours, and it will bring the company over £6O in cash. It would take 78 men and lads the same time to get the coals it the risk of their lives, and !t would bring them £2O in cash, out of which a good many deductions have to be made. Cymro you are a very poor friend to the collier, and in future mind what you write about, or you may, per- haps, catch a Tartar and make soother exhibition of yourself. As I could not ask the editor to grant me any more space for useless arguments, I will bid you adieu on this question. I have been thinking over the municipal elections,and read the sermons of our parsons and ministers, so next week, with the editor's permission, I will let Cymro and John Peers have a rest and talk to their reverences.— Yours, Sm., A. BRUCEIEMITE.
MR. R. PIERPOINT AND THE EMPLOYERS'

div.head: LIABILITY BILL.
div.p: LIABILITY BILL.

Sir,—Mr. R. Pierpoint has been speaking in favour of rendering it right and lawful for employers to still con- tinue to maim and kill as many as they think fit of their workpeople as it is profitable for them to do. Such is the sole underlying meaning of compelling employees to contract out of the Liability Bill.

Workingmen need to remember with distrust, the majority of their foes—the Tories; but with confidence and thanks, the majority of the Liberals past and present, for these Liability Bills ; the vital principles of which aim at saving working people from being maimed and slaughtered like dumb-driven cattle. Alas ! Cattle are much more valued than human beings by those employers, and members of Parliament who are unwil- ling to grant any act in order to save all possible loss of limb and life in coal mines, railways, sea, or any other kind of employment. For years past the Trades Con- gress have pleaded, all in vain, with tie late Tory gov-

div.p: THE tiii_4lKEli, 'sAitifiljAY, NOVEMBER ?5, 1893.

ernment for the amendment of the 1880 Act, solely on i two grounds. (1) To amend the Act so as to prevent employers compelling workpeople to contract out of it. When the Act first came in force, Ist January, 1881, I, and tens of thousands were locked out becat4erwe, declined to contract out of the Act. The 'strUggle,b4ted' ht weeks. Because I addressed mass meetings' January, 1881, when we were locked put for refusing to contract out of the 1880 Act. I was victimised, black- listed," and others besides me likewise suffered. After two monthsedriflict, tens of thousands of minds, who had subscribed thousands of pounds to secure the pass- ing of the Act, as well as the loss of their forefathers, and relations by needless slaughter were &sit-melted to starve for bread, or throw themselves,. and their sons in the scale. It was then that the plea was raised which has never ceased to sound like distant thunder in the labouring atmosphere, plying its part in trades unions, trades congresses, etc., to 'l. amend the' etnplcyers liabil- ity Act so that employers t. shall not he able to force their workpeople to el7ptcact out of the act" The principle inculcated ,tlrlll4 and ROW' by such speeches as Mr. R. Piernoint's uniaermine all human ex- istence. Should the house of 'Lords as 99Me of the blind Tory guides, editors, lcc..' who are now'praving their lordships will do the right thing, and insert Mr. McLaren's amendment " at the right time," then those eternal foes of all that appertains to the well being and just government al the toiling masses of England, and of the British Empire will surely fill np the cup of their crimes inflicted on the vast host of honest toiling men and women who will set their faces against the Lords and hasten the completion of their doom ! (2) Another of the principle arguments for the Bill is that it may prove as a lifeboat to the seamen of the empire, and so save them from perishing in " coffin ships." They need all the protection they can get from being drowned like old cats and dogs. Why should such trades as minersand sailors be forced into starvation for refusing to contract out of the Act ? Mr. Pierpoint says several communications have been sent him in favour of the clause of the hon. member for

- Jo oz. putaile and general import- ance, Mr. Pierpoint ought to publish the communica- tions, and the names of the persons said to have sent them : also whether those persons sent to him on their own authority only ; or state how, when and where such persons were authorised. If Mr. Pierpoint fails to do so, workingmen will know that he is an enemy to them, while professing to be their representative and friend. In fact all workingmen may see that he is so, in speak- ing against Mr. John Burns. the workingman's represen- tative of many thousands of railway, &c.. employees. He spoke about a large number of trains passing near both his back door and his front door, ever since the London and North Western Railway had been made. Having no sound reason to urge-azainst the Bill, he thus wasted the time of the House of Commons to hinder the passing of that important Bill, and others which we to follow for the good of the working class. Can he see either from his back or front door, trains passing his house? No wonder he was laughed at for such twaddle. He praised the London and North Western Railway for paying £lOO in case of death. How few poor widows get the £lOO. I know some get not a tenth of that sum after much trouble. Year after yearthe Trades Con- gress passed the following resolution against the late Tory Government : " That this congress expresses its strong dissatisfaction with the Governmep t for not giv- ing facilities for the consideration of the bill to amend the Employers Liability Act of 1880." It is thus clear as noonday that Tories are and have been opposed to the true interests of workingmen. Under present arrange- ments puffed up by Mr. R. Pierpoint it takes yearly more money to secure what little is got as compensation for accidents to men than what is obtained out of the fund subscribed to by masters and men. Further, the miners in Lancashire and Cheshire have to subscribe 75 per cent, to the Permanent Relief So- ciety. The colliery master pays 25 per cent, of the sum paid in. Therefore, they are compelled to contract out of the Act, and likewise pay three to one towards their own compensation in cases of getting maimed or killed. So much for the present system of so-called good ar- rangement, which Mr. R. Pierpoint strives to prevent being rectified. Workingmen. note the views of all labour representatives in the House of Commons. Be- yond all possible disproof,the Conservatives are opposed to the best reforms of labour laws, moral laws, and reli- gious equality. But they are the greatest foes of them- selves in opposing the general elevation of the masses of the nation, and the suppressing of their darling hobby— drink, which keeps the toiling masses in subjection, poverty, ignorance, crime, and misery. Shun all such thraldom, workingmen. Why be Tories ?—Yours, &c., R, STOREY. 18th Nov., 1893.

THE COALOWNERS AND THE MINERS. notice that your correspondent, Mr. John Peers, who has distinguished himself as an enemy to the cause of labour, can speak of nothing but the tyranny of the Miners' Federation. It is a poor argument, but as it appears to be about the only one he has, it is per- haps only natural he should try to make the best of it. Let us see what there is in it. A few men have used violence to a few others, will have taken the places of men who were perfectly justified in resisting a substan- tial reduction of their wages. A few paltry instances of this nature hive OCT,serred, and it is creditable to the , miners that they have not been more numerous. It speaks volumes for their self control and heroic fortitude. But to describe a whole body of men, hundreds of thou- sands of them, as " tyrants " for the excesses of a few whom you can count upon your fingers and toes is a gross misuse of an odious epithet. -In depriving the worker of the right to resist what he regards as an un- reasonable demand (and as things are he can only resist it by a cessation of work) Mr. Peers would take away from him the only weapon with which he can defend himself. Now John admits that it is absurd for a coalowner to assume ownership of a mineral he has never seen. But it would be more than absurd to enable him to get it on terms dictated by himself. Yet this would be the effect of a practical application of Mr ' John Peers' doctrine. A , coalowner who is paving say 2s. ed. a ton to a collier for getting coal says to him "You must get this coal at 2s. a ton." The collier replies," no," and therefore, accord- ing to Mr. Peers, it lathe duty ~f the collier to pick up his tools leave his work and allow somebody else to come in who will do it for 2s. The result is that both work- men .laffer.,a.nrl the coalowner puts the extra 6d.into his own pocket. Under this system the coalowner would grow rich and the condition of his workmen would never improve. It might be objected that this demand of the coalowner is possibly a reasonable one. Who is to decide this? II Mr. Peers' system prevailed (and it does exist) a number of unemployed would take the places of the workers, thatworkers would take the places of the un- employed, the condition of the workeq would be worse than -before, and the position of tllls rich coalowner would be better. The reasonableness of the demand would thus be decided by the coalowner who takes ad- vantage of the poverty of the 'worker, and this is what Mr. John Peers calls the "liberty of the subject." The words sound well, but they are misapplied, John, just as you misapplied the word " tyranny. ' A better des- cription would be, "a mean and contemptible form of robbery." I remember reading two years agl Ruskin's "Crown of Wild Olives," in which this subject is beauti- fullytreated, and the great teacher exposes in all its hideous nakedness this fine doctrine of the "liberty of the subje;ct." It is this same argument of beating down; as I said in my last letter,the setting off of one starving man against another, wealth utilizing the necessities and the miseries of the poor for selfish greed, for the poor must eat, the poor must live, even though their lives may not he worth the living. No, there is no such thing as "liberty of the subject" under such circumstances ; it is one of the ugliest and vilest forms of compulsion And this is why I hail with unfeigned satisfaction the pros- pect of the advent of what Mr. Peers is pleased to call a "labour tyranny," which will have no more resem- blance to the tyranny and insolence of wealth than the fertile plains of Lebanon have to the arid desert of Sahara.

But why, it may be asked did not the colliers accept Arbitration early in the struggle ? In all arbitration pro- ceedings there mnsr be a principle agreed upon for the guidance of the arbitrators. If you take only prices rul- ing lit A given period as a basis to an upon,the suggestion of arbitration would be nothing short of an insult to the men. Competition presses against the weakest, and if in order ti) obtain a contract a coalowner agrees to sup- ply coat at an unprofitable price what course does he take? Ask for a reduction of royalties ? No. Cut down the manager's salary? No. Effect economies in the management of his private establishment ? Oh, no. Deprive himself of luxuries and dispense with all the paraphernalia of refinement, and reduce himself to a condition only of a plentiful supply of food and clothing? Not a hit of it He goes straight to the collier, who in the heat of summer and the cold of winter picks and digs ceaselessly and toilsomely; who exposes himself to the dangers of deadly gases and the terrible roof-falls which are the daily incidents of his life frofh the cradle to the grave; whose home is designed merely as a shel- ter, and sometimes a poor one at that, and whose sur- roundings aro such as to discourage every impulse for the development of his better nature. It is to him the coalowner goes—he takes the line of least resistance— and thrusts him deeper still into his inferno of slavery. And it is of these men and their toil that the coalowner holds his .tata.

'Aye, "half mad." It may be so John Peers I will not deny it. In the dark days of the fourteenth century when 'twere even a bigger crime to be poor Moan it is to day there a priest of Kent who shook the founda- tions of feudalism to the core. This priest was John Ball. who gave utterance to the terrible cry of the people , as they staggered under the tyranny of property. And the confortable men who believed that the poor existed I only for their special benefit, men of the same class who now torn up the whites of their eyes and declare that the colliers are flyirm in the face of the "inexorable laws of political economy," said then that this champion of 1 the on of toil was mad, "The mad priest of Kent.' 1 And there was William Lonalsnd the silent and moody' tong t4ill " author of "Piers the Plowman," who de- vaed himself to the cause of the peasant,and the reward he got from his betters was their description of him as a mailman. Need I run up the whole gamut of madmen right through the centuries down to the" mad "Kier Hardie and • he " fanatical " Ben Tillett, No, John, my services in the course of Is tour do not entitle me vet—l say it with some regret for time wasted—to the Hatter-

ing des-oription which you have bestowed upon me. Figet-a my life is end NI I hope to have rendered such sem ice as will really justify the application of the full tile. At least I can work for it if I do not achieve it.

If reliance is to be placed upon parliamentary returns, 'there ware IRst year 300,000 coal getters who received in wages £15,000,000 being an average of 1.93. 21d. per week. Sir George Elliott in a letter to the" times" urging the formation 01 a Coal Trust said the profits of the coalowners were £11,000,000 which, reckoning these men at 3,000, gives an average of £lOB per week. And trade is being ruined by foreign competition, and the wealthy coalowners "can't make it pay" on £lOB a week. And yet it is of us and our toil that these men hold their Rtate.

" Cymro " says the masters have offered to prove that they cannot pay the late rate of wages with coal at late rates and they offer inspection of their books in proof. But Mr. Bayley M.P., a coalowner himself, says." the coalowners who have entered into these big contracts hive sold the men's•labour before they boughtit,and that is where they have made a mistake and that the coal war was initiated by Ting of coal owners, on their own account. And yet it is of us and our toil that these men hold their state. The coal war has had a disastrous effect,ws all admit;

its duration is unprecedented for at least a generation ; as " Cymro " says it has left bare walls and empty clothes chests, but it is not the colliers, it is the coal- owners who have -made him £2O the poorer and ruined many a hundred homes. In the name of eternal justice apportion the blame aright The coalowner has had a steaming ink dinner every day, his family have been carefully tended; the miner has borne the pangs of hunger like a sturdy man that he is, his wife has been growing thinner every day, but she has been as resolute aS he, and ,children have risen in the morning and gone totbed.without food at night, and have fainted at school from :sheer exhaustion. And all for what? Because thev.resisted their 193. 21d. being still further whittled claim to sixteen,because the £lOB man was not satisfied. DO these arm-chair critics know what hunger is I won- ; have they ever felt its cessele:s gnawing, its untold miseries, miseries that must be felt before you can even attempt to describe them. And not a word of consola- tion from you,John Peers and you, Cymro ; nothing but blame. And mat one single, solitary, syllable of censure of the cralowners who have caused all the trouble. And yet it is of Us andourtoil that these men hold their state " Charity "says Idr.John Peers "begins at home." I hare erased that monstrosity from my list of proverbs. It covers a multitude of sins of selfishness. When a genuine case of distress appeals to you button up your coat and mutter " charity begins at home." When you are asked to subscribe for the alleviat'on of distrait; caused by a mining explosion which sends eighty ' men into eternity and occasions widespread mourning and suffering—there have been three such within these last three years—think of the miseries of this coal strike and let the naelliffuenti words trip gaily from your tongue. But never, whatever.. happens, say one disrespectful word against the coal- owners ; it is much better to slander the collier—herause he wears a black face and rough clothes. Besides he is used to it. And yet it is of these men and their toil that their masters hold their state. For Many years I have asked myself the question —what are we here for ; what are we living for. I see men every morning going to their work, and I meet them returning perhaps a trifle dirtier, a shade paler, and with a look sometimes of weariness at night. From day to day, from week to week, from month to month, and from year to year, I see the same old faces going the same old round,and I often repeat to myself the words slowly and distinctly, " What—are— we—here—for ; what—does—it—all—mean 2" And I see the business man hurrying along, anxious on his money getting Frauds, the rich man and the rich lady passing away their time in comfortable leisure, and I sometimes wonder if they are ever troubled with the same problem. Surely there is some destiny for the race, there must be some goal to which we are all tend- ing ; there is some object in our existence, but if it be' not to lift the race to a higher level of ,physical and moral life then I know not what it is..
" Yet I trust that somehow good Will be the final goal of ill; That nothing welks with aimless feet, That not one life shall be destroy'd Or cast as rubbish to the void,
When God bath made the pile complete." —Your!, &C. "COMMON JUSTICE."

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.

RUGBY Foorwsarr.. Blackley—the team with whomWairrington filled an open date on Saturday—are 'known .as the "Wooden Spoonists." This is simply an appellation bestowed up- on them to signify the fact that'they are at one end— 'and that not the top—of the second •division of the Lancashire Rugby Championship competition. So that Warrington may be said to have had an easy thing on with them. Nevertheless, the game was of a very en- joyable character, or at least it would have been, had there been a greater absence of boisterous wind. As it required to withstand this, the hardy qualities of a viking, there- was naturally a great decrease in the " gate." Only a thousand spectators graced the game with their presence! Warrington were without most of their usual men—and, besides drawing upon the A team for support, they generously brought forward two jun. players, Burton and Clark. Both these players are in possession of what are known as " bumping" reputa- tions, in their own teams, and they were quite willing to see if they were able to maintain them ,among the champions of their town. This they did, for they ac- quitted themselves in a very praiseworthy manner.

• Burton is a tall youth, and with a little coaching should be able to hold his own in very good company. He is very speedy and kicks excellently,shewing in every respect good capacity fur three-quarter play. Clark showed himself to be generally active and displayed qualities which should enable him, by a little coaching, tdibe " licked into shape," for almost any post. " Smack " Bate and Jolley were, of course, both away doing their best to enable Lancashire to appropriate the honours of victory in the match against Cumberland. From what I can hear both players splendidly repaid the honour conferred upon them by their selection. But, for all that, " Smack" Pate was not quite able to play with the brilliancy which he has shown in local matches. This was in consequence of his being transferred to a side in the scrimmages to which he has not been used. Then, in addition to this, he was very obviously neg- lected by his partner at the other side of the scrimmage. However, this will be remedied in the match neat week, for the other Bate has been selected also to play. This will give the fullest satisfaction to Warrington, and gives corroboration to a rumour that has long been abroad, that the" two Bates are the two leading half- backs in the county." Like other of their admirers, I shall look to them for a record to-day (Saturday), when they face the doughty "Tykes."

But to revert back to the match with Blackley. It was an easy victory for Warrington, and a source of assurance to Blacklev that they need not fear losing the "wooden spoon." That is, unless they go and throw reckless improvement into their play, and then they might lose the honour. Warrington's victory consisted of a dropped goal and a try,buth of which were scored by that energetic threequarter, Putts. In the first half of the game, when Blackley were " plunging "on "flying" kicks at goal, Heesom rendered capital service by the prompt manner in which he returned the bill. By this means he certainly" kept the ball a rolling," and what was more necessary,kept it in the visitors' domain. The A. team men, especially Hampson, showed what fine substitutes they make for their premiers.

I see that the following is the team chosen t 9 repre- sent Lancashire against Yorkshire on Saturday :—D. Foulkes (St. Helens), back; M'Cutcheon (Oldham), Barratt (Salford), Valentine (Swinton), and Lees (Old- ham), three quarter backs ; John T. Bate and James T.* Bate (Warrington), half backs; Simpson (Rochdale), Unsworth (Wigan), Goold (Liverpool Old Boys), Case (Swinton), Woodward (Tyldesley), Jolley (Warrington). Ashworth (Rochdale Hornets), and Wilson (Liverpool Old Boys), forwards. The changes from last Saturday are—Valentine and Lees vice Holmes and Lewis. John T. Bate vice Chapman (Barrow), and Ashworth and Wilson in lieu of King (Salford) and Andrew (Old- ham).

An interesting ceremony will be performed next Mon- day at a meeting of the Warrington Football Club. Two of the oldest players, who have retired upon their "laurels," are going to have those rather unsubstantial trophies augmented by a timepiece each. The retired " Knights of the Leather " in question, are W. Speak- man and W.Povey. The latter acted as touch judge last year. Both were popular and hardworking players of the club in their day, and the recognition of their past services which is to be bestowed upon them, will, I am sure, be accompanied by the good wishes of both the football public and the members of the club. Speakman has been connected with the club for almost 17 years, and Povey joined in 1877.

div.head: CYCLING.
div.p: CYCLING.

In response to an appeal a deputation of the Warring- ton Cycling Club joined in the cyclist parade at Widnes, an Monday evening. One of them, Mr. S. Cook, who was" got up" as Mephistopheles, took the first prize for the best turrout. E. Pickavance, was attired in his " Jack Point "costume, whilst the following were in " fine fantastic get-up" :—Messrs. W. Leatherbarrow, A. Booth, W. Bellian, G. Whitham, G. Smith, C. H. Holt, W. Mounfield, T. Barnes, J. Worsley and A. Pritchard. The parade was in aid of the Widnes Distress Fund, and the sum of £56 13s. 6d. was collected.

By the way,while speaking of cycling, I am reminded that Mr. E. Pielavance has resigned his office as secro- tary of the club, and what is worse, the club have gone and accepted his resignation ! From what I can hear, the genial Edward has taken this course because, after some years at the work, he thinks he might have a rest. His intention has caused a large amount of regret in local cycling circles, for he has been recognized as one of the hardest workers and best organizers which any local club has been lucky enough to obtain. Mr. Pickavance can claim to have had much to do with the rapid growth of the W.C.C., and the club are loosing in him a most capable officer.

div.head: ANTECEDENTS.
div.p: ANTECEDENTS.

This week the subject of our sketch is ".Fair." Turner, than whom Warrington has yet not turned out a better all-round athlete. At least I cannot find a trace ot any such predecessor. The stalwart "Fair." has been des- cribed thus by a Liverpool contemporary :—"The name of 'Fair.' Turn& is a household word in Warrington, where he reigns as the beau ideal of an all-round athlete. He is the pride of the rising generation—aye, and of the well advanced generation, too—and is an honour to Lancashire and all England. . . His talent does not Pe all in one direction, for all the various forms and re- quirements of the gymnasium, football, bicycling, run- ning, jumping, and swimming find him at his ease. No athletic diary would be complete without a sketch of Fair- field Turner. To all of which I ejaculate " Hear, hea-.- "Fair.'s" football career commenced with the old Pad- gate team, to which I have before alluded in these antecedents. He has always played a forward game. He was, indeed, one of the few present players who laid ,the foundation of the present club. He joined it when it first became possessed of the name of "The Warrington , Football Club," and has continued to play with it since without cessation. The good service he performed as an enthusiastic worker, and player, at a time when the , club was struggling against adverse circumstances, is proverbial. He captained the club in 1984 and in 1890. And in 1887 he was twice selected to play with the county against Durhatn and Somerset,and he did so with credit to himself and the ‘Varrington Club.

But "Fair." Turner's achievement; in other de- partments of athletics are more than worthy of a mention. Probably, of his many ac- complishments, the stalwart athlete is proudest of his prowess as a swimmer. At the age of ten Fairfield. we are told by his admirers. "took to the water like a duck." 1n the year 1879 he began to build up his repu- tation by winning the championship of the Warrington Swimming Club. He has held on to this honour ever since. In 1884 he surprised the natives of Manxlancl by winning the 100 yards amateur swimming championship , of the North of England, at Douglas. But in the follow- ing year, in consequence bf heing "done up" from hard ' work, he was beaten in the same competition at Roch- dale by Nuttall. After this Turner entered into aquatic competitions right and left, and emerged from most of them with immense success. He once performed the novel feat of swimming the canal at Warrington with his hands and feet tied together. This was done in res- ponse 'to a challenge. He has in his possession i.en medals for swimming, an honour of which few amateurs can boast.

" ,air Turner was also one of the leading originators of the Warrington Gymnasium and the present Warring- ton Athletic Club. It was when the former was in its infancy that he won at Liverpnol,the 200 Guineas Shield of the National Physical Recreation Society, for the best feats as an all round athlete. fie also holds several medals for foot racing and enjoys the unique distinction of having been a leader in every institution in Warring- ton connected with physical recreation. He is indeed an athlete of whom Warrington and Lancashire have cause to be proud, and that the Warrington football club are all the richer for numbering him as one of their team everyone is ready to admit. May his stalwart frame long lend weight to their forward forces.

Councillor F. A. Burt, of St. Helens, had a narrow escape from serious injury on Wednesday. He was rid- ing in a trap with Mr. Houghton, of Parr Old Hall,along Blackbrook-road near to Chain-lane, when the pony shied at a steam tram coming in the opposite direction. The pony swerved across the road,and in eoing so slipped on the tram rails. The occupants were thrown out,Mr. Burt alighting in f'tbrit of the tram engine. The driver immediately stopped the engine, the wheel of which I must otherwise have passed over Mr. Burt's leg. In fall- ing Mr. Burt injured his left arm. The pony received a nasty cut onthe hind leg. The Mayor of St. Helens (Mr. Sinclair) was unable to attend the Corporation Committee meeting at St. Helens Town Hall on Wednesday on account of indisposition. His worship has contracted a severe cold, and his medical adviser has ordered him to remain indoors.

div.head: WARRINGTON DEBATING SOCIETY.
div.p: WARRINGTON DEBATING SOCIETY.

"ONE MAN ONE VOTE." At the weekly meeting of the Debating Society held in the Masonic Hall on - Tuesday night, Mr. C. Lyon gave a paper on the subject ef " One man one vote." There was a fair attendance, and the chair was occupied by Mr. J. Horton. The essayist said that in the vast field of social and commercial pzo- gress that had ripened and bunQ fialit in the !Ast three-quarters of this Century, nothing wee mo:e remarkable than the change which had come over the relative positions of the classes that fornaed the community. The working man had risen from being a mere beast of burden, to claim with those who for ages past bad been les owners, his masters, and his lords, an equal voice in the government of the nation's affairs. The demand at present went no further than tor an equal share, but if steps were not taken to accede to the demand,it would grow equally irresistibly and, perchance, not so silently, to claim as complete a monopoly in the management of the nation's affairs as the to-called lords exercised for generations past, and a government monopoly by the democracy might prove as tyrannical as the government monopoly by the aristo- cracy.flitherto it had all been for pocket and escutcheon, all for birth and soil,but it was to be hoped that the days of these graven images wche passing away, and that the dawn of a loftier hero worship was now breaking on our shores. It was essentially necessary when considering the direct question before them to keep in mind the foregoing panorama of historical events, even although great men's deeds had been made to look like little things and centuries :as but yesterdays. The divine right of kings ad the divine right of nobility had gone ; there yet temainad the divine right of landed property to hold political supremacy in the land. Political supremacy and social distinction were as apart from each other as the poles were asunder, there was scarcely an atom in common between the two. A man might have as many residence in as many counties as he chose, and might justly claim the social and local privileges that respec- tively appertained thereto, hut he could only live in one nation, he could only live the one life in that one nation and ought not therefore to exercise the privileges of tens, twenties, or fifties of lives according as his wealth might buy. Tho incongroity of allowing a separate political vote to ono person for every bit of property he might have scattered over the country, had oaly to be looked at to be revealed in its gross unfairness. Those properties might justly entitle him to the exercise of Municinal votes and other such privileges, but that, , was a different matter entirely to exercising separate parliamentary votes. He was told that as the one who invested in property had the privilege of paying taxes upon the different properties, he ,ought t o have the privilege of voting upon them. He had, however' but one life to live in the nation, and when he had done with it, the nation looked upon his properties 'as a single possession • whether situated at John '0 Greats or Land's Et;el, his properties were lumped in one for Government purposes. That the principle of plural vot- ing 'as at present in vogue was an erroneous one as ad- mitted by the legislature in the cases of those borotighs which were divided into parliamentary divisions and municipal wards. In such cases although a man might possesaand pay taxes upon property in everydivision and every ward he was only allowed one parliairientary and municipal vote, he being given the option of which division 'hr which ward in which to do so. If such corporations were considered compact ard undivided, still more so 'might the nation to be considered compact andoindivtlied, and still greater was the necessity that onemember should not exercise the functions of several members. the rich man had no greater issue at stake than the poor man, although his direct contribution to the exchequer might be greater. The 'poor man's wife and children, and home, were dearer and more valu- able te him than the various material possessions to the rich man. Plural voting was unjust to the very , class`which it favoured so largely, for one property owner might possess a whole county and have only one vote, although he paid treble the amount in taxation than another property owner did, who had four or live votes because he had four or five smaller properties in as many counties.—A discussion followed in which Messrs. narrington, Neil& Flan, Robinson, and the chairman took part. The expression of the meeting was unanimously opposed to the continuance of plural voting.

div.head: WATt RINGTON MUSEUM.
div.p: WATt RINGTON MUSEUM.

The mnseum has recently received a most valu- able accession in the shape of a series of casts from ancient engraved gems, presented by the trustees of the British Museum. The 230 gems represented illustrate most, if not all, of the known stages of the glyptic art,as practised by the Greeks,Etruscans, and Romans, from a period not later than the beginning of the 7th century 8.C., down to about the 3rd century AD,, or even later. The casts are beautifully mounted in two glazed frames, and fully labelled, and the value of the gift is much increased by its being accompanied by a number of copies of a printed catalogue of the casts. The catalogue briefly describes each gem of which a cast is shown, and refers for further details to the " Catalogue of Engraved Gems in the British Mos.,- urn," a copy of which is in the Reference Library,havin,g been presented by the Trustees some span ago. The usual annual change in the objects constituting the loan frona the South Kensington Museum 'has just been made. One picture has been sent viz, an oil paint- ing by De Jongh, of Old London Bridge, as it appeared near the end of the 17th century. The remainder of the loan consists entirely of specimens of rrench art, includ- ing silk brocades, pottery and porcefain, Ironwork, wood and ivory carving, bronzes, gold and silversmith's work, and enamels. The framed illustrations comprise sj mens of furniture, and a series of facsimile reprodu. tions of drawings by Watteau. The loan although rtre presenting the art of only one nation, is more varied and., generally attractive tban.tisnal.

div.head: NEW BOOKS.
div.p: NEW BOOKS.
CHRISTMAS PUBLICATIONS, &c.

Every year we think and are tempted to exclaim that it is Impossible for Messrs. Raphael Tuck & Sons to im- prove in any way on their splendid collection of booklets, cards, calendars, and every following year we are bound to adrojt that they have done so. For the years 1893-4 they lave produced an endless variety,both literary and artistic. The designs are novel, the colours are novel, and the inscriptions are novel. One of the prettiest cards is the " Minuet Tableau," with charming quaint figures going through the stately dance, another the " Salon," a three-fold card ornamented with cherubs' heads, bells, and floral sprays. Other series are the " Ribbon." the " Cameo," the " Horse-shoe," the "Sacred," the " Mosaic," the "Photogravure," and the " Celluloid," and for the little folks there are the three- fold " Fairy-tale" cards, with a Christmas letter on the back of each one. We must not omit to mention the ever-popular" Autograph "cards, which for variety and refined production surpass those of previous seasons. The" Hundred and One Year "calendar (patent), is cer- tainly a novelty. The great calculator—Jacques Inaudi —has worked out a marvellous scheme, showing by one movement the day of the week of any date between 1791 and 1920, a most useful and interesting acquisition. It is supplied with a cord for hanging, as is also the " Golden Ladder," a calendarsuitable'for the bed-room, with a religious motto for each month of the year. "Yule Tide " is an exceptional shilling's-worth alike for quantity, quality and variety. It contains no less than seven presentation plates, the largest a coloured picture, " Don't tell," from a painting by A. G. Elsley, and two smaller ones, both coloured, reproduced from original drawings by Yeend King, RI. The remaining four are printed in three tints, from drawings by W. Paget and Bernard Munn. Mr. Stanley J. Wevman contributes a very good illustrated story, " rhe Man in Black," and an original carol, by A. T. Quiller Couch, set to music by C. V. Stanford (in music size), and printed separately is included. G.Manville Fenn supplies a comedy in miniature, and set cf ingenious puzzles.

The principal literary features of "The Illustrated London News "are two complete stories ; the first by Rudyard Kipling, and a short one by John Strange Win- ter, both valuable contributions to the good things of the season, and well illustrated. " The Additional Guest," six scenes in a country house, by N. E. Norris, is just the thing for amateur theatricals. A fairy tale by Canon Atkinson, and a short story by George Gissing, in addition to a large presentation plate," Grandfather's Pet" by the same artist as "Don't tell," and two small coloured pictures" Une Col6mbe," and " Say please," complete the number. " Holly leaves "is well recognised now as the Chtist- mas number of the " Sporting and Dramatic News." Two coloured supplements are given with it, the largest a reproduction in fac-simile. by photographic transfer, of J W. Godward's picture, " Memories," a most artistically finished copy. An illustration by Louis Wain, " Cat's Ice," is alone worth the price of the magazine ; each cat is a study, and the whole picture most amusing The literary contents are all well written and numerous, the illustrations number nearly a score, and the letter- press and general finish of the number ars excellent. Thera is a great deal of admirable literature in the first Christmas number of " The Sketch." It is decidedly smart, and clever, full of fun, and funny pictUres. The artists include Phil May, Dudley Hardy, R. Caton Wood- ville' Leslie Wilson, Louis Wain and others, and the authors are Max Pemberton, Clara Saville—Clarke, E. Nesbit, and Arthur T. Pask. We anticipate a successful career for "The Sketch," and hope to welcome many more of its Christmas numbers. " Father Christmas" is the children's number of "The Illustrated London News," and we are quite sure it will please them every one, both young and old. The rhymes are simple, catchy, and humorous, and are ap- propriately illustrated on every page. The coloured presentation plate, " I'se Biggest," is a copy of an ori- ginal picture by Arthur J. Elsley. The same artist supplies the big picture presented with "The Penny Illustrated Paper," " Happy Days." which represents a see-saw with a frightened little dog at one end of the plank, and a merry, buxom lassie at the other, who with her little sister is having some fine-fun at the doggie's expense' as ke clings to the end of the plank in mid-air. The "Christmas Rases" are different types and all pretty. The authors include Archibald Forbes, I. Zangwill, Clement Scott, G. Manvill Fenn and others, and among the artists are Sir John Gilbert, R.A., Fred. Barnard, and E. N. Downard. The wonder is that so much that is good and clever can be had for sixpence.

Among so many comparatively new Christmas publi- cations, it is as pleasant as the sight of an old friend to see" Hood's Comic Annual "among the rest, which for twenty-five years has done its best to make a merry Christmas merrier, and so far succeeded admirably.

In a crtver blooming all over with flowers we b-ave a copy of" Our Village" (Macmillan) by Mary Russell Mitford, which as its title suggests is a number of sketches descriptive of the village in which the authoress lived and died. They are written in a manner and with a charm peculiarly her own ; enthusiastic, quaint, old- fashioned:serious, playful, pathetic, each one in turn' and none too much. It is a long time since we reads book that was so refreshing ; it is like a holiday in the country in all seasons of the year. To make it more valuable as well as attractive, it is illustrated on a hundred pages by Hugh Thompson, who has just the knack of picturing village characters and vinare scenes. A lengthy, interesting introduction is lovingly contri- buted by Anne Thackeray Ritchie. An uncommon little book by' Ralph Iron (Olive Schreiner) called " Dream Life and Real Life," an African story, is published by T. Fisher Unwin. It is ingenious,and imaginative,with a purity of thought and expression, eminently poetical and powerful. Two other sketches are bound in the same cover, making altogether a charming little volume.

" Everybody's Book of Acting Charades" is as season- able as any Christmas literature, and certainly as useful. Not only " the word "given, but a number of complete charades, dialogues, tableaux-vivants, and debates are fully supplied, with the costumes, acts,and characters explained in detail. " The Lads's Companion" includes a pretty picture in colours, " Waiting for Papa," and gives a special illustrwed article on Christmas decorations for the home, arid the art of draping, in addition to the usual number of stories.

There is undoubtedly a need, and a demand for such an entirely new and original work as Warner's " Royal Natural History " promises to be. It is issued in thirty- six monthly shilling . pvts, (first part ready now), in twelve quarterly sections bo,und in cloth at five shillings each, and in six half-yearly volumes at nine shillings each, and when complete will be adorned with seventy- two coloured plates, and sixteen hundred other illustra- tions. Its responsible editor and chief contributor is Mr. Riehard Lydekker, 13. A., P.G.S., F.Z.S. ; the pre- face being written by Dr. P. L. Sclater, F.R.S., the secretary of the Zoological Society of London. From the prospectus we learn that no expense has becn spared to produce the work in a form and quality worthy of its literary and scientific value. Its paper is of the best ; its type has been specially cast ; and it is printed on entirely new machines, in order that every advantage may be given to its letter-press and engravings.

div.head: GOVERNMENT AND THE
div.p: THE GOVERNMENT AND THE
UNEMPLOYED.
In the House of Commons, yesterday, Mr. Keir Hardie

, asked the President of the Local Government Board ! whether his depaement contemplated taking any action and if so of what kind, to provide work of a productive and non-pauperising, kind for the great, numbers of men and women who are at present unable to find employment. Mr. Fowler said cn the 30th September a circular was issued to all sanitary authorities reminding them of the scarceness of employnaent in all parts of the country and the probability of its becoming more general during the winter months, and urging upon them the great import- ance of proceeding with sanitary or improvement works. In a number of cases the Board had received satisfac- tory replies stating' that works were in progress, or would be expedited or provided if necessary arose. In other cases application had been made for the sanction of loans which would afford employment. The Local Government Board had no power themselves to under- take, nor were they empowered to request any local au- thority to carry out work. They had no control what- ever in the matter except in cases were the cost of the projected work was to be defrayed by a loan. In such cases the sanction of the Local Government Board was necessary, and they were desirous of and were assist- ing the Local Government authorities as far as they could.

Mr. John Bums asked whether it was outside the power of the Board to compel local authcrities to act on the suggestion sent them. Mr. Fowler said it was, and he was sorry to say that in one or two eases the local authorities refused in no very courteous terms to pay any heed to the recommen- dations of the hoard.

Mr. Kier Hardie asked leave to move the adjournment of the House in order to call attention to the widespread destitution among the large masses of the working classes, due to so many out of employment, and to the inadequacy of the measures adopted for dealing there- with. As only 36 members rose at the :speaker's call, the speaker declared that that noes had it. Thereupon Mr. Hardie claimed that in accordance with the standing orders a division he taken. The House divided and there were for the motion 44 and against 142, majority 96. The motion was therefore negatived. Mr. Hardie said he trusted the unemployed would take he matter into their own had. The Chairman said ninetee,be twentieths of the Scotch miners were idle, being w largest number in the history of Scotch mining troubeogi" The Scotchmen made a foolish mistake in not supPerti 0 the English strikers. div.head: BUCKLEY MYSTERY.
div.p: THE BUCKLEY MYSTERY.
EXTRAORDINARY _ SCENE ON THE MANG

ROYAL EXCHANGE. The section of the Manchester Royal Exchange sPe„et. ally set apart for the cotton trade was, yesterday Inv, ing, the scene of extraordinary and unusual excitet caused by the appearance on the boards of Mr.. 6, worth Read, who was on Thursday acquittql of charge of murder in connection with what is knosfo, the" Blackley Mystery." Directly Mr. Read put ind appearance, and was recognised, he was surrounde an indignant, and very demonstrative crowd of , members and subjected to hooting and strong eicr)e sions with reference to recent events. Whenever he,', about on the boards Mr. Read was followed by lug crowd, until finally he had to seek refuge lo private office of the Master of the Royal Exchalg Finally he left the building, but was even followed 111 the streets across into Barton Arcade by an Incligo crowd, who continued to hoot him in a very vocifero fash on.

The exciting incident was afterwards a matter of /be general comment, and surprise is expressed t, Mr. Read should under the circumstances have an appearance at all. The demeanour of the indigs3 crowd by which he was surrounded was at one tioiel threatening that some violence was feared, esPecia as Mr. Read at first showed rather a disposition to 10;1. matters out, and the Master of the Exchange though" advisable to protect Mr. Read from any possible violess tcooffer him a temporary place of safety in his offi:e behind the bar at the Exchange. Even when Eead had sought refuge in tho Master's office an in' mut crowd surrounded the bar, and eventually it 5'7 considered advisable that lie should leave the Exchan_ altogether, as his continued presence would, in aliP' btbility, lead only to some further turbulent scenes.

George Vanderbilt, the American millionaire, who has bought the larger part of a county down in .iortti Caro- lina with the intention of founding a sort of baronial estate, finds himself much in the position of an Irish landlord. The natives of the district, who are Baptists, moonshiners, and free-born Americans of the most ag- gressive type, imagine that he is trying to establish a monarchy or some other form of despotism, and all the Winchesters and six-shooters in the mountains are being put in order to give him a warm reception if he ventures into that locality. A fiwe-storeyed factory in Square-road, Halifax, was gutted by fire on Thursday morning. It was chiefly occupied by electrical engineers, and the damage is estimated at from £lO,OOO to £12,000.
